1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation
on the observations/recommendations as contained in its Two Hundred and Third Report on
“Privatization of Services at Airports”, which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on
17
th December, 2013.
2. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of these recommendations/observations,
which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest.
3. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee
contained in the Two Hundred and Third Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and
recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the
succeeding paragraphs.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
4. Initially, when Delhi and Mumbai airports were restructured under PPP mode in 2005, it
was decided at the level of the Prime Minister that Chennai and Kolkata airports will not be
privatized. A tripartite agreement was also signed between AAI, the Employees Union and the
Government to that effect. It was also decided by COI headed by the Prime Minister himself way
back in 2006 that the services on the air side and in the terminal building would be assigned to
AAI only; it would not be given to private people. The Ministry could not give a convincing
explanation as to (i) how can these two airports be given under PPP now; and (ii) how can the
services on air side and in terminal building be given to the private people. Therefore, the Model
Concession Agreement, the Committee feels, cannot be amended to assign the services on airside
and in terminal building to the private people as contended by the Ministry/Planning Commission.
It is strange that within six years the perception of the Task Force has changed and it has come
to an opposite conclusion and the decision of the COI is also given a go by. No reasons have been
for taking contradictory stand on this issue by the Planning Commission/Ministry.
(Recommendation at Para 24 of 203rd Report)
Reply of the Government
5. The Task Force in its Report on “Financing Plan For Airports” published by Planning
Commission in July, 2012 states the following as a reason for its recommendation for undertaking
the operation and management of AAI airports (both city side and airside) through Public Private
Partnership basis:-
“…The next challenge for AAI would be to ensure their management and upkeep at a level
commensurate with the high quality of these terminals. Moreover, the potential for non-
aeronautical revenues from car parking, cargo facilities, hotels, passenger amenities,
shopping etc. cannot be fully harnessed by AAI due to the inherent constraints of a public
sector entity. The anticipated shortfall in nonaeronautical revenues is bound to lead to higher
passenger and aeronautical charges. Problems related to monitoring and supervision of the
large number of sub-optimal service contracts being awarded by AAI could also be
eliminated if a single PPP concession for operation and maintenance of the entire airport is
granted to an experienced and competent authority”

2
6. Subsequently, the Prime Minister took a meeting on 28.06.2013 to approve the targets for
infrastructure sector for the financial year 2013-14 for the Ministries of Railways, Road Transport
and Highways, Civil Aviation, Shipping, Power and Coal. In this meeting it was decided that Airport
Operations and Maintenance in AAI airports would be awarded on PPP basis. Accordingly, Ministry
of Civil Aviation (MoCA) has taken up 20 select airports under PPP on the basis of Operation
Management and Transfer (Copy enclosed).
7. Report of the Task Force does not have any reference of the tripartite agreement signed
between AAI, the Employees Union and the Government and the decision of Committee on
Infrastructure that the services on the air side and in the terminal building would be assigned to
AAI only; it would not be given to private people.
8. It is further mentioned that a Tripartite Committee was constituted comprising AAI, AAI
Employees Joint Forum and Government of India, in 2006. The Committee submitted its
recommendation in June, 2009 in which it was inter-alia  recommended that Chennai and Kolkata
Airports would be developed/modernized by AAI besides other non-metro airports. The private
players’ involvement for non-metro airports shall be r estricted for maintenance/commercial
operations of Terminal Building and City Side development including cargo operations. In a related
development in the year 2009, Planning Commission had also prepared a Model Concession
Agreement for Non-Metro Airports which covers only city side development including maintenance
and commercial utilization of the Terminal Building and Cargo Operations. On the line of above,
Bids for Amritsar and Udaipur airports were also called for but could not materialise due to absence
of finalisation of scope of work.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
9. The Committee does not agree with the Task Force/Ministry that potential for ‘non
aeronautical revenues’ from car parking, cargo facilities, hotels, passenger amenities, shopping etc.
“cannot be fully harnessed by AAI due to its inherent constraints”. But the Committee was neither
informed specifically about those constraints, nor about the efforts, if any, made by the
Government to enable AAI to overcome them. The Ministry of Civil Aviation did not have
convincing answers for these queries raised by the Committee. Even the Task Force report itself
has acknowledged the development of 35 non metro airports by AAI during the Eleventh Plan, of
which, development of 27 airports has been completed with the investment of 
R4565 crores (upto
March, 2012) and the development work of remaining airports is in progress. Thus, Airport
Authority of India has just shown its ability to modernize and operate 35 airports, of which several
airports including Kolkata and Chennai Airports are the profit making ones. The Government has
invested thousands of crores for modernizing these airports and unfortunately, now it is proposed
to hand them over to private people. The Committee feels that instead of privatizing these airports,
their management can be retained by AAI and a subsidiary of AAI or a Special Purpose Vehicle can
be formed to acquire the necessary expertise in managing those airports. (Para 25 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
10. Post implementation of PPP at DIAL, MIAL, BIAL and HIAL, non-aero revenue for these
airports increased substantially i.e. about 50% to 60% of total revenue. Whereas, in AAI airports,
non-aeronautical revenue even today is restricted to 16%. Therefore, it is evident that AAI has not
been able to maximize their non-aeronautical revenue due to various restrictions including delay in
tendering of F&B counters, availability of city side etc.
11. Many of the AAI land in City Side is under encroachment and being a Government
organization, AAI finds it difficult to get the encroachment vacated. AAI has not been able to
exploit the potential of non-aeronautical revenue.

3
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12. The Committee notes the reply giving the reasons for Airports Authority of India not
being able to maximise their non-aeronautical revenue. The Committee is of the view that
the Ministry should endeavour to empower the AAI also to maximize its non aeronautical
revenue.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. During the deliberations the Committee was informed that privatization of Delhi and Mumbai
Airports helped the Airports Authority of India to garner a lot of resources which was not possible
otherwise. The Committee does not accept this argument. While arguing repeatedly in favour of
privatization having been beneficial to AAI, the Government conveniently tries to overlook the fact
that if the AAI had been allowed to run Delhi and Mumbai airports by itself, the magnitude of their
earnings would have been much higher. The Committee feels that Model Concession Agreement
signed at the time of privatization of airports at Delhi and Mumbai allowed the private airport
operators to generate huge revenue with minimum investment. (Para 26 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
14. It is a fact that the non-aeronautical services at IGI, CSI and AAI airports, are not run by
the airport operators. Almost all of non-aeronautical activities are concessioned out. However, private
airport operators are able to exploit the potential of non-aeronautical services more than AAI.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
15. The Committee notes the reply and strongly feels that issues relating to generating
more non-aeronautical revenue at Indira Gandhi International Airport, Chatrapathi Shivaji
International Airport and Airports Authority of India need to be examined by it in detail
in future. The Committee will be in a better position to make an informed comment on this
issue only after going into Model Concessionaire Agreement, Operation, Maintenance and
Development Agreement, etc. of these airports. Cost of services and social obligations are
also issues to be taken into account.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
16. The Committee, therefore, recommends that at the first instance AAI be allowed to operate
the airports at Chennai and Kolkata and other non-metro airports for a few years. When asked
whether AAI is incapable of managing the newly modernized airports, the Chairman, AAI stated that
there were certain issues and these are being resolved but nowhere did he say or accept that AAI
is incapable of carrying out this responsibility. The Secretary of the Civil Aviation, however, tried
to argue that the AAI will not be able to do the job, almost toeing the line taken by the Task Force
of the Planning Commission in this regard. (Para 27 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
17. As explained in reply to para 24 above, as per the recommendations of the Task Force and
directions of PMO, MoCA has decided to take up these airports under PPP in order to maximize
all the revenue streams and introduce greater efficiency in the running of these airports.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
18. The Committee notes the reply and reiterates its comments made above.

4
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
19. The Committee is of the view that efficiency of AAI and constraints, if any, can be
assessed precisely only after they are allowed to manage and run/operate these airports themselves.
An agency which has been managing our airports till now may not become inefficient just one fine
morning. Such a decision is based on presumptive conclusions that AAI does not have the
expertise, that it will not be able to mobilize required resources, that it will not be able to manage
non-aeronautical services and that it will not be able to manage so many agencies by itself. It
appears that the decision to give the airports under PPP has been taken merely on fallacious
conclusions based merely on assumptions, with no concrete bases. (Para 28 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
20. AAI has the expertise to run the airports. However, expertise of private sector in marketing
and exploitation of all sources of income results in the success of PPP model.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
21. The Committee notes the reply and feels that the Ministry should explore
possibilities of taking positive initiatives to empower AAI, which will have to run those
airports which will not find private people to run them on commercial reasons.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
22. The Committee is dismayed that instead of strengthening AAI by giving it much needed
financial and administrative autonomy to enable it to take its own decisions without being
influenced/advised by either the Ministry or the Planning Commission, a decision to give our
airports on platter to private parties was taken. The Committee fails to understand the logic behind
privatizing all these airports after spending tax payers’ money. The public utilities created by public
fund cannot be given to private parties for commercial considerations. (Para 29 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
23. Airports Authority of India has mini-ratna status and as per the AAI Act, 1994, the
authority already has financial and administrative autonomy. During the PPP process it will be
ensured that the financial interests of AAI are fully protected and AAI gets a higher return on
their investment.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
24. The Committee notes the reply.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25. The Committee was informed that commercial space in the terminal buildings of both
Chennai and Kolkata airports could not be utilized to generate revenue from the available huge
space in terminal buildings. Entire blame for this has been laid on the Airports Authority of
India and the Ministry had nothing to show about the efforts made by itself to help Airports
Authority of India. It appears that AAI is being made a scapegoat in this regard. The
Committee feels that it was due to negligence more on the part of the Ministry of Civil Aviation
than the AAI. (Para 30 of ibid)

5
Reply of the Government
26. As per ICAO standards, the percentage of total floor area that can be used for commercial
activities in an airport has been fixed and space for commercial utilisation at Chennai and Kolkata
airports, have been earmarked accordingly. Any additional usage of floor area for commercial
activity may fetch additional non-aeronautical revenue but would compromise the floor area
available for users of the airport. In addition, the additional floor area usage for commercial
activities within the terminal building may affect the aesthetic look of the terminal building.
Therefore, considering all these aspects, AAI has struck a balance in fixing the commercial floor
area in its airports.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27. The Committee notes the reply of the Government and would like to know the
details in respect of percentage use of floor area for commercial activities to the total floor
areas at Indira Gandhi International Airport, Chatrapati Shivaji International Airport,
Bangalore International Airport and Hyderabad International Airport.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28. The Committee notes the argument that large number of sub-optimal service contracts being
awarded by AAI could also be eliminated if the operation and maintenance of the entire airport is
granted to a single PPP concessionaire. The Committee fails to understand why AAI itself cannot
be allowed to adopt a ‘single agency model’ which the Ministry/Planning Commission is visualizing
under the PPP mode. Even in the airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad and Bangalore, services
including commercial operations in the terminal buildings have been given to several agencies. The
Committee, therefore, does not agree with the contention of the Planning Commission/Ministry in
this regard. (Para 31 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
29. In case of Chennai and Kolkata airports, AAI has already adopted ‘single agency model’ for
Food and Beverages. Contracts have already been awarded by AAI under this model to optimise
the non-aeronautical services and also increase the revenue from this source while taking into
account the interest of users of these services.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
30. The Committee notes the reply and reiterates its comment made above.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
31. The private players in airport infrastructure sector are using entirely the money borrowed
from Indian Financial Institutions. The Committee is at a loss to see that the Government generally
does not allow the AAI to issue tax free bonds for mobilizing project finance and sanction of grants
for funding of non-viable small airports. AAI’s finances are highly constrained due to huge pending
dues from various airlines, particularly Air India. The Committee would like to know the steps
taken by Government to recover such dues from private players so far. (Para 32 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
32. AAI has been allowed to raise tax free bond as announced in 2013-14 budget. AAI is
expected to raise R500 crore in the Year 2013-14.

6
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
33. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee may be furnished a status report on
the steps taken by Government to recover outstanding dues from private as well as
Government air service providers.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee finds it strange that AAI is now being forced to build, operate and manage
smaller and non-metro airports which are loss-making. Thus, with the metro and other profit-
making airports going to private people, AAI will be left with economically unviable ones. Earlier,
Airports Authority of India was in a position to off-set the losses of non-metro airports by revenue
earned from metro airports through cross-subsidy. The Committee fails to understand how the AAI
will be able to carry out its mandate with the depleted resources. Other lucrative activities of AAI
are being taken out and being given to a separate corporation. (Para 33 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
35. Presently, AAI is getting a revenue share of about R2000 crore from JVC airports viz DIAL
and MIAL. This may increase further in the coming years. Also some of the major airports of AAI
are profit making airports and thus profits are used to cross subsidize the low cost / loss making
airports. AAI is also ensuing construction/upgradation of non-operational airports through PPP/State
participation.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
36. The Committee notes the reply of the Government.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
37. The Committee is of the view that construction, operation and maintenance of airports
should remain with Airports Authority of India. It should be empowered to take decisions to
generate resources rather than handing over the core activities of the airports newly constructed
with public money to the private players. (Para 34 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
38. As explained in reply to para 24 above, as per the recommendations of the Task Force and
directions of PMO, MoCA has decided to take up these airports under PPP.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
39. The Committee notes emphasis laid on “direction from PMO/MoCA” in
Government’s reply. The Committee reiterates that Airports Authority of India should be
empowered with more financially and administratively as it has to eventually operate and
maintain non-lucrative airports in the country.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
40. The Committee is surprised to see the unusual haste being shown in the process of
privatization right from the constitution of Task Force, constitution of three Inter-Ministerial
Groups (IMGs) one after another, placing the matter before Cabinet and obtaining its clearance,

7
process of pre-bidding, etc. The Committee also was not given a final view regarding whether the
existing Section 12A of Airports Authority Act and the relevant Rules/Regulations do adequately and
clearly provide for allowing all the services – airside, terminal building and city side to private
parties. The Committee would like to have clear opinion of the Law Ministry in this regard.
(Para 35 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
41. Both CSI and IGI (both city side and airside) airports are given to private companies for
operation, management and development under Section 12A of AAI Act, 1994. Hence, it is
permissible as per AAI Act to go in for PPP.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
42. The Committee notes the reply and feels that these aspects of IGI and CSI need
deeper study.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
43. The Committee expresses its concern about the fate of employees of both Chennai (1050)
and Kolkata (1200) airports, after they are put under PPP. The Committee would like to remind
the Ministry and the Planning Commission the poor handling of employee related issues after the
airports in Delhi and Mumbai were privatized. Employees in these airports had to undergo tough
times and ultimately, most of them either had to take voluntary retirement or were transferred to
remote locations where they did not have any work and the AAI had to pay them full salaries and
allowances. The private parties generally try to stall the absorption of existing employees with them
even if they are required to do so under the agreement. The Committee feels that same thing is
going to be repeated this time as well. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
fate of the existing employees needs to be tackled first at both the airports before taking any step
in this regard. (Para 36 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
44. While finalising the Concession Agreement, interest of the employees will be fully protected
by making adequate provisions to this effect in the Concession Agreement.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
45. The Committee notes the reply of the Government and reiterate its earlier
recommendation of protecting the interest of AAI employees in consultation with them.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
46. By giving away more and more airports to the private sector on long term transfer (it has
been proposed to give these airports on 60 year long-term lease) for management and operations,
the role of private sector will increase and the airports will be controlled by only private companies
leading to a situation where there will be private sector monopoly and a strong public sector will
be sacrificed. AAI will end up in managing only the loss making airports and other non-operational
airports and also airports in remote areas which are being considered for development at present
for improving air connectivity to remote areas and tourist destinations, medical tourism, etc.
(Para 37 of ibid)

8
Reply of the Government
47. Even after PPP of AAI airports, ATC/ANS services will be fully managed by AAI and 100%
revenue from that activity will accrue to AAI. Further, AAI will also get revenue share from JVC.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
48. The Committee notes the reply of the Government.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
49. The Committee would like to remind the Ministry that India is a vast country and its civil
aviation sector is growing fast. Large parts of the country need to be connected by air for which
we need modern airports, and AAI is the agency which has to undertake this mammoth task. The
Committee feels that by cutting AAI into size or shrinking its area of operation, the Government
of India is not facilitating the national task of air connectivity to the length and breadth of the
country. (Para 38 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
50. Government of India is in the process of establishment of 50 low cost airports for
providing air connectivity to tier-II and tier-III cities with a view to provide regional connectivity.
The task of establishment of these airports has been assigned to AAI. The resources after
developing these airports will be raised from the profit making AAI airports and PPP airports of
AAI.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
51. The Government should address these issues before embarking on the process of operation
and management of these airports through PPP mode. (Para 39 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
52. While finalising the Concession Agreement observations of the Committee will be taken into
account to protect the interest of AAI and its employees.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
53. The Committee notes the reply of the Government. The Committee would like to
know if the resources earned by AAI from its profit-making airports will be adequate
enough to meet expenditure of the airports in tier-II and III cities, which may not be profit
making.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
54. Even if it is a question of bringing in external management expertise to augment the internal
expertise of AAI in managing these airports, this could be achieved even without leasing out these
newly-built airports to the private sector. A better way to achieve efficiencies in operations can be
through awarding a ‘management contract’ to an entity with expertise in this domain by the AAI
itself. (Para 40 of ibid)

9
Reply of the Government
55. While finalising the model of PPP, the observations of the Committee will be taken into
account in the best interest of AAI.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
56. The Committee notes the reply of the Government and hopes that interest of the
AAI would be well protected while taking such a major policy decision.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
57. The Committee feels that the PPP model has its own pitfalls. We have seen in development
of national highways that due to poor margins in road projects, concessionaires are abandoning the
projects in the recent years as toll collection did not turn out as per their expectations. The private
airports developers, we have seen, no doubt gave world class facilities but at a prohibitive cost
to the passengers. These are not being run as for public service. The Committee feels that they
tend to increase user fees, as they have done in the past, on the pretext that operations in the
terminals and city side areas are not profitable. The Committee is of the considered opinion that
our people need good facilities at airports but not which are unaffordable. It could be done by a
public owned body and not by private agencies. In fact, motto of AAI is to develop and provide
affordable facilities to the people. (Para 41 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
58. As against the observations of the Committee, the PPP model is very successful in the
airport sector. Further, Airports Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA) has been put in place as
a regulator. Airports Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA) conducts extensive stakeholder
consultation before fixing any airport charge.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
59. The Committee notes the reply of the Government. However, the Committee feels
that even the role of Airports Economic Regulatory Authority of India as a regulator also
needs to be reviewed. It is said that AERA has not been able to fulfil its desired mandate.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
60. In view of what has been mentioned above, the Committee recommends that AAI may be
permitted to manage and operate all its airports, including the lossmaking ones, with a rider that
there should be time bound delivery of world class passenger services in a more efficient and
transparent manner, matching with those being rendered by private airport operators.
(Para 42 ibid)
Reply of the Government
61. As explained in reply to para 24 above, as per the recommendations of the Task Force and
directions of PMO, MoCA has decided to take up these airports under PPP.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
62. The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Government will protect the
interest of Airports Authority of India and its employees.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this Two Hundred Sixteenth Report on “Action taken by the Government on the
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee contained in its Two Hundred Eleventh Report on
the Upkeep of various Monuments in Delhi, National Museum and other important issues pertaining
to the Ministry of Culture”.
2. The Two Hundred Eleventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented on the 19
th February, 2014 to the
Parliament.
3. The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Two
Hundred Eleventh Report were received from the Ministry of Culture on the 15 th September, 2014.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 10 th December, 2014.
DR. KANWAR DEEP SINGH
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
December 10, 2014 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Agrahayana 19, 1936 (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
This Report deals with the Actions Taken by the Ministry of Culture on the observations/
recommendations of the Committee as contained in its Two Hundred and Eleventh Report on
“Upkeep of various Monuments in Delhi, National Museum and other important issues pertaining
to the Ministry of Culture”, which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on
19
th February, 2014.
2. The Action Taken Replies have been received from the Ministry of Culture vide their O.M.
dated the 15 th September, 2014 in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the
Report.
2.1. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of all the further
recommendations/observations, which have been made in this Report should be furnished to
the Committee at the earliest.
3. After scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made its further
observations/comments on each item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry of
Culture. The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Two Hundred and Eleventh
Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and recommendations/observations of the Committee
on each item of action taken have been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
4. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made by the Ministry to get back the
original Mughal era charm of Red Fort. This can happen only when its surrounding is also
developed tastefully in a contemporaneous style of the Monument. It is a sad story that nothing
has been done to renovate this great monument and compensate for the loss and deliberate
destruction that took place during the colonial period by converting it into military barracks. The
Committee recommends that the Ministries of Culture and Tourism should make a joint effort for
this purpose. The Committee emphasizes the need to integrate the Red Fort to Shahjahanabad as
the entire Mughal City, including Red Fort, has been nominated as part of a World Heritage City
of Delhi. (Para 4 of 211
th Report)
Reply of the Government
5. The Comprehensive Conservation Management Plan (CCMP) for the Red Fort has been
prepared on the basis of which necessary conservation and development works are in progress as
per the availability of resources. Most of the identified modern constructions of colonial period in
the Fort Complex, as identified in the Management Plan have been dismantled. Originality of
surrounding areas of Mugal structures is being restored by re-orientation of gardens of Mugal
pattern. In this regard a workshop was also held at Red Fort, Delhi in October, 2013 to discuss
about various issues related to development of historic gardens. The renovation work is in
progress.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
6. The Committee appreciates that most of the identified modern constructions of
colonial period in the Fort Complex have been dismantled to restore the old charm of the
Red Fort. The Committee would like to know about the efforts made to integrate Red Fort
into Shahjahanabad as recommended by it. The Committee may also be apprised of the

2
outcome of the workshop held in October, 2013 to discuss about various issues related to
development of historic gardens.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
7. The Committee also took note of several important museums like Freedom Fighter’s
Museum, Indian War Memorial Museum and Red Fort Archaeological Museum housed inside Red
Fort which preserve many important historical antiquities. But, adequate steps have not been taken
to improve their visibility. The Committee also learnt that many posts are lying vacant and many
museum staff are working as casual labour in these museums almost for two decades and have
not been regularized despite their eligibility. The Committee recommends that steps be taken to fill
these vacancies in time and also to regularize the eligible casual appointees to boost their morale
so they would contribute best in their service career. (Para 5 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
8. A proposal for regularization of temporary status workers is under consideration in DOPT.
A separate case for regularization of casual labour with special exemption for age and educational
qualification has been referred to DOPT at the level of Hon’ble Culture Minister.
9. In addition to the above, the creation of a cadre for museum officials has been included
in re-structuring proposal submitted to Ministry of Finance. A proposal is also in hand to upgrade
a few museums resulting in increase of sanctioned manpower.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
10. The Committee further recommends that Museums are storehouse of knowledge
pertaining to the rich cultural heritage of the country. The direct experience gained by the
museum staff by working for such a long time should be harnessed duly and they may be
regularized on priority.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
11. The Committee therefore emphasizes the need for proper and adequate illumination of the
Qutub Minar to enhance its beauty as well as its visibility. The Committee found that the flood light
at night is too bright that it might harm the monument. The Committee recommends to improve
this at the earliest. (Para 7 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
12. Lighting arrangements at Qutub Minar have been installed by the Delhi Development
Authority (DDA). Electrical Engineers of DDA have assessed the intensity of illumination and
thereafter provided required illumination. However, Archaeological Survey of India, Delhi Circle has
again requested to the DDA to examine the illumination status of the Qutub Minar afresh.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. The Committee takes note of the fact that ASI has taken up the matter of
appropriate illumination at Qutub Minar with Delhi Development Authority. However, the
final results are yet to be intimated. The Committee, therefore, desires that the DDA may
do the needful in respect of adjusting the intensity of lighting arrangement at Qutub Minar
so that it does not have an adverse impact on the monument.

3
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
14. The Committee also feels that Qutub Minar, like any other monument, should not be dealt
with in isolation from its surroundings. This world famous Heritage Monument, therefore, must be
developed as an integrated site including historic Mehrauli Village and Mehrauli Archaeological park.
(Para 8 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
15. The surroundings of Qutub Minar has eleven other centrally protected monuments like
Adham Khan’s Tomb, Jamali Kamali Tomb, Marhi Masjid, Wall Masjid, Walls of Lal Kot, Rai
Pithora’s Gate and Sohan Gate, including the ditch where there is an outer wall, Walls of Lal Kot
and Rai Pithora, where they meet together, Wall of Rai Pithora’s Fort including gateways and
bastions, Gandakki Baoli, Zaffar Mahal, Jehaz Mahal and Mehrauli Archaeological Park. There are
3 monuments protected by ASI, some of them looked after by State Department Archaeology and
DDA. However, entire park is in ownership of DDA. There are some other areas owned by private
colonies.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
16. It is evident that all the eleven odd monuments mentioned above are under protected
category. No one knows the exact number of monuments under DDA and State
Archaeological Department and how many of them are unprotected as some of them lie in
private owned areas. This gives a very bleak picture about the whole thing. The Committee
would like to have monument-wise position in respect of their protection either with ASI,
DDA, State Governments or unprotected. In this way, Delhi has already lost hundreds of old
monuments to the encroachers and we are perhaps allowing same thing to happen in areas
around Qutab Minar as well. The Committee is of the view that better co-ordination
between the ASI and the concerned State agencies is needed in the matter of protection of
monuments.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
17. The Committee appreciate the work done by Agha Khan Trust for Culture and INTACH and
recommends that such good initiatives should continue in future for other monuments also.
Partnership with people and developing a larger synergy and coordination among several
stakeholders/agencies for protection and preservation of our iconic Monuments/ Heritage Sites is
the need of the hour. But, we also cannot lose sight of the majority of our monuments that are
lying unattended. Through our own resources as also having partnership with international
organizations such as UNESCO, and other bodies like Aga Khan Foundation, resources may be
generated for renovation, upkeep and beautification of monuments. Since maintenance is a
continuous affair, this can best be done through increasing people’s participation. The MOC should
put in place a credible system to encourage and motivate a large section of the local populace in
the task of upkeep and maintenance of historical and cultural monuments. Once the people treat
these monuments as their own assets and develop a sense of ownership, their maintenance become
assured. (Para 12 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
18. On the lines of engaging Agha Khan Trust for Culture and INTACH conservation projects
for few other monuments are also being executed by funding from National Cultural Fund and
World Management Fund etc. The public awareness programmes are regularly conducted by the
field offices in the form of organizing exhibitions, lectures, interviews, painting competitions etc.

4
to educate the students/public about the rich cultural heritage of the country and its preservation.
The regular conservation work is being attended by the Archaeological Survey of India for
protected monuments.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
19. The Committee notes the reply and further recommends that public awareness
programmes should be more action oriented involving mass engagement in cleaning,
beautifying and protecting the monuments. Much more efforts need to be taken for this
purpose for making its impact visible.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
20. The Committee is glad to note that as a result of its prolonged persuasion, now the Ministry
has given in-principle approval to include Lal Mahal in the list of centrally protected monuments
under the ASI. (Para 19 of ibid)
21. However, it appears to the Committee that in case of Lal Mahal, land grabbers and various
authorities were conniving with each other. They could successfully destroy the precious
monument and illegal constructions took place while Government authorities remained silent
spectators. Even now the ASI people are being denied entry into the illegally encroached premises
of Lal Mahal. The Committee recommends that since a decision has been taken to protect this
important monument, no laxity should be shown to the encroachers and they should be removed
with the help of police force and suitably renovated. (Para 20 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
22. Lal Mahal is located in a thickly populated locality and is heavily encroached. The structure
has recently been declared as a heritage building. The proposal for protection of the structure by
ASI was first submitted in August, 2013. However, there was strong resistance against declaration
of Lal Mahal as a protected monument due to the restriction on construction, repair etc. in the
prohibited/ regulated areas, which protection by ASI would entail. Efforts by ASI officials to pursue
the case for preliminary notification have been hindered by the fact that this is a living monument
and ASI has not even been able to carry out even basic assessment of the structure. DG, ASI has
referred the matter to the Chief Secretary, Government of NCT, Delhi on 12.06.2013 requesting
him to declare the said monument as a state protected monument. The State Government is being
pursued for early action in the matter.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
23. The Committee feels that we have come back to square one in respect of protection
of Lal Mahal. The Committee feels that the concerned authorities failed to act in time due
to reasons better known to them and area around Lal Mahal was allowed to be encroached
in such a manner that it has become next to impossible to even take that under ASI
protection. It would entail massive demolition of houses/buildings built illegally there. The
Committee would like to know stand of Delhi Government in this regard.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
24. The Committee is of the view that even if some important monuments are privately owned,
it does not authorize the private owners to alter, deface or demolish the monuments. Appropriate legal
and institutional mechanism need to be put in place to make such private persons accountable and
face severe legal consequences for destroying such monuments/ancient sites. (Para 21 of ibid)

5
Reply of the Government
25. There are very few monuments which are privately owned and have been taken by ASI for
protection and conservation by signing an MOU. No such incidents of damages to these
monuments by the owners have come to the notice. However, the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Sites and Remains (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010 to take action against any
defaulter/ miscreant.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
26. The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
27. The Committee observes that the Ministry of Culture has the domain knowledge about the
specifications of art and architectural traditions and innovativeness of each monument/site.
Therefore, they should impart the training to tourist Guides. The Committee learnt that there is no
system for on the spot booking of guides at our premier cultural sites. As a result, tourist are left
to be cheated by fake/untrained guides. The Committee also observes that just like counters to sale
entry tickets to visit a monument, a counter should also be there for guided tour/visit of the
monument. Moreover, the specialized Guides should be available with each monument/heritage sites.
(Para 23 of ibid)
28. The Committee observes that several agencies are involved in the process and they meet on
various fora; yet, communication gaps have been often noticed on important matters. The Committee
recommends that both the Culture and Tourism Ministry should develop a closer synergy for
preserving and promoting our heritage and culture. For instance, the Ministry of Tourism is nodal in
imparting training to the Tourist Guides whereas the Culture Ministry has the domain knowledge of
all monuments sites. As a result, many touts are passing on half cooked information to innocent
visitors at various monuments and tourist destinations. (Para 25 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
29. The Archaeological Survey of India conserver, preserve and maintain the monuments/sites
declared as of national importance. However, as per the Government of India Notification No.
S.O.429(E) Dated 20.5.2010, the statutory authority under the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 for framing and issuing guidelines for issuance of
guide license, approval and registration etc. of qualified persons selected through due process to
operate in the protected monuments of national importance is the Additional Director General of
Tourism, Ministry of Tourism, Government of India. However, at present both the Department of
Tourism and Culture are under the same Ministry, hence there will be no such information gap and
closer synergy will be developed.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
30. The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
31. The Committee observes that our heritage sites are neglected and left unattended in Delhi
and so also at other places in the Country. The ASI is not in a position to render appropriate care
and protection to monuments. Numerous cases of encroachment and unauthorized construction in
and around these sites have been noticed. The Committee strongly recommends that an Authority

6
should be created under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (Amendment
and Validation) Act, 2010. On receiving a complaint from the public or any other private/public
organization the proposed authority should be empowered to take strong action immediately. The
Committee also recommends that creation of database on existence of heritage buildings/
monuments/ancient sites should be completed in a time bound manner and progress in the matter
should be informed to this Committee at the earliest. Further, efforts should be made separately to
identify the potential ones for declaring them as protected. A comprehensive assessment of
preservation works should also be done. (Para 28 of ibid)
32. The Committee also understands that creation of mechanisms under the provisions of
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remain (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010
has been very slow so far. The Committee earlier had asked the Ministry about it but was not
informed about the efforts made in this regard and the reasons for delay. The Committee would
again like to remind the Ministry about the Para 42 of 192
nd Report and recommend to be proactive
for putting the required mechanism in place at the earliest in order to save our ancient sites/
monuments and the Ministry may also apprise the Committee about it through an explanatory note.
(Para 29 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
33. There are 3679 centrally protected monuments/sites in the country including 174 in Delhi
which have been declared as of national importance. The Archaeological Survey of India undertakes
their regular conservation and preservation by way of structural repairs, chemical treatment, laying
of gardens and day to day maintenance as per archaeological norms subject to availability of
resources. There are instances of encroachments in some of the centrally protected monuments.
As there already exist the provisions contained in the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites
and Remains 1958 (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010 and Rules framed thereunder, the
Archaeological Survey of India undertakes action for removal of encroachment in the premises of
the protected monuments and protected areas and unauthorized constructions in the prohibited and
regulated areas.
34. In order to contain the such encroachments and removing them, the Superintending
Archaeologist in charge of the Circles have already been vested with the powers of an Estate
Officer to issue eviction notices/orders to the encroachers under Public Premises (Eviction of
Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. They are also authorised to issue show cause notices under
the provisions of Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains 1958 (Amendment and
Validation) Act, 2010 and Rules 1959 followed by a direction to the District Collector/Magistrate
by Central Government to remove such encroachment under section 19 (2) of the Act and
Section 38 (2) of the Rule. Assistance in containing and removing encroachments is also sought
from the respective State Government/police force and where there are no fruitful results, actions
are initiated against the encroachers by filing cases in the court of law. In addition to the regular
watch and ward staff, private security personnel, State police guards and CISF have also been
provided for the safety and security of selected monuments. Removal of encroachments is an
ongoing process and is carried out under the provisions of the Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Sites and Remains 1958 (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
35. The Committee’s real concern is that the existing system is not yielding the desired
impact; it leaves a lot to be desired. It would like to know the progress about its
recommendation for creation of database on existence of heritage buildings/monuments/
ancient sites in Delhi.

7
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
36. The Committee further notes that the 90 years old John and Marshall Guidelines for
preservation of monuments are still followed in India whereas new conservation and preservation
policy has not taken shape so far. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the
Government must frame new updated conservation policy incorporating latest technology and

98. The Central and the respective State Governments, have jurisdiction and responsibility over

18

of monuments/sites for declaring them as of national importance. However, the protection of
monuments as of national importance is a continuous process.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
99. The Committee understands the limitations posed due to Ancient Monuments and
Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 as well as State laws in increasing the number
of monuments under the protection of ASI. But it feels that the Ministry and ASI with a far
more closer interface with the State Archaeology Departments can sensitize, help and
facilitate them for taking over of monuments for protection and conservation. The Committee
recommends that the number of important monuments languishing should be reviewed and
a national database with regard to number of monuments under different jurisdiction
prepared under two categories i.e., “already protected” and “yet to be protected”.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
100. The Committee takes strong exception to the fact that the dossiers sent to the UNESCO
for including our Heritage sites in the List of World Heritage Sites are generally found not to be
in order. As a result, these are sent back for corrections, etc. This has happened several times in
respect of our different sites. The Committee has taken up this issue earlier also with the Ministry
and had expressed its concerned about this. It feels that with the kind of vast technical and other
expertise that we have in this regard, we are unable, to present our case properly to the UNESCO.
It appears we do not do our homework seriously and send dossiers to UNESCO casually. It is a
serious matter that our dossiers have been returned several times. The Committee recommends that
“Dossiers Committee” should be constituted comprising eminent persons from relevant area as well
as other professionals for the purpose so that National does not have to hear again about our
proposals being returned. The Para 45 of the 192nd Report may be referred to this regard.
(Para 46 of ibid)
101. The Committee in this context would like to site the case of Majuli Island, Assam, which
was recommended by the Ministry for being adopted by UNESCO as a World Heritage Sites. But
the said request was returned by the World Heritage Centre (WHC) in March, 2012 as it was not
complete and not accordingly to the Guidelines framed by WHC. (Para 47 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
102. Every Nomination dossiers is considered and recommended for by the ACWHM before it
is submitted to WHC for inscription on World Heritage List. The nomination dossier of Majuli
Island. Assam was recommended by the Advisory Committee on World Heritage Matter. The
proposal of Majuli had been returned because it was not completed as per the latest Operational
Guidelines i.e. 2011.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
103. The Committee notes the reply and feels that we have lost lot of precious time
because it appears, we are preparing dossiers without doing our home work seriously. It is
very odd to receive back paper on the ground that those were not complete.

19
104. The Committee desires that concrete steps should be taken to ensure that
incomplete/improper dossiers are not forwarded to the UNESCO.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
105. The Committee also learnt that the Government of NCT of Delhi has submitted the detailed
dossier to nominate Delhi as a World Heritage City to the UNESCO. In view of this, the Committee
recommends that this may be pursued more seriously. A coordinated and holistic approach is
required to conserve the cultural heritage of this ancient city instead of adopting an isolated
monument approach. (Para 48 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
106. The dossier on Delhi Imperial Capital Cities was sent to W orld Heritage Centre for
completeness check in September, 2013 and as per the suggestion given by WHC modification,
were carried out and finally submitted in January, 2014.
107. Acc ording to the intimation of PRI it has been evaluated and found correct.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
108. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made regarding Delhi  vide para
48 of 211
th Report which inter alia states that: “The Committee recommends that this may
be pursued more seriously. A coordinated and holistic approach is required to conserve the
cultural heritage of this ancient city instead of adopting an isolated monument based
approach.”
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
109. The Committee emphasizes the urgent need for strengthening of all wings of Archaeological
Survey of India like Monument, Conservation, Exploration and Excavation, Epigraphy, Chemistry,
etc. due to increase in the quantum as well as nature of these works. The Committee observes
that the workload of Horticulture Wing has increased manifold with the increase in number of
gardens under maintenance from 100 to 500 with no corresponding increase in the manpower. As
a result, sites, monuments, etc. are not being properly maintained and landscaped. Their upkeep is
generally not upto the mark. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be a
commensurate increase in the workforce engaged in all the Departments of ASI, particularly in
Horticulture for showcasing our heritage sites. The Committee also recommends that vacancies at
all levels should be filled up on priority and revival of posts whenever necessary also be expedited
with the Ministry of Finance. It is taking lot of time. The Committee desires the Ministry to keep
it informed about the recommendations of the Manpower Management and Planning Consultants
and status of its implementation. The Committee’s recommendations at Para 50 of 192
nd Report in
this regard may also be referred to. (Para 49 of ibid)
Reply of the Government
110. The recruitment process for filling up vacant posts under direct recruitment has been
started. Roster points have been issued to Circle/Branch offices of ASI for recruitment to 300
vacant non-gazetted posts through Staff Selection Commission/open market ASI engaged
M/s Manpower Management and Planning Consultants, K-107-B, Sheikh Sarai, Phase-II, New
Delhi-110017 on 21.5.2010 on the work measurement study to restructure and strengthen the
Archaeological Survey of India, who submitted their report on 14
th March, 2011. Keeping the report
of Manpower Management and Planning Consultants in view a comprehensive proposal for overall

20
strengthening of all wings of ASI like monument, conservation, exploration and excavation,
epigraphy, chemistry, horticulture, planning, budget and account, security, Institute of Archaeology
and introducing a new cadre for the Site Museums, was prepared and has been taken up with
Ministry of Finance.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
111. The Committee desires that the Ministry may pursue the matter of strengthening of
all wings of ASI with the Ministry of Finance, so that adequate funds are allocated for the
same and accordingly desired number of posts be created.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee desires that final replies in respect of all the further
recommendations/observations, which have been made in this Report should be furnished to
the Committee at the earliest. (Para 2.1)
The Committee appreciates that most of the identified modern constructions of
colonial period in the Fort Complex have been dismantled to restore the old charm of the
Red Fort. The Committee would like to know about the efforts made to integrate Red Fort
into Shahjahanabad as recommended by it. The Committee may also be apprised of the
outcome of the workshop held in October, 2013 to discuss about various issues related to
development of historic gardens. (Para 6)
The Committee further recommends that Museums are storehouse of knowledge
pertaining to the rich cultural heritage of the country. The direct experience gained by the
museum staff by working for such a long time should be harnessed duly and they may be
regularized on priority. (Para 10)
The Committee takes note of the fact that ASI has taken up the matter Of
appropriate illumination at Qutub Minar with Delhi Development Authority. However, the
final results are yet to be intimated. The Committee, therefore, desires that the DDA may
do the needful in respect of adjusting the intensity of lighting arrangement at Qutub Minar
so that it does not have an adverse impact on the monument. (Para 13)
It is evident that all the eleven odd monuments mentioned above are under protected
category. No one knows the exact number of monuments under DDA and State
Archaeological Department and how many of them are unprotected as some of them lie in
private owned areas. This gives a very bleak picture about the whole thing. The Committee
would like to have monument-wise position in respect of their protection either with ASI,
DDA, State Governments or unprotected. In this way, Delhi has already lost hundreds of old
monuments to the encroachers and we are perhaps allowing same thing to happen in areas
around Qutab Minar as well. The Committee is of the view that better co-ordination
between the ASI and the concerned State agencies is needed in the matter of protection of
monuments. (Para 16)
The Committee notes the reply and further recommends that public awareness
programmes should be more action oriented involving mass engagement in cleaning,
beautifying and protecting the monuments. Much more efforts need to be taken for this
purpose for making its impact visible. (Para 19)
The Committee feels that we have come back to square one in respect of protection
of Lal Mahal. The Committee feels that the concerned authorities failed to act in time due
to reasons better known to them and area around Lal Mahal was allowed to be encroached
in such a manner that it has become next to impossible to even take that under ASI
protection. It would entail massive demolition of houses/buildings built illegally there. The
Committee would like to know the stand of Delhi Government in this regard. (Para 23)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 26)

22
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 30)
The Committee’s real concern is that the existing system is not yielding the desired
impact; it leaves a lot to be desired. It would like to know the progress about its
recommendation for creation of database on existence of heritage buildings/monuments/
ancient sites in Delhi. (Para 35)
The Committee notes the reply and would like to have a copy of the Conservation
Policy for the protected monuments of the Archaeological Survey of India. (Para 38)
The Committee would like to have a roadmap from the Ministry about renovation of
galleries. The Committee desires that a comparative “assessment of the actual work done
vis-a-vis the target and financial allocation made for the purpose should be furnished to the
Committee. (Para:40)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 42)
The Committee recommends that the ASI should vacate the premises at the earliest
so that extra space would be available to the National Museum. It appears that the Ministry
has not at all acted upon the recommendation made by this Committee. (Para 44)
The Committee is aware of the fact that CPWD is looking after the building
maintenance of National Museum like any other Government building. However, despite this
the Committee had earlier found that the building and precious collection of National
Museum was in a pitiable condition due to seepages etc. In view of it, the Committee
desires a more concrete answer from the Ministry. (Para 46)
The Committee would like to know from the Ministry whether the existing security
is found adequate by the museum authorities. (Para 48)
The Committee feels that ASI is not vacating the place due to certain constraints
which should be sorted out at the earliest and recommends that Phase–III work should
commence before the next budget atleast. (Para 50)
The Committee notes the reply. (Para 52)
The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the fact that Art Acquisition
Committee has not been constituted till date and reiterates its earlier recommendation to
expedite the constitution of Art Acquisition Committee which is defunct for the last several
years. The Committee sincerely feels that it is an unfortunate situation. (Para 54)
The Committee observes that out of the total collection of 2,06,169 objects, physical
verification of only 55,644 objects have been done which is only a negligible percentage. The
Committee strongly feels that this should be done in a time bound manner and the
Committee may be apprised about it from time to time. (Para 56)
The Committee would like to know how much more time it would take to complete
the process of digitization. (Para 58)
The Committee notes that the action taken process in this regard is still on. It,
however, feels that it has already taken a long time and still it is likely to take some more
time. The Committee strongly recommends that the amendment of recruitment rules be
expedited and all the vacancies be filled at the earliest. (Para 60)
The Committee may be apprised of the data regarding the total number of exhibits
in the collection of National Museum, number of exhibits handed over taken over and
number of exhibits physically verified. (Para 62.3.1)

The Committee feels that the process of filling up the vacancies is quite slow. The
Committee is of the view that the pace at which the Recruitment Rules are being finalized
should be expedited. .(Para 62.4.1)
The Committee is not satisfied with the fact that only three Galleries have been re-
opened in the year 2013-14. The Committee may be apprised of the road map in this regard.
(Para 62.6.1)
The Committee is surprised to note that only one Exhibition was held and four
publications were brought out and feels that the lead Museum of the country should have
done much more. The Committee desires that the range and frequency of the activities in

The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Ministry. (Para 63)
The Committee may be apprised of the outcome of its earlier recommendation for

The Ministry may inform the Committee about the steps taken to ensure that under

REPORT
The Anti-Hijacking Bill, 20 14* was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 17 th December, 2014.
The Chairman, Rajya Sabha had referred the Bill to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture on the 29
th December, 2014 for examination and
report.
2. The Anti-Hijacking Bill, 2014, seeks to achieve the following objects:–
(a) to expand the scope of the definition of hijacking;
(b) to define the term “in-service” so as to cover the offence against aircraft even when
it is on the ground or under preparation for departure;
(c) to provide capital punishment to all offenders including hijackers whose actions result
in deaths of hostages and security men while carrying out the act of hijacking;
(d) to provide capital punishment to conspirators and abductors, besides hijackers, for any
of the offences committed under the Act so that all persons involved directly or
indirectly in hijacking get similar punishment;
(e) to include confiscation of movable and immovable property belonging to offenders as
part of the punishment;
(f) to widen the provisions relating to jurisdiction and extradition;
(g) to confer powers of arrest, investigation and prosecution on officers of the Central
Government and to empower them to seize and attach the properties belonging to
offenders;
(h) to provide that all offences under the Act shall be triable only by the Designated Court;
3. The Committee discussed the provisions of the Bill with the representatives of Ministries of
Civil Aviation, External Affairs, Home Affairs, Department of Legal Affairs and Legislative
Department, Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, Central
Industrial Security Force, Intelligence Bureau, National Investigation Agency, National Security
Guard and National Security Council Secretariat and also received written memoranda from Air
Passengers Association of India, Association of Private Airport Operators and Business Aircraft
Operators Association.
4. The Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 was enacted to give effect to the Convention for Suppression
of Unlawful Seizure of the Aircraft signed at Hague in 1970. The Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 was last
amended in 1994. The hijacking of Indian Airlines Flight IC-814 on December 24, 1999 from
Kathmandu to Kandahar, the hijacking incidents in USA on September 11, 2001 when hijacking
civilian aircrafts were used as missile for causing mass destruction and subsequent attempts
worldwide to hijack aircraft and also the threats to hijack aircrafts by the outlawed groups/
organizations necessitated a fresh and thorough examination of the preparedness of all concerned
to face such exigencies. It also enjoined upon the policy makers and planners in-charge of Civil
Aviation Security to reassess the strengths and weaknesses of the existing strategies for handling
such exigencies.

10. It was felt that the penalties provided in the present law on anti-hijacking were not
commensurate with the gravity of the crime to deter the prospective offenders. It was also
insufficient to deal with these new situations and the impending threats of hijacking. Therefore,
there was an absolute necessity and urgency to have a more comprehensive legislation in order to
cover all kinds of hijacking and to have stringent provisions like awarding penalty to offenders and
conspirators of hijacking. It was also felt necessary to give effect to the provisions of the Beijing
Protocol, 2010 in India. It was accordingly decided to include certain provisions of Beijing Protocol
2010 as well as other provisions as detailed below, in the existing statute dealing with hijacking:–
– to include Beijing Protocol, 2010 in the Preamble;
– to extend the scope of the Act;
– to widen the scope of certain definitions and to insert a new definition “inservice” to
cover the offence against aircraft even when it is on ground or under preparation for
departure;
– to widen the scope of ‘hijacking’;
– to include confiscation of movable and immovable property as part of punishment;
– to widen the jurisdiction and to widen the provisions relating to extradition by inserting
new sub-sections (3) and (4);
– to provide procedures for seizure and forfeiture of property;
– to provide for powers of investigating officers for forfeiture of property and appeal
against order of Designated Authority; and
– to empower the Central Government to make rules.
11. The Committee was informed that during the inter-Ministerial consultations, Ministry of Law
and Justice (Legislative Department) advised that it would be better to go in for a fresh Bill
incorporating whole provisions of the law rather than going ahead with the Amendment Bill.
Secondly, Ministry of External Affairs advised the Ministry of Civil Aviation to seek ex-post facto
approval of the Cabinet for signing of the Beijing Protocol, 2010 and approval for ratification of
the same.
12. Accordingly, a draft Cabinet Note along with a fresh and comprehensive draft Bill on Anti-
hijacking, entitled “Anti-Hijacking Bill, 2014”, covering all the required provisions, was submitted
to Cabinet Secretariat with the following proposals:–
I. To seek ex-post facto approval of the Cabinet solicited for signing of the Beijing
Protocol 2010;
II. To seek approval of the Cabinet for –
(i) ratification of the Beijing Protocol, 2010;

22. Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft signed at the Hague on
16th December, 1970 known as the Hague Convention, 1970 is basically for Civil aircraft and not
for State aircraft used by State i.e. Military, Police/armed forces or Customs.
23. Taking into account the International Conventions and also to ensure continuity in
definitions, related issues and existing Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 and Anti-Hijacking (Amendment) Act
1994, no change was made in the draft Anti-Hijacking Bill, 2014. Ministry of Law and Justice has
vetted and drafted these definitions.
24. The enactment of Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 was done to implement the provisions of Hague
Convention 1970. The Convention only relates to civil aircraft as defined in Convention on
International Civil Aviation held at Chicago on 7 th December, 1944, not the State aircraft used for
the purpose of military, police or customs. The hijacking of military, police or Customs aircraft
cannot be brought under the preview of the Anti-Hijacking Bill 2014.
25. Therefore, the definitions ‘aircraft’ and ‘military aircraft’ may continue without any change.
Hijacking and connected offences (Chapter II)
Clause 3(1)
26. When asked about the significance of the term ‘intentionally’ used in Clause 3 of the Bill
and whether hijacking done unintentionally will not be a crime under the Bill, the Committee was
informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation that in commission of any crime by any person the basic
ingredient in our judicial system is to prove intention for ensuring commission of crime for
punishment and that the language of the Clause 3 is retained as per the existing Anti-Hijacking
Act, 1982 by Ministry of Law and Justice.
27. To a specific query on the need for defining the definition of term ‘seizes’ in Clause 3(1),
the Committee was informed that there is no need to define the expression ‘seize’ in the Bill. As
per the Tokyo Convention, 1963, Pilot-in-Command is empowered as Law Enforcement Officer and
lawfully commands the aircraft. Any person attempting to seize the command of aircraft from
Pilot-In-Command will do it unlawfully. The language of Clause 3 is as per existing Anti-Hijacking
Act,1982, enacted to implement the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft
known as the Hague Convention, 1970.

34. During the deliberations of the Committee, the Ministry of External Affairs informed that
regarding extradition of hijackers who are foreign national, in the absence of bilateral extradition
treaty the Protocol may be used as basis for seeking extradition of such foreign nationals and once
extradited, they would be tried in accordance with law of the land. The Bill also provides that all
offences under the Act will be deemed to have been included as extraditable offences in all
extradition treaties made by India with Convention countries. In accordance with the Extradition
Act, 1962 as well as the proposed Bill, none of the offences mentioned under this Act shall be
regarded as political offences for the purposes of extradition.
Clause 15
35. When the Ministry of Civil Aviation was asked about the requirement of previous sanction
of the Central Government under Clause 15 for prosecution for an offence under this Act and in
what manner it would obviate the possibility of misuse of this provision, it was informed that
Section 10 of the existing Anti-Hijacking Act, 1982 is retained as Clause 15. As per Union list, civil
aviation is subject under the domain of Central Government. All permission and approvals relating
to civil aviation matters all over India are granted by Ministry of Civil Aviation and its attached
departments/organizations only. Aircraft Act, 1934, Aircraft Rules 1937, The Aircraft (Carriage of
Dangerous Goods) Rules, 2003, Carriage by Air Act, 1972 etc. are most important legal documents
implemented by Central Government through its attached departments.
36. The Ministry of Civil Aviation further stated that the main reason to have prior permission
of Central Government is to control probable misuse by State governments by registering cases,
which would be difficult to prove in court of law due to various legal aspects of broadening of
definition of hijacking. Moreover, as proposed in the Bill, the cases of hijacking will be investigated/
prosecuted etc. and handled by National Investigation Agency, the condition of prior approval of
Central Government is essential to have in the proposed Bill and also to avoid duplication at any
level.
Clause 19
37. Clause 19 of the Bill deals with confiscation and forfeiture of property wherein it is stated
that where any order is made by the Designated Court under Section 4 for confiscation of movable
or immovable property or both, of the accused, then such property shall stand forfeited to the
Government free from all encumbrances.
38. The Ministry of External Affairs further clarified that as far as the issue of confiscation/
forfeiture of property of a hijacker who is a foreign national is concerned, all would depend on the
judgment of the Court and the treaty on mutual legal assistance between India and that foreign State.
Recommendations/observations of the Committee
39. The Committee finds that the Anti-Hijacking Bill, 2014 seeks to give effect to the
Beijing Protocol of 2010, which itself supplemented the Hague Convention of 1970 for the
Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft. The Bill is also designed to give effect to the
provisions of the Protocol and includes a couple of other provisions. The Committee is happy
to note that its main recommendations contained in its 161
st Report on the Anti-Hijacking
(Amendment) Bill that was referred to it in 2010 have been accepted by the Government
and incorporated in the new Bill. The Committee also notes that the 2014 Bill seeks to
impose death penalty for offenders and extension of the jurisdiction of the Act.

Clause 20 of the Bill empowers the Central Government to

not practicable to provide for them in the Bill itself. The delegation

REPORT
The civil aviation sector in the country is the world's ninth largest civil aviation market and
ranks fourth in domestic passenger volume. It is one of the growing sectors of the Indian economy.
India's scheduled airlines carried 67.73 million passengers in 2014 compared to 61.42 million
passengers in 2013. Air traffic in India grew between 20 and 40 per cent for six years starting from
2003, when the Low Cost Carrier module was launched. The civil aviation market in India is all set
to become the world's third largest by 2020. During the next five years, aircraft movements,
passengers and freight at all Indian airports are expected to grow at a rate of 4.2%, 5.3% and 5%
respectively.
2. The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation and implementation of national
policies and programmes in the civil aviation sector. The Ministry oversees the development and
regulation of civil aviation in the country including establishment of new aerodromes, maintenance
and upgradation of existing aerodromes, regulation of carriage of traffic by air and ensuring civil
aviation safety and security.
3. The civil aviation sector is monitored and regulated by two separate organizations under the
Ministry of Civil Aviation i.e., Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Bureau of Civil Aviation
Security. The Commission of Railway Safety, which deals with matters pertaining to safety in rail
travel and operations and performs certain statutory functions specified in the Indian Railway Act and
the Rules framed thereunder, is also under the Administrative control of Ministry of Civil Aviation.
Ministry of Civil Aviation has the following Public Sector Undertakings/Companies/Autonomous
Bodies under its administrative control:
(i) Air India Limited and its subsidiaries viz. Hotel Corporation of India Limited, Air India
Charters Limited, Air India Air Transport Services Limited, Air India Engineering
Services Limited and Airline Allied Services Limited
(ii) Airports Authority of India
(iii) Pawan Hans Limited
(iv) Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi
(v) Airports Economic Regulatory Authority of India

AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA (AAI)
36. Airports Authority of India (AAI) is developing airport infrastructure along the length and
breadth of the country including remote and far flung areas. AAI came into existence on 01.04.1995
with the merger of National Airports Authority and International Airports Authority of India. The
merger brought into existence a single organization entrusted with the responsibility of creating,
upgrading, maintaining and managing civil aviation infrastructure both on the ground and air space
in the country; with a view to accelerate the integrated development, expansion and modernization
of the air traffic services, passenger terminals, operational areas and cargo facilities at the airports
in the country. It manages 125 airports consisting of 68 operational airports (11 International airports,
8 Customs and 49 Domestic airports), 26 Civil Enclaves (3 International, 4 Customs and 19
Domestic) and 31 Non-Operational Domestic Airports. In addition, AAI provides Air Navigation
Services (ANS) at all civil airports including 9 other airports that are not managed by AAI. AAI also
provides Air Traffic Management Services (ATMS) over entire Indian Air Space and adjoining oceanic
areas with ground installations at all airports and 25 other locations to ensure safety of aircraft
operations. AAI is a Mini Ratna Category-1 Public Sector Enterprise.

40. To a specific question on the implementation of Advanced Navigation System, it was informed

already been implemented at Mumbai, Delhi and Ahmedabad Airports and are likely to be implemented

42. The Committee raised the issue of the decongestion of major Indian airports and the status of
introduction of 'Centralized Air Traffic Flow Management' at major airports. The Ministry informed
that AAI has implemented state of the art technology, modernization of ATM/CNS facilities and
advance ATM procedures at all major airports in the country. Further, following initiatives have also
been taken by AAI to decongest major Indian airports:
1. Reduction in Runway Occupancy Time (ROT).
2. Implementation of Airport Collaborative Decision Making system in Delhi to ensure
optimum slot utilization and slot monitoring.
3. Implementation of Performance Based Navigation procedure in Terminal and Enroute
Airspace.
4. Optimization of A TS Routes under Flexible Use of airspace and introduction of shorter/
direct routes and new ATS routes to provide better connectivity to various airports
whether directly and indirectly.

two phases. In first phase (PHASE-1), it will be implemented covering six metro airports namely
Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad and Bengaluru. In PHASE-2, it will be implemented
covering all other airports.
