REPORT  
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action T aken by the Ministry of Road Transport 
and Highways on the observations/recommendations as  contained in its Two Hundred and Twentieth 
Report on Demands for Grants 2015-16 of the Road Transport and Highways which was presented to both 
the Houses of Parliament on 28 th  April, 2015. 
2.  Action Taken Replies were received from the Min istry in respect of all the 
observations/recommendations contained in the Report have been categorized as follows:– 
(i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government: 
Paragraph Nos. 8,18,49,52,96,110,157        
(ii)  Recommendations/Observations which the Commit tee does not desire to pursue in view of the 
Government replies:– 
Paragraph Nos.19,31,43,47,48,50,53,54,55,56,61,65,7 0,79,84,89,107,116,121,133,136,139,141,142, 143, 
      
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted 
by the Committee: 
       
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are still awaited. 
      
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect  of those recommendations/observations which 
have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished at the earliest. 
4.     On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the  Committee has made Observations on each item of 
Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee contained in 
the Two Hundred Twentieth Report, action taken ther eon by the Ministry and 
recommendations/Observations of the Committee on ea ch item of action taken has been given in the 
succeeding paragraphs: 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
5.     The Committee finds that the allocations for  the Ministry were reduced at RE stage for its 
programmes and projects as in the past. But while t he Ministry was able to spend 96.82% allocations 
during the year 2014-15, it could spend only 91.25%  during 2013-14. The Committee feels that the 
reduction of allocation of funds for this important  infrastructure sector at RE stage should be avoide d 
particularly when the expenditure percentage has be en very good. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the Ministry should take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance.                    
      (Recommendation at Para 5  of the 220 th  Report) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
6.     Noted for compliance.  The issue will be tak en up with Ministry of Finance at appropriate time.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
7.     The Committee notes the reply of the Ministr y and further requests them to apprise the 
response to be received from the Ministry of Finance on this issue to the Committee. 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
8.     The reasons submitted by the Ministry for un der-utilization of funds under some 
schemes/programmes are of routine nature. The Commi ttee feels that proper planning, timely monitoring 
and taking preventing steps anticipating the routin e bottlenecks would ensure timely completion of 
schemes/projects and programmes. The Committee desi res that shortcomings with regard to 
implementation of projects may be identified in con sultation with the stakeholders involved in road 
Paragraph Nos. : 51
144,145, 146,147,148,149,150,151,152,153,154,155,156
Paragraph Nos: 5,9,11,20,71,86,90,95,97,103,112,128

projects so that such things are not repeated in fu ture. The Committee hopes that the spending pattern  of 
the Ministry will see an improvement in the coming years. 
 (Para 8  of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
9.     The Observations of the Committee noted for compliance.  However, due emphasis is being given i n 
the quality of project preparation ensuring that th ey reflect ground realities and considering previou s 
experiences.  Further, periodic review meetings are  held at various levels to monitor the progress of 
project, identify bottlenecks and take up necessary  corrective action for expediting progress of proje cts.   
In this regard, consultations are also held with va rious stakeholders during project preparation, 
implementation, and for identification of major bottlenecks resolving them, etc.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
10.    The Committee notes the reply and hopes that  with the existing co-ordination mechanism and 
consultations with the stakeholders, the Ministry will be able to improve its spending pattern during 
the current fiscal.  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
11.    The Committee finds that the Ministry was no t able to utilize Rs.22.20 crore provided from the 
Central Road Fund for State roads in Delhi for the year 2014-15. Though this fund is non-lapsable, the  
reasons submitted by the Ministry for non-utilizati on due to less number of proposals received from th e 
Delhi Government are not impressive. The Committee hopes that the Ministry should impress upon the 
State Governments in such cases to send their propo sals in time so that the allocated funds could be s pent 
fully. 
 (Para 9 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
12.        All the State Governments have been advi sed to submit their proposal for development of Sta te 
roads under Central Road Fund timely.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
13.      The Committee notes the reply of the Minis try; but the Committee wants to know further as 
to the reasons why the State Governments fail to send their proposals in time. 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
14.      The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s c oncern in this regard. However, the Committee notes  
that the Ministry did not actively pursue the matte r with the Ministry of Finance as could be understo od 
from the reply furnished by the Ministry to the rec ommendations made by the Committee in its 193rd 
Report in this regard. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should pursue the issue of removal of 
ceiling of expenditure for the last quarter with th e Ministry of Finance vigorously. The Committee urg es 
upon the Ministry of Finance to consider the remova l on ceiling of expenditure for road projects durin g 
the last quarter. It will help the Ministry of Road  Transport and Highways to spend the allocation ful ly 
and also to complete the projects in time without cost overrun. 
 (Para 11 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
15.     This Ministry has been consistently taking up the need for relaxation of Scheme-wise restricti on of 
33% of total expenditure for the last quarter and 1 5% in the last month considering the less working 
season for road works in the country due to long du ration of monsoon and snow fall in hilly areas.   

However, matter will be taken up with Ministry of F inance during the last quarter of the financial yea r 
after reviewing the expenditure.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
16. The Committee feels that unless the ceiling on spending of funds during the last quarter is 
not removed, the Ministry will not be able to spend  much of the allocated funds.  The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the M inistry should pursue this issue with the 
Ministry of Finance vigorously.  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
17. The Committee is pleasantly surprised to find t hat the Ministry was able to get Rs. 82,697.15 
crore (including IEBR) as against its projected dem and of Rs. 54,692.49 crore (including IEBR) for the  
year 2015-16. The Committee also finds that the GBS  component for the Ministry has seen an increase 
from Rs. 26,288.00 crore in 2014-15 (BE) to Rs. 40, 655.65 crore (BE) in 2015-16 which is a good 
54.65% increase. But this increase, Committee notes  is more apparent than real because the IEBR 
component has been calculated by the Ministry of Finance to be Rs 42,694.50 crore against this Ministry’s 
projection of Rs 20,980 crore. In other words, the financial burden on the NHAI would tend to increase . 
The Committee wishes all the best to NHAI and hopes  that it would be able to mobilize IEBR amount as 
is expected. 
 (Para 18 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
18. Comments of Committee have been noted. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
19. The Committee notes the reply with greater expe ctations. 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
20. However, the Committee finds that as against th e projected demand of Rs. 6,004.00 crores, the 
Ministry was able to get Rs. 4,211.56 crore only fo r NH (O) which is a cause of concern. The Committee  
feels that this reduction may result in diversion o f funds from NHAI meant for development of National  
Highways under NHDP to undertake projects under NH (O). The Committee desires that additional funds 
be allocated to the Ministry for projects of NH (O)  at RE stage to avoid diversion of cash flow from 
NHAI. 
 (Para 19 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
21. The additional demand would be projected at RE stage appropriately as per assessed estimated 
requirements.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
22. The Committee hopes that additional funds will be a llocated for NH (O) projects at RE 
stage.  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
23. The Committee finds that although there has bee n an increase in allocation of funds for Road 
Transport Sector from Rs.200 crore in 2014-15 (BE) to Rs.803.00 crore for 2015-16, major chunk of this  
allocation has been made for ‘Safety for women on p ublic transport’ (Rs.653.00 crores). This would mean 
that Rs.150 crore only is left for the Road Transpo rt Sector. The Committee is constrained to observe that 
the transport sector has not received the required attention during all these years. The Committee fee ls 
concern about Nirbhaya Fund being non-starter till date. It hopes that operationalisation of scheme un der 

‘Nirbhaya Fund’ for security for women and girl chi ld in public road transport in the country would be  
done in a time-bound manner and the funds allocated under this head will be spent judiciously. 
 (Para 20  of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
24. The Scheme-“Security for Women in Public Road Trans port in the country”, envisages setting 
up a National Level Vehicle security & Tracking sys tem and City Command & Control Centre with 
installation of GPS/CCTV/panic buttons in public ro ad transport in the country in 32 cities out of 53 
million plus population cities. This scheme is fina nced from ‘Nirbhaya Fund’ set up by Ministry of 
Finance. Under this scheme, Concept Report, Technol ogy Analysis Report and detailed specification of 
GPS & CCTV devices for setting up of National Level  vehicle Security & Tracking System has been 
finalized and uploaded on MoRTH website. Detailed P roject Report & Request for Proposal document is 
being examined. Now, as per directives from PMO, fu nds may be utilized only after the report from 
Secretary, Department of Electronics and Informatio n Technology on integration of schemes of Ministry 
of Home Affairs, Women and Child Development and this Ministry is received and deliberated upon. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
25. The Committee may be apprised of the further de velopment of the implementation of the 
Scheme -“Security for Women in Public Road Transport in the country”.  
National Highways Authority of India 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
26. The Committee hopes that the performance of the  Ministry in achieving the fixed targets under 
various categories will continue in the current fiscal also as in the last year. 
 (Para 31 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
27. All efforts are being made to achieve the set t argets.   
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
28. The Committee notes the reply. 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
29. The Committee observes that though there is a b etter performance in achieving the target of 
award of works during 2014-15 as compared to 2013-1 4, the performance in completion of projects has 
not seen any remarkable improvement. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will strive hard to achieve  
the targets under NHDP during the current fiscal. 
 (Para 43 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
30. All efforts are being made and various measures  are being taken to achieve the targets.   
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
31. The Committee after scrutinizing the informatio n provided by the Ministry expresses its deep 
concern over the functioning of NHAI and the unsati sfactory progress of development of National 
Highways in the country. NHAI was able to spend Rs.  6,208 crore only out of Rs. 23691.8 crore allocate d 
during 2014-15 at RE stage. The Committee is dismay ed to note that when the private players are 
withdrawing from National Highways projects due to non-availability of equity and loan to carry forwar d 
the projects, NHAI was able to spend just 26% of th e allocated fund. The Committee feels that with thi s 
spending trend, NHAI would not be in a position to achieve its targets in the coming years. 
 (Para 47 
 of ibid ) 

REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
32. The factual position is that during 2014-15 NHA I recorded total cash outflow/expenditure of 
amounting to Rs. 23,696.19 crore.   NHAI has used b orrowings amounting to Rs. 2,876.40 crore to bridge  
the gap between resources from the Government and its cash outflows. 
33. As on date, NHAI has 195 projects under executi on. 77 of these are under EPC and 118 under 
BOT. As regards projects being executed under BOT m ode, part of the capital expenditure is met by the 
private sector. As per information compiled the private sector has invested Rs. 17,293.12 crore in highway 
projects during 2014-15. Hence, during 2014-15, the  actual expenditure over seen by NHAI, public as 
well as private is Rs. 40,989.31 crore. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
34. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry w ith respect to paras 43 & 47 of 220 
th  
Report and hopes that the spending pattern of the NHAI will remain the same during the current 
fiscal also. 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS   OF THE COMMITTEE 
35. The Committee finds that the performance of dev elopment of National Highways under NHDP 
has not seen any remarkable improvement during the last year. Projects under NHDP III to VII are 
progressing at a snail pace and there are no takers  for projects under NHDP VI. The Committee feels th at 
the Ministry should address the bottlenecks causing  the delay at various stages of NHDP which was once  
considered as an ambitious project for providing ro ad connectivity even to the remote places of the 
country. 
 (Para 48 
 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
36. During the last 3 years, the highways sector is  going through a difficult phase. Public Private 
Partnership (PPP) projects through Build Operate Tr ansfer (BOT) (Toll) mode are not able to attract bi ds. 
Major highway developers in the country which are l imited in number have capacity constraints includin g 
over-leveraged financials due to excessive exposure  to infrastructure projects including highways. 
Another inherent issue for the sector is lack of av ailability of debt products aligned with revenue st ream 
profile of highway projects resulting in financial stress in projects during the initial construction years. In 
addition, there have been issues like some banks re aching the ceiling as per sectoral exposure norms. 
Quite a few projects have got stalled in the construction stage due to these reasons. These are discouraging 
prospective bidders to participate in new project bids.  
37. In order to revive the Highways Sector and to e xpedite the implementation of road projects, this 
Ministry has taken following steps: 
(a) With the constant interaction with Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change, a number o f 
specific bottlenecks for speedy execution of National Highways Projects have been resolved.  
(b) Three meetings of the Group of Infrastructure h eaded by Hon’ble Minister (RT&H,S) have 
been held and a number of inter-Ministerial issues have been resolved. 
(c)  Government on 13.05.2015 has approved the poli cy which permits 100 % equity divestment 
after two years of construction completion for all BOT projects irrespective of year of award. This wo uld 
facilitate infusion of liquidity in the sector by e nabling existing developers to release their locked -in 
equity in completed projects. Out of the 115 Conces sion Agreements signed up to 30 
th  September, 2009 
on BOT (Toll) and BOT (Annuity), 80 such projects h ave been completed, and the locked in equity of 
such completed projects works out to approximately Rs.4500 crores. This amount of equity by itself

(d) Government on 13.05.2015 has also approved the policy for one time fund infusion to revive 
and physically complete languishing BOT projects. F or any languishing highway project in BOT (Toll) 
mode that has achieved at least 50% physical comple tion and it is also established that infusion of 
moderate funding can quickly bring this project to completion, NHAI will provide financial assistance to 
such a project from the overall budget corpus of NH AI on loan basis for a short tenure and with a pre-
determined return.  This assistance (say bridge fun d) will be provided on a loan basis at Bank Rate +2 % 
drawing a parallel with the provisions of the Model  Concession Agreement. This proposal would help 
physical completion of languishing projects bringin g relief thereby, to the citizens /highway users in  the 
area. 
(e)  This Ministry has also adopted a new Hybrid An nuity model for implementation of highway 
projects in order to encourage private sector parti cipation through adequate incentives. The objective  is to 
maximize the quantum of implemented highway project s within available financial resources of the 
Government. As per this model, 40% the Project Cost  is to be provided by the Government as 
‘Construction Support’ to the private developer dur ing the construction period and the balance 60% as 
annuity payments over  the concession period along with interest on outstanding amount to the 
concessionaire. There is separate provision for O&M  payments by the Government to the concessionaire. 
The private party does not have to bear the traffic  risk. All the payments have been inflation indexed  by a 
Price Multiple Index which is a weighted average of WPI and CPI (IW) on 70:30 bases. This mitigates the 
inflation risk for the developer.

Ministry of Finance 
Relaxation of Scheme-wise restriction of 33% of tot al expenditure for the last quarter and 15% in 
the last month for the year 2014-15 
156. Ministry of Finance every year reiterates its instructions of the need for adhering to the 33% 
ceiling on expenditure for the last quarter and the  15% ceiling for the last month of the financial ye ar. 
Since the effective working season for road sector commences from October onwards till the end of the 
financial year, both for new construction & mainten ance and hence the bulk of the budget allocated to the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is spent in these months. The payment to contractor engaged in 
the activities of road development and maintenance is made on completion of the project/work or at 
different stages of the work as per the agreement. Besides, for a portion of payment to the State we f ollow 
system of adjustment which takes time in reflecting  the expenditure. In view of these circumstances 
Ministry of Finance has been requested to relax the above limit in respect of this Ministry. 
 (Para 143 
 of ibid ) 
Non- payment of unspent balance of CRF 
157. The Central Road Fund is created by the CRF Ac t 2000 and the Act provides that proceeds of 
cess levied on petrol and Diesel shall be first credited to the consolidated fund of India. The Parliament by 
appropriation credit such proceeds to the fund from  time to time, after deducting the expenses of 
collection, for being utilized exclusively for the purpose of this Act. Fund is non-lapsable and unuti lized 
portion remains as unspent which can be used in the subsequent years for the same purpose. Large amount 
of money unspent has been accumulated.  
158. Ministry of Finance has instructed Controller General of Accounts for writing back the sums 
from specific Funds in Public Accounts to consolida ted fund as non-tax receipts as assumed in BE 2014-
15. Accordingly CGA has written to CCAs/CAs concern ed for carrying out the transaction immediately. 
The principal Chief Controller of Accounts, MORTH h as transferred an amount of Rs. 4479.33 the 
unspent balance of CRF to CFI.

utilized for the purpose of development of NHs as w ell as State Roads. Though there has been increase in

Problems with respect to compliance of Forest Rights Act, 2006 
162. It was informed that vide circular dated 28.10.2014, MoEF&CC facilitated line ar projects by 
dispensing with the requirement of submission of co pies of resolutions of Gram Sabhas (and other 
committees) where diversion of forest land is invol ved from plantations notified as forest, provided s uch 
land is located in villages having no recorded popu lation of Scheduled Tribes, as per the census 2001 and 
2011. On face of it, this dispensation appears fine . However, MoEF&CC mandated a certificate in the 
prescribed format to be issued by the Collector alo ng with submission of records of meetings of Gram 
Sabhas and other Committees. In many cases certificate by the collector, that there are no tribal in the area 
and hence there is no question of any rights gettin g affected, has not been accepted by MoEF&CC, and 
they insist on submission of certificate in exactly in their format. This defeats the purpose of exemption.

 of ibid )

th  Lok

192. The Authority will have its own Secretariat.  The Central Government will appoint a Member 
Secretary, who shall be a Government employee of th e rank of Additional/ Joint Secretary to the

broad framework for the Government both at the Cent ral and the State level, to take measures for 
improvement of road safety scenario in the country.

128. The average age of Indian fleet is marginally higher i.e. 17.91 years as compared to 
16.7 years for international fleet. This indicates that not many new vessels are being added to 
Indian fleet.  However, in the past few years, SCI has added new vessels to its fleet in

owned by other Indian shipping companies would be higher than 17.91 years. 
129. Here it may be noted that higher average age o f Indian fleet is due to slow pace of 
growth of Indian tonnage over the years.   There ar e various reasons for slower growth of 
Indian tonnage.  These include higher incidence of taxation, stiff global competition 
accentuated by supply demand imbalance, absence of dedicated cargo support policy for 
Indian shipping companies and lack of access to fun ds at affordable cost for acquisition of 
ships.  
130. In order to make the shipping industry more at tractive and competitive, the 
Government has initiated several facilitative measures for the Indian shipping sector such as:- 
i. Acquisition of all type of ships, through import ha s been brought under the Open 
General Licence (OGL). 
ii. To attract investment for the growth of this sector , the Government has allowed 100% 
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in the shipping sector. 
iii. With a view to provide a level playing field to the  Indian shipping sector, the 
Government has introduced tonnage tax system during  2004-2005 which has 
effectively brought down the tax liability of the s hipping companies to a level 
comparable to the international level from the prev ious levels of the corporate tax 
regime. 
iv. Government has exempted Customs and Excise Duty lev iable on bunker fuels used in 
Indian flag vessels for transportation of EXIM and empty containers between two 
or more ports in India.  
v. Realising the need for encouraging transportation o f goods through coastal shipping 
rather than road or rail, the Government has, in th e Union Budget 2015-2016, has 
brought the abatement of service tax at par with road and rail i.e. 70%.      

vi. Keeping in view of the Government’s policy of stren gthening and promoting the 
Indian shipping industry in a competitive framework , the Indian flag vessels have 
been allowed to exercise Right of First Refusal (Ro FR) provided they match the 
lowest rate quoted by the foreign flag vessel. 
vii. Government has taken a policy decision to allow shipping enterprises based in India to 
acquire ships abroad and flag them in the country o f their convenience.  This 
will facilitate Indian ship-owners to get access to finance and business abroad.

Taxation in the Shipping Sector 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
204. The Committee recommends that the Government m ay consider granting NRI status to 
seafarers serving in Indian flagships.  The Committ ee also recommend for tax incentives for 
income from sale for qualifying vessels and other t ax incentives requested by the Ministry of 
Shipping during the pre-budget memorandum.  The Com mittee further recommends that

country.  The Ministry should take up the issues wi th the concerned Ministries/Departments 
and submit a note to this Committee along with the responses from them. 
(Para No. 138 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
205. Indian shipping industry is going through a di fficult period since the global meltdown 
of 2008.  Even though some signs of growth have bee n witnessed, the shipping and the ship-
building industry in particular face a tax regime i n India which renders them non-competitive 
in domestic as well as in international markets.  T herefore, despite 100% FDI being permitted 
in these sectors, no foreign shipping company has s et up a base in India which also points 
towards the lack of a level playing field.  To tide  over the situation this Ministry in its pre-
budget memorandum has sought undernoted tax incenti ves for the Indian shipping and 
shipbuilding industry so as to provide them a level  playing field in the intensely competitive 
global environment. 
206.  DIRECT TAX: 
• Grant of NRI status to Indian seafarers serving on Indian flag ships to bring them at 
par with their counterpart serving on foreign flag ships. 
• Income from sale of qualifying vessels to be leviable to Tonnage Tax. 
• Income resulting from deployment of tonnage tax res erves to be leviable to Tonnage 
Tax. 
• Relaxation of criteria for entry, continuation, dis qualification and exclusion from 
Tonnage Tax Scheme. 
• Amendment in Tonnage Tax Scheme to include all types of dredgers. 
• Amendments in Section 80-IA(1) of Income Tax Act, 1 961 for inclusion of dredging 
as an Infrastructure facility.  
207.  INDIRECT TAX: 
Although the tonnage tax scheme introduced in 2004-05 provided relief from corporate tax, 
some changes in the direct and indirect taxation su bsequently have diluted the benefits 
provided. The fiscal policy and lack of level playi ng field for Indian shipping companies has 
adversely affected the growth of the domestic shipp ing industry and the share of Indian 
shipping in carrying the EXIM trade from the country. These taxes include:- 
• Tonnage Tax is paid for relevant shipping income i. e. income arising from core and 
incidental shipping activities. 
• Corporate Tax or MAT is paid on income obtained fro m sale and transfer of ships 
which is an integral part of shipping activity. 
• Corporate Tax or MAT is paid on income arising from  deployment of tonnage tax 
reserve, which is meant for acquiring new tonnage. 
• Service Tax is not paid on voyage chartering of ves sels as well as on inland waterway 
transportation as the services are presently under negative list of service tax. This, 
however, blocks CENVAT credit for the tax already p aid on the inputs and prevents 
passing the tax credit to the service user thereby increasing the cost of transportation 
for the service user. 
• Service Tax is paid on time chartering of vessels, over a period of one month for 
transportation of goods. 
• An abatement of 70% on the taxable value is present ly available for payment of 
Service Tax for coastal transportation of cargo. 
 
 

208. Steps taken by the Government till date  
To encourage the Indian shipping industry the Gover nment has taken the following 
measures, namely, though more needs to be done:- 
• Acquisition of all type of ships, through import ha s been brought under the Open 
General Licence (OGL). 
• To attract investment for the growth of this Sector , the Government has allowed 100% 
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in the Shipping Sector. 
• Indian Shipping industry has been provided cargo su pport in the form of right of first 
refusal and policy of Free On Board (FOB) import is  being followed for Government 
owned/controlled cargoes. 
• In the Union Budget 2015-16, Government has announc ed an increased abatement from 
taxable value for levy of service tax on coastal tr ansportation services from 60% to 70% 
which has resulted in decrease of service tax incidence on end users. 
• To keep pace with the growth in EXIM trade and to e ncourage Indian controlled 
tonnage owned by Indian entities, Government has al lowed flagging of ships owned by 
Indian entities outside the country, subject to con ditions. This measure is expected to 
facilitate Indian shipowners to get access to finan ce and business abroad. Indian 
controlled ships shall be eligible for a priority h igher than non-Indian ships i.e. they 
would be given the right of first refusal next in the hierarchy after Indian flag vessels. 
209. The Ministry of Shipping had proposed relaxati on of residency criteria of Indian 
seafarers employed on Indian foreign going vessels while in Indian coastal waters.  The 
Hon’ble Finance Minister in his Budget speech for 2 015-16 has proposed to provide an 
enabling power to CBDT to  prescribe in the rule a uniform method of computation of period 
of stay in India for the purposes of determination of “Resident” status in the case of a Indian 
seafarer, whether working on a Indian-ship or foreign ships.   
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
210. The Committee notes that tax regime in India in the  shipping and shipbuilding 
industry renders them non-competitive in domestic a s well as in international 
markets.  Therefore, despite 100% FDI being permitt ed in these sectors, no foreign 
shipping company has set up a base in India which also points towards the lack of a level 
playing field. The Committee recommends that necess ary amendments to tax laws 
should be made in order to strengthen the shipping and shipbuilding industry in the 
country. 
Legislative Measures 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
211. The Committee, in its 197 th  Report, had made recommendations on the Merchant 
Shipping (First Amendment) Bill, 2014 on the Anti F ouling Systems for control of chemical 
pollution in the seas. The Committee understands th at the legislation has been implemented 
w.e.f. 1 st  April 2015 and hopes that this legislation would h elp in controlling the use of 
harmful anti-fouling systems on ships. 
(Para No. 140 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
212. The Ministry noted the observations of the Com mittee. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
213.  The Committee notes the reply. 
 
 
 

Maritime Labour Convention provisions incorporated in Merchant Shipping Act, 1958  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
214. The Committee, in its 202 nd  Report, had made recommendations on the 
implementation of Maritime Labour Convention 2006 f or the benefits of the Indian seafarers.  
The Committee notes that seafarers are facing vario us problems, cheating and other atrocities 
even from ship owners and life threat from pirates etc throughout their career.  Even though 
there are provisions for their protection under the Merchant Shipping Act. 1958, they have not 
proved to be effective in addressing their grievanc es.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
for an early implementation of the Maritime Labour Convention 2006. 
 (Para No. 142 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
215. Merchant Shipping (Second Amendment) Act 2014 incorporating the provisions of Maritime 
Labour Convention 2006 of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) has been passed by the 
Parliament and has been implemented on 01.04.2015. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
216. The Committee notes the reply. 
Vacancies  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
217. The Committee notes that due to non-availabili ty of sufficient personnel in the 
customs department, the ports are not able to make swift cargo movement or work round the 
clock.  Customs is income carning venture of the ex chequer.  Therefore, the Government 
should augment its income carning capacity by deput ing sufficient number of officials to man 
the customs activities at the ports.  Recruitment o f customs personnel will help the already 
struggling ports to streamline its operations.  The  Committee recommends that this matter 
should be taken seriously and adequate steps for re cruiting enough staff members should be 
made immediately. 
      (Para No. 144 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
218. The matter of deployment of Customs Officials at Major Ports comes under 
administrative control of Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.  
 FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
219. The Committee notes the reply and recommends that Ministry of Shipping may 
pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
220. The Committee takes strong exception to the pr oposal of Ministry of Finance for 
installing container scanners in every port in adeq uate numbers.  But this work is not being 
done with required scale and pace.  As a result we are still running the risk of radioactive and 
other hazardous material including lethal weapons i nto the country.  The Committee would 
like to have a status note on installation work of scanner at our Ports reflecting the 
requirements and actually installed/sanctioned, Port-wise.  
(Para No. 145 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
221. The issue of installation of X-ray scanners at  Major Ports is being done by Department 
of Revenue (Central Board of Excise & Customs). CBE C has informed that installation of 7 
container scanners (3 Mobile Gamma Ray Scanners and 4 fixed X-ray Scanners) at the port(s) 
of Mumbai, Chennai, Kandla and Tuticorin have been initiated since 2010-11 with the 
approval of the Cabinet. Out of these, two Mobile S canners have been installed at the ports of 
Tuticorin, and Chennai in the month of March 2014 a nd June 2014 respectively and the third 
Mobile Scanner is under installation at Kandla Port . Balance four fixed X-ray scanners at 
Chennai, Kandla, Tuticorin and Mumbai Ports will be  installed by June, 2015. In the 2 
nd  

Phase, Three X-ray based Drive Through (Road) Conta iner Scanners are being installed at the 
ports of JNPT, Mundra and Cochin. A proposal to ins tall two Drive Through (Rail) Container 
Scanners on Pilot basis at the gateway ports of JNP T and Mundra has also been approved.  
Requirement of 22 additional container scanners at 8 ports was identified for installation in 
phase III at port(s) of Kolkata(3), Vizag(1), Cochi n(1), Mundra(1), Bangalore(1), Goa(1), 
Mumbai(10) & Chennai(3). Procurement of additional scanners for installation at various 
ports in the next phase may be taken up only after observing the result of installation of Drive 
Through Container Scanners (Road) and (Rail). 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
222. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee recom mends that priority should 
be given to those Ports like ICTT and JNPT which ar e exclusively doing container 
handling among the other Major Ports. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
223. The Committee notes the vacancies existing in the Ministry  and  recommends that the 
Ministry should take steps to ensure that the vacancies are filed up without delay. 
(Para No. 147 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
224. The recommendations have been noted for compli ance.  Ministry of Shipping is taking 
up the case for filling up of all Group ‘B’& ‘C’ po sts with Department of Personnel & 
Training which is the cadre controlling authority f or Group ‘B’posts (Gazetted & Non-
Gazetted) of Central Secretariat Service (CSS), Gro up ‘B’ & ‘C’posts of Central Secretariat 
Stenographers Service (CSSS) as well as Group ‘C’po sts of Central Secretariat Clerical 
Service (CSCS). 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
225. The Committee notes the reply. 
Komagata Maru Memorial 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
226. The Committee notes the initiatives taken by t he Ministry of Shipping on the 
construction of a Memorial Hall on Komagata Maru in  the land of Kolkata Port.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture s hould provide the required grant for 
construction of the memorial.  The Committee also n otes that the Ministry of Tourism has a 
scheme to fund the Central Government agencies for maintaining monuments.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism m ay also be approached for appropriate 
funding for construction of the monument as it can attract a large number of tourists. 
(Para No. 154 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
227. The issue relating to construction of a Memori al Hall on Komagata Maru on the plot 
of land of KoPT has already been taken up by the Mi nistry of Shipping with Ministry of 
Culture.  Ministry of Shipping has informed the Min istry of Culture that KoPT can build the 
Memorial Hall with Museum provided Ministry of Cult ure may give cost of construction to 
KoPT as grant.  Ministry of Culture has  
 
agreed to pay the cost of construction to KoPT. The  estimated cost of construction of 
Memorial Hall with Museum and a copy of draft Memor andum of Understanding (MoU) to 
be signed between Ministry of Culture, Kolkata Port  Trust and Komagata Maru Martyr’s 
Memorial Trust has been forwarded by KoPT to Minist ry of Culture for 
consideration/approval. Till date, the matter is pending with Ministry of Culture.  
 
 
 

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
228. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee recom mends that the matter may 
be pursued with the Ministry of Culture and further  action may be initiated at the 
earliest.  
Other Issues  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
229. The Committee understands that low lying struc tures along the NW- 3 cause hindrance 
to the development of the Waterways in Kerala and a t many stretches, the issue is a major 
one. The Committee hopes that the new Bill will be able to address such issues and that the 
pace of development of National Waterways will increase after the implementation of the Act.  
 (Para No. 156 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
230. To regulate the cross structures on inland wat erways of the country, a notification for 
classification of waterways has already been made i n 2006 and the same was circulated to 
Chief Secretaries of all the States for compliance.  As per classification of waterways, rivers/ 
canals/ creeks etc. have been classified in differe nt categories and the cross structures 
constructed on the waterways require minimum horizo ntal and vertical clearances according 
to category of waterways mentioned in the notificat ion.  Further, as per the notification, the 
State Governments are required to obtain No Objecti on Certificate (NOC) from IWAI prior to 
commencement of construction of any cross structure s on the waterways in their respective 
States.   
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
231. The Committee notes the reply and desires to know the response from various 
State Governments in this matter. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
232. The Committee notes that insufficiency of rake s is a perennial problem and despite 
being pointed out year after year, resolution of th is issue is still out of sight.  The Committee 
feels that this is happening because of the inefficient planning by the agencies concerned.  The 
Committee recommends that a solution to the problem  may be found out urgently keeping in 
view the long term requirements.   The Committee ho pes that the Infrastructure Committee 
would be able to address the infrastructure related  issues in consultation with all the other 
agencies concerned.  
(Para No. 158 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
233. The issue of insufficiency of rakes has been t aken up with Ministry of Railways 
several times in respect of Visakhapatnam Port Trus t. We have also written to Container 
Corporation of India (CONCOR) in respect of heavy c ongestion at ICD, Tughlakabad. We 
have also requested Ministry of Railway to enable G overnment run Major Ports to be allowed 
to procure their own wagons under Special Freight T rain Operator (SFTO) Scheme. The 
matter is pending with Ministry of Railways.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
234. The Committee recommends that procurement of wagons  under SFTO Scheme 
may be pursued with the Ministry of Railways in ord er to meet the shortage of wagons/ 
rakes in the Ports.  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
235. During deliberations, one of the Members of th e Committee raised the issue of 
shortage of accommodation for staff of Kandla Port Trust and thereby the employees had to 

resort to strike to highlight their grievance. The Committee urges the Ministry to look into the 
matter urgently and apprise the Committee, the steps taken to alleviate the problem. 
(Para No. 160 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
236. There has been no shortage of accommodation fo r the staff of Kandla Port and many 
flats are lying vacant as staff of the Port have no t occupied the flats.  Ministry has formulated 
Land Policy Guidelines, 2014 which has come into ef fect from 02.01.2014.  As per the Land 
Policy Guidelines, 2014 there is no provision for a llotment of Port Land to Port Employees. 
Ministry has been implementing measures to curb enc roachments and to ensure there are no 
new encroachments. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
237. The Committee notes the reply. 
General Observations and Recommendations 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
238. During the discussion on Demands for Grants, t he Members of the Committee 
highlighted the need for better utilization of the vacant land available with the Major Ports. 
The Committee recommends that un-utilized land with  the Major Ports should be utilized 
appropriately in public interest such as hospitals,  schools etc. The Ministry should also ensure 
that encroachments from its land removed and that n ew encroachments are not allowed to 
happen.  
(Para No. 161 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
239. The Ministry of Shipping has advised all the M ajor Ports to digitalize and do GIS 
mapping of their Land Records. This would enable th e Ports to identify and keep track of all 
the land available with them and the various usages  to which it has been put in use. The Ports 
have also been instructed to construct boundary wal ls around their land areas so as to check 
any unauthorized encroachments. Vacant lands are allotted/utilized as per the Land use Plan. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
240. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee recom mends that the Ministry of 
Shipping may encourage the Ports to make the vacant  land available for hospitals, 
schools, etc., as mentioned above, once the digitalization of land records is completed. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
241. The Committee emphasizes the need for greater autonomy- financial and 
administrative- to be given to Major Ports, so that  they may be able to tackle the rough 
patches in the execution of projects without delay and execute their projects timely.  
(Para No. 162 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT  
242. The financial powers delegated to Major Ports have been enhanced in February, 2015 
to speed up decision making and infrastructure crea tion. The Powers for sanctioning and 
incurring expenditure on capital works have been en hanced from Rs. 50 crore to Rs.100 crore 
for new and replacement works; and to Rs.200 crore for all capital works, facilitating speed 
up of decisions on Port development works. 

FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
243. The Committee notes the reply.  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
244. The Committee recommends that Vizhinjam Port i n Kerala which has natural draft of 
16 meter should be developed properly with the aid of the Central Government. The 
Committee also recommends that the present cabotage  regulations which are preventing the 
Port from getting a suitable bidder should be revis ited and corrective measures should be 
taken promptly. 
(Para No. 163 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
245. The State Government has informed that Vizhinj am Port is being developed as a 
Greenfield port to reduce the reliance on foreign p orts for transshipment. It is  proposed to be 
set-up as a PPP venture and bidding process to sele ct a PPP operator has been completed and 
M/s Adani Ports and SEZ Limited has been selected to implement the project. 
246. The Empowered Committee under Department of Ec onomic Affairs (DEA), Ministry 
of Finance had given in-principle approval for providing Viability Gap Funding (VGF) for the 
Vizhinjam International Deepwater Sea Port.  
247. The Ministry is undertaking comprehensive revi ew of Cabotage Policy. This issue will 
be finalised as part of cabotage policy which is be ing reviewed. A policy note on Relaxation 
of Cabotage Policy has been circulated for comments of the stakeholders.   
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
248. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee may be apprised about the future 
developments in the case of Cabotage Policy for its reference. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
249. The  Committee  observes  that  oil  pilferage   is  a  huge  environmental  issue  and 
recommends that the Government should take correcti ve measures to contain  this  menace.  
The Committee desires that environmental pollution from asbestos due to ship breaking also 
needs to be addressed effectively.    
(Para No. 164 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
250. This Ministry has taken a number of steps viz. , deployment of CISF, installation of 
CCTV, to enhance the security of Major Ports.  It i s now very difficult for any person to gain 
unauthorized entry into the port premises or take anything unauthorisedly out of port area. 
251. So far as spillage of oil in port waters, due to collision between vessels or otherwise, is 
concerned, all the Major  Port have been directed t o acquire facilities for combating tier-I oil 
spills in their waters. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
252. The Committee desires that environmental pollution  from asbestos due to ship 
breaking also needs to be addressed effectively.    
 

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
253. The Committee urges the Ministry that for skil l development in the various trades of 
the Shipping Sector, the Ministry, Shipping Corpora tion of India, Ports etc. should sponsor 
such courses in the IITs and other reputed Institutes of the country. 
(Para No. 165 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
254. SCI has been constantly training its manpower ashore and afloat in the various reputed 
institutes. SCI have their in-house Maritime Training Institute (MTI) at Mumbai and Tuticorin 
for mainly training the shipboard personnel. Furthe r, they have been arranging training of the 
ashore personnel at various management levels to ke ep them abreast of the dynamics of 
shipping sector. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
255. The Committee notes that the Ministry is reemphasi zing the status quo. The 
Committee desires that the Government should do mor e to develop skill and qualified 
personnel in large numbers. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
256. The Committee recommends that small barges up to 500 tonne capacity should be   
given adequate subsidy to improve transportation through inland waterways. 
(Para No. 166 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT  
257. During 10 
th  Plan, there was a scheme termed as ‘Inland Vessel Building Subsidy 
Scheme (IVBSS)’ under which 30% of the cost of the vessel was provided to the applicant, 
who constructs the inland vessels for plying on NWs . The same was discontinued from 
01.04.2007. For revival of the scheme, matter was p ursued with the Government However, 
the then Planning Commission did not agree with the proposal. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
258. The Committee recommends that the matter may be pu rsued with the NITI 
AAYOG and Ministry of Finance for the resumption of a modified Scheme for IVBSS. 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE  
259. The Committee also observes that due to scarci ty of large sized scanners, 
customs/security checking of the large sized cargo get delayed in the Ports. The Committee 
recommends that necessary remedial steps should be taken in this matter.  
(Para No. 167 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
260. Central Board of Excise & Customs (CBEC) has b een entrusted with the responsibility 
of installation of Container Scanners at all Major Ports. 2 Container Scanners are already 
operational in JNPT since 2004-05.  Installation of  Scanners at Chennai, Kandla, Tuticorin 
(V.O. Chidambaranar) and Mumbai Ports is in progress.  
261. In the 2 
nd  phase, three X-ray based Drive Through (Road) Cont ainer Scanners having 
higher through put of scanning more than 100 contai ners per hour are being installed at the 
ports of JNPT, Mundra and Cochin. Seeing the result  of installation of Drive Through 
Container Scanners (Road) and (Rail), CBEC proposes  to install 22 additional containers at 8 
ports in phase III.   
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
262. The Committee notes the reply.

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Transport, Tourism and Culture, having been auth orized by the Committee to 
present on its behalf, do hereby present this Two H undred and Twenty Ninth  
Report on “Action Taken Replies by the Ministry of Tourism on the 
observations/recommendations as contained in its Tw o Hundred and Twenty Second 
Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) of the Ministry of Tourism”. 
2.  The Two Hundred and Twenty Second Report  of the Department-related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tour ism and Culture was presented 
on the 28 th  April, 2015 to the Parliament. 
3.  The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations  of the Committee contained 
in its Two Hundred and Twenty Second Report was rec eived from the Ministry of 
Tourism on 21st August, 2015. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 
24 
th  November, 2015.   
 
 
KANWAR DEEP SINGH  
NEW DELHI;                      Chairman,  
November, 24,  2015                                  Department-related  Parliamentary Standing  
Agrahayana, 03, 1937 (Saka)    Committee on  Transport, Tourism and Cult ure. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 

REPORT 
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action T aken by the Government on the 
observations/recommendations as contained in its Tw o Hundred and Twenty Second Report 
on Demands for Grants 2015-16 of the Ministry of To urism which was presented to both the 
Houses of Parliament on 16 th  April, 2015.   
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the  Government on the 21 st  August, 2015 
in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. The replies have 
been categorized as follows:– 
(i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government: 
Paragraph Nos. 9, 10, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 2 6, 27, 28, 32, 38, 39, 40, 44,45, 46, 47, 48, 
49, 50, 53, 54, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 68, 74, 77, 82,  83, 84, 87, 93, 94, 95, 100, 102, 107, 108, 
113, 114, 118, 119, 120, 123, 124, 129, 130, 132, 133, 137, 138, 139, 140, 143, 147 (i), (ii) & 
(iii), 151, 153, 154, 159, 160, 161, 162, 163, 164, 165, 166 and 167. 
Total: 73 
(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committ ee does not desire to pursue in view 
of the Government replies:– 
Paragraph Nos. 17, 20, 21, 27, 32, 33, 38, 39, 40, 46, 47, 48, 50, 62, 63, 68, 71, 74, 82, 87, 
93, 95, 118, 129, 130, 139, 151, 153, 154, 159, 160, 163, 164   
 (iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of w hich replies of the Government have not 
been accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos. : 16, 19, 26          
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of whi ch final replies of the Government are 
still awaited. 
Paragraph Nos.: Nil                                                                        
3. The Committee desires that final replies in resp ect of those 
recommendations/observations which have been catego rized as interim replies by the 
Committee should be furnished at the earliest. 
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Com mittee has made observations on each 
item of Action Taken/proposed to be taken by the Mi nistry. The recommendations of the 
Committee contained in the Two Hundred and Twenty S econd Report, action taken thereon 
by the Ministry and recommendations/observations of  the Committee on each item of action 
taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs: 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
5.  The Committee notes that even though Planning Commi ssion had made a very 
ambitious plan for tourism promotion in the country  during the 12 
th  plan Period by making  
an outlay of Rs. 15190 crore, the sanctions made du ring the first three years of the Twelfth  
Plan period was  Rs 2930.00 crore only, which is ju st 19.28% of the  total outlay. If the 
actual spending is taken into consideration, it sta nds at Rs.2566.48 crore which is 16.89% of 
the 12 th  Plan outlay.  The Committee finds that expenditure and allocation have not been upto 
the mark.  It is a matter of concern as the targets  also could not have been achieved due to 
less spending. The Committee, therefore, is constra ined to observe that such a pattern does 

not augur well for Tourism, as it has highest poten tial for employment as well as revenue 
generation for our economy.               
6. The Government does not make adequate allocation  for this Sector. The Committee is 
afraid that if such a trend continues, the country may not be able to sustain the current tourist 
inflow, not to speak of increasing it upto the desi red level.  It, therefore, may result in the 
decline of not only the tourism industry as a whole  but also so many other sectors associated 
with it.            
      (Recommendation at Para No.9 & 10 of the 222 
nd  Report) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
7. During the 11 
th  Plan period the Ministry of Tourism was able to sp end about 99.23% 
of its budgetary allocation.  During the 12 th  Plan period i.e. during the first three years, the  
average utilization of funds have been as under:- 
Year  BE (Rs. In crore) RE (Rs. In crore)  Expenditure. (Rs. In 
crore) 
% Utilisation 
2012-13 1210.0 950.0 865.96 91.15 
2013-14 1282.0 980.0 957.80 97.73 
2014-15 1882.0 1000.0 * 910.39 91.39 
* An additional amount of Rs. 100 crore was allocat ed but not released to Ministry of 
Tourism.  
8. Ministry of Tourism recognizes the fact that the  tourism sector has the potential for 
employment and revenue generation for our country. Hence it is the endeavour of Ministry of

160. Basically, service tax is leviable only on the  service portion of the services provided.

actual duty incidence comes only 7.416% at present,  when service tax is levied @12%.  
While, after the rate of service tax is increased t o @ 14%, actual duty incidence after

abatement would be 5.6% and net increase would be 0 .66%, which is again a very nominal 
increase.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary S tanding Committee on 
Transport, Tourism and Culture, having been authori zed by the Committee, do hereby 
present on its behalf this Two Hundred Thirtieth Re port on “Issues related to Security 
at Airports in India". 
2. The violent incident which occurred at Karipur I nternational Airport at 
Kozhikode on 10 th  June, 2015 involving the employees of Airports Aut hority of India 
and Central Industrial Security Force was an eye op ener regarding the security system 
available at Indian airports.  With this backdrop, the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Cultur e decided to take up the Issues 
related to Security at Airports in India for examination and Report.   
3. The Committee heard the views of the Ministry of  Civil Aviation, Ministry of 
Home Affairs, Airports Authority of India, Bureau o f Civil Aviation Security, Central 
Industrial Security Force and Intelligence Bureau d uring its meeting held on the 10 th  
July, 2015.  The Committee visited the Delhi Intern ational Airport to have on-the-spot 
study of the security arrangements at the Delhi Air port on 31 st  August, 2015 and heard 
the security agencies, Ministry of Civil Aviation, Home Affairs, and GMR on various 
aspects of security at Delhi Airport. The Committee , during its study visit to Mumbai 
and Kochi in October, 2015 also heard the views of MIAL, GVK and CIAL, the 
Airport operators as well as various agencies invol ved in providing security to these 
airports.  
4.  The Committee wishes to express its thanks to t he officers of Ministries of Civil 
Aviation, Home Affairs, Airports Authority of India, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, 
Central Industrial Security Force, Intelligence Bur eau, Government of Maharashtra and 
other stakeholders for placing before the Committee , the material and information 
desired in connection with the subject and for clar ifying the points raised by the 
Members. 
5.  The Committee considered and adopted the Report  at its meeting held on the 
18 
th   December, 2015.

Report 
Airport Security is integral part of National Security. The objective of providing 
security to airports is to safeguard the passengers , crew, ground personnel, the general 
public and the airport infrastructure against unlaw ful acts as per International Civil 
Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommen ded Practices laid down in 
Annexure-17 to the Chicago Convention.  Annexure – 17 (Security) of International 
Civil Aviation Organization  requires that all Cont racting States shall establish and 
implement a written National Civil Aviation Securit y Programme (NCASP); shall have 
a designated appropriate authority to be responsibl e for development, implementation 
and maintenance of NCASP; shall allocate tasks and co-ordinate activities related to 
aviation security.  
2. The Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) is the designated agency for 
providing security in accordance with the Internati onal Civil Aviation Organization 
(ICAO) regulations.  The broad security architecture is laid down by the BCAS in terms 
of codified five documents.  They are called Nation al Civil Aviation Security 
Programme, National Civil Aviation Security Trainin g Programme, National Civil 
Aviation Security Quality Control Programme and Bom b Threat Contingency Plan to 
deal with hijacking. 
3.  Airport security in the country is looked after  by specialized Police agencies, 
State Police and airport security organizations, de pending on the security conditions 
prevalent in a particular area. Bureau of Civil Avi ation Security co-ordinates the 
working of the various agencies to ensure that all security norms are followed by them. 
4. The violent incident which occurred at Karipur I nternational Airport at 
Kozhikode on 10 th  June, 2015 involving the employees of Airports Aut hority of India 
and Central Industrial Security Force was an eye op ener regarding the security system 
available at Indian airports.  With this backdrop, the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Cultur e decided to take up the Issues 
related to Security at Airports in India for examination and Report. 
5. The Committee heard the views of the Ministry of  Civil Aviation, Ministry of 
Home Affairs, Airports Authority of India, Bureau o f Civil Aviation Security, Central 
Industrial Security Force and Intelligence Bureau d uring its meeting held on the 10 th 
July, 2015.  The Committee visited the Delhi Intern ational Airport to have on-the-spot 
study of the security arrangements at the Delhi Air port on 31 st  August, 2015 and heard 
the security agencies, Ministry of Civil Aviation, Home Affairs, and GMR on various 
aspects of security at Delhi Airport  
6. The Committee, during its study visit to Mumbai and Kochi, also heard the 
views of GVK and CIAL, the Airport operators as wel l as various agencies involved in 
providing security to these airports.  

10 
 
7. The issues dealt with by the Committee on the is sues related to Security at 
Airports in India and the response of the Ministrie s of Civil Aviation and Home Affairs 
and other agencies thereon and the observations/ re commendations of the Committee 
have been enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs. 
Policy on security at airports 
 
8. The Committee was informed that the Commissioner  of Security, Civil 
Aviation (COSCA), Bureau of Civil Aviation Security  (BCAS) is designated by 
Ministry of Civil Aviation (MCA) as appropriate aut hority for development, 
implementation and maintenance of National Civil Av iation Security Programme 
(NCASP) of India in line with Annexure 17 of Chicag o Convention of International 
Civil Aviation Organization. COSCA has been empower ed to issue directions under 
Section 5A of Aircraft Act 1934 with respect to civ il aviation security matters. He is 
also empowered to exercise all powers and duties co nferred under the Aircraft 
(Security) Rules 2011. Ministry of Civil Aviation i s the nodal Ministry for all matters 
relating to Civil Aviation.  
9. The Advisory Committee for Civil Aviation Securi ty is headed by the 
Secretary (Civil Aviation) which meets every year. This Committee is responsible to 
advise Government on matters relating to Civil Avia tion Security, recommend and 
review the effectiveness of security measures and procedures, and suggest enactment of 
such legislation as is found necessary and provide for co-ordination, at the national 
level, of all matters relating to the security.  
10. Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS)  lays down Aviation Security 
(AVSEC) norms in accordance with ICAO Annex-17 for Airport Operators, Aircraft 
operators, Regulated Agents, Caterers, Ground Handl ing Agents, Central Industrial 
Security Force/Aviation Security Group and State/Union Territory Police personnel.  
11. It was further informed that implementation of security rules and regulations is 
monitored by BCAS through Quality Control activities (security audits and inspections, 
security surveys and security tests to check profes sional efficiency and alertness of 
security staff and mock exercises to test efficacy of contingency plan and operational 
preparedness). AVSEC training is imparted to securi ty personnel of all agencies 
concerned with civil aviation. BCAS also carryout p lanning and coordination of 
AVSEC matters.  
Present status of security at airports  
12. On the matter of present status of security at Indian airports, the Committee 
was informed that major threats (acts of unlawful interference) are hijacking – unlawful 
seizure of aircraft; hostage taking on board aircra ft / aerodromes; forcible intrusion on 
board aircraft / aerodrome / aeronautical facility;  sabotage of airport / aircrafts and 
terrorist attack on airport.  
13. India is amongst the most terrorism affected co untries. Latest threat inputs 
include surgically implanted explosives for unlawfu l interference in civil aviation 
operations, Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) hid den in printer ink and toner 

11 
 
cartridges, inputs like Terrorists looking to hijac k aircraft from airports using trained 
pilots and inputs point to increasing sophisticatio n in terrorist Modus Operandi and the 
threat to hijack aircrafts / forcible intrusion at smaller airports.  India has been rated 
highly in terms of aviation security in the last ICAO audit in 2011. The parameter, Lack 
of Effective Implementation (LEI) for India stood a t 10.75% against global average of 
34.01%. 
 
Security arrangements at airports 
 
14. On the subject of existing security arrangement s at the airports in the country,  
the Ministry informed the Committee that Standard O perating Procedures (SOPs) have 
been issued by BCAS in the form of AVSEC Circulars/  Orders regarding some 
important issues like procedure of passengers and c arry-on baggage screening, items 
banned for carriage on-board the aircraft, dealing with cases of detection of arms and 
ammunition during screening of passengers or baggag e, screening of hold baggage, 
security of cargo, courier and mail, access of vehi cles up to the aircraft and the list of 
persons exempted from pre-embarkation security checks.  
15. Categorization of airports, on the basis of int elligence inputs as well as threat 
and risk, has been made for the 98 airports (Hyper- sensitive – 26, Sensitive –56 and 
Normal – 16).  
16. It was also informed that in the aftermath of h ijacking of IC-814 in December 
1999 from Kathmandu, the Committee of Secretaries t ook a decision to deploy CISF at 
the airports. The security of Airports is covered b y the State / Union Territory Police, 
Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) and Centra l Reserve Police Force (CRPF)/ 
India Reserve Battalion (IRB). CISF was inducted in to airports consequent to IC-814 
hijacking (24 th December, 1999) as decided by Committee of Secretar ies in a meeting 
held on 7 th  January, 2000. CISF was first inducted at Jaipur A irport on 3 rd  February, 
2000.  As on date, Central Industrial Security Forc e (Aviation Security Group) has 
taken over the security of 53 airports of Airports Authority of India and 06 Joint 
Venture/ Private Airports. The airports at Jammu an d Kashmir, Mizoram, etc are 
covered by State Police with the support of CRPF / IRB and rest of the airports are 
manned by Local Police.  
17. In view of potential security threats and curre nt aviation security scenario, 
State/UT Police have been requested to ensure that all operational airstrips / 
aerodromes in their jurisdiction including those be longing to flying clubs are properly 
guarded and all necessary measures are taken to ens ure that no unlawful interference 
takes place with civil aviation operations, especia lly with regard to hijacking and 
operation of rogue aircrafts which may be used as w eapons. Also to ensure that all 
those airstrips / aerodromes which are not in use c urrently are actually made non-
operational so that no rogue aircraft can make use of the same.  
18. The security infrastructure is provided by the Airport Operators. Some 
security functions are allocated to Airport Operato rs (in-line hold baggage screening), 
Aircraft Operators (screening of registered baggage , cargo, mail, catering, company 

12 
 
stores and security of aircraft) and Regulated Agen ts (screening of cargo / courier / 
mail).  
19. All authorized persons, employees, casual labou r, passengers and vehicles 
while gaining entry into airside from any gate(s) a re subject to security checks/frisking, 
baggage search, if any, by the Airport Security Personnel manning those gates.  
20. Screening of passengers, staff and visitors at the entry gates of the airport 
through Door Frame Metal Detectors (DFMD)/Hand-held  Metal Detectors (HHMD) 
and physical frisking on random basis are carried o ut depending on local situation and 
inputs received from the intelligence agencies.  In case of suspected baggage, additional 
measures like screening through X-ray Baggage Inspe ction System (XBIS) and 
Explosive Trace Detection (ETD) may also be taken.  
21. It was further informed that Closed-circuit Tel evision (CCTV)   is mandatory 
at all operational airports.  Monitoring of CCTV is to be done by all agencies concerned 
at unified CCTV Control Room.  It is the responsibi lity of Airport Security Unit of 
State Police and ASG (CISF) to monitor CCTV coverin g all areas of the airport.  Other 
agencies like AAI, Customs, Immigration and Airline  operators are authorized to 
depute their representatives in the Control Room fo r monitoring activities in their 
respective areas.  The recorded cassettes are retained for a period of one month to allow 
any concerned agencies to review later.  
22. Perimeter wall of 8" with 1½" overhang fencing has been prescribed around 
the airport.  Watch towers are to be installed ever y one km or as per the local survey 
keeping in view the threat to a particular airport.   Similarly, perimeter lighting and 
perimeter roads are prescribed for mobile and foot patrolling to prevent any 
unauthorized entry / intrusion into the airports. P erimeter Intrusion Detection System is 
also prescribed for installation.  
23. Manpower for surveillance in and around the air ports is also provided on the 
basis of requirements assessed by joint security survey team.  
24. All authorized personnel working with Ground Ha ndling Agents (GHA) while 
leaving airport from any gate(s) are subject to security checks (frisking/baggage search) 
by the airport security personnel manning those gat es.  Similarly, all staff when exiting 
the security restricted area of airports is to be f risked on random basis so that any 
element of preparation of an unlawful act can be detected.  
25. Airport Operators, Airline Operators, GHAs and other agencies are required to 
have security clearance and approved security programme before operation.  
26. All persons operating in the aviation environme nt need to undergo Aviation 
Security (AVSEC) awareness training.  Security rela ted personnel need to qualify in 
AVSEC Basic Training.  Screeners are mandated to qu alify in screener training.  
Refresher courses are prescribed for various training programme.  
27. The Ministry submitted that the following is th e mechanism existing to deal 
with hijacking situations:  
i. Aerodrome Committee at airport level;  
ii. Central Committee at National level; 

13 
 
iii. Committee of Secretaries on Aircraft Hijack (COSAH); and  
iv. Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS): Apex Body. 
28. The Cabinet Secretary is the Chairman of COSAH.  DGCA is the Chairman of 
Central Committee with COSCA as the Convener. 
29. The Quick Reaction Team (QRT) of State Police /  CISF / CRPF is responsible 
for cordoning of hijacked aircraft till the arrival of NSG, strengthening of perimeter and 
crowd management.  Counter Terrorism Contingency Pl an including various agencies 
i.e ., CISF, NSG, Local Police, etc. are in place at Airports.  
Role of Ministry of Home Affairs in Civil Aviation Security 
 
30.  When asked about the role of the Ministry of Home A ffairs on  the issue of 
Security at Indian airports, the Committee was info rmed that the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA) has an important role in ensuring Civ il Aviation security in the country.  
Whereas BCAS frames the rules and regulations for c ivil aviation security, Central 
Industrial Security Force, which is functioning und er MHA, acts as the implementing 
agency for the guidelines framed by BCAS.  CISF is also entrusted with drawing up 
airport-wise Counter-Terrorism Contingency Plans (C TCP) and is at the forefront of 
activities in this regard.  Currently CTCP is avail able only at Delhi and Mumbai 
airports where CISF has been entrusted with securit y of the city side area. CISF also 
has its own intelligence wing and is part of the mu lti agency centre which disseminates 
intelligence and coordinates action at the airports. 
31. The Intelligence Bureau also plays an important  role in providing intelligence 
inputs related to civil aviation security.  Further , Bureau of Immigration under 
Intelligence Bureau screens incoming and outgoing p assengers from and to other 
countries.   
32. It was further informed that the National Secur ity Guard (NSG) under MHA is 
involved in Civil Aviation Security through deploym ent of Sky Marshals on aircrafts 
operating on sensitive sectors for prevention of an d to act as first responders to any 
incident involving hijacking of an aircraft.  NSG i s also the primary Contingency 
Response Force for anti-terrorist operations at airports. NSG maintains a Task Force for 
this purpose ready to move at 30 minutes notice.

33.  As per the status note furnished by the Ministry of  Home Affairs on the subject, 
the following agencies are involved in civil aviation security:- 
i. Airlines  - Airlines are responsible for screening of registere d baggage and

ii. Airport Operators -  Airport Operators are responsible for provision of

• Airports Authority of India (AAI) Operates 125 airp orts (including non-

Threat perception and Security Categorization of airports  
34. When asked about the threat perception and the provision of adequate security 
at the airports in the country, the Committee was i nformed that threat perception to all 
operational airports in the country is reviewed by BCAS in consultation with the 
Intelligence Agencies and based on the inputs recei ved, airports are categorised into 
three categories viz ., Hypersensitive, Sensitive and Normal. Currently,  out of 98 
operational airports in India, 26 airports are cate gorised as Hypersensitive (18 under 
CISF security cover), 56 categorised as Sensitive ( 37 under CISF security cover) and
