Existing Regulatory measures for Infrastructure Lending by Banks
47. The Committee was informed by RBI that they are seized of the importance of
infrastructural development in the country and thus the RBI has initiated a number of regulatory
measures/concessions for facilitating increased flow of credit to infrastructure projects. The special
dispensations given by RBI in this regard are briefly outlined below:
(a) Liberal Single/Group Borrower Exposure Limits
 In view of the generally large requirements of funds for infrastructure projects, the
existing RBI guidelines provide for enhanced exposure ceilings for the infrastructure
lending. Exposure to single borrower may exceed the general exposure norm of 15
per cent of the bank’s capital funds by an additional 5 per cent ( i.e. up to 20 per
cent) provided the additional credit exposure is on account of infrastructure finance.
Exposure to borrowers belonging to a group may exceed the general exposure norm
of 40 per cent of the bank’s capital funds by an additional 10 per cent ( i.e. up to
50 per cent), provided the additional credit exposure is on account of extension of
credit to infrastructure projects.
 However, the current dispensation is under review subsequent to the publication of
the BCBS Standards on Supervisory Framework for Measuring and Controlling
Large Exposures.
(b) Liberal Norms for ‘security’ recognition
 While assignments/rights/receivables are not allowed to be treated as ‘tangible’
securities, banks have been allowed to treat annuities under build-operate-transfer
(BOT) model in respect of road/highway projects and toll collection rights, where
there are provisions to compensate the project sponsor if a certain level of traffic
is not achieved, as tangible securities subject to the condition that banks’ right to
receive annuities and toll collection rights is legally enforceable and irrevocable.
 In case of PPP projects, the debts due to the lenders has been allowed to be
considered as secured to the extent assured by the project authority in terms of the
Concession Agreement, subject to the following conditions:
(a) User charges/toll/tariff payments are kept in an escrow account where senior
lenders have priority over withdrawals by the concessionaire;
(b) There is sufficient risk mitigation, such as pre-determined increase in user
charges or increase in concession period, in case project revenues are lower
than anticipated;
(c) The lenders have a right of substitution in case of concessionaire default;
(d) The lenders have a right to trigger termination in case of default in debt
service; and;

17
e) Upon termination, the Project Authority has an obligation of (i) compulsory
buy-out and (ii) repayment of debt due in a pre-determined manner.
48. The Committee observes that initiatives taken by RBI recently has broaden the
scope for borrowers to get more funds on account of enhanced infrastructure finance.  It
is further heartening to note that banks have been allowed to treat annuities under BOT
model in respect of road projects and toll collection rights where there are provisions to
compensate the sponsor. Change of norms in PPP projects are also a welcome move where
debts due to the lenders has been allowed to be considered as secured. Lenders have got
first charge over escrow account and also a right of substitution of concessionaire if he
defaults.  The Committee hopes that these changes in existing models will help lenders and
it will pave the way for getting the stalled projects completed soon.
(c) Long Term Bonds
49. To ensure adequate credit flow to infrastructure sector and affordable housing needs of the
country by encouraging banks to optimally utilize the long-term financing avenues, Reserve Bank
in July 2014 allowed banks to issue long-term bonds with a minimum maturity of seven years to
raise resources for lending to these sectors. As an incentive, these bonds have been exempted from
the regulatory pre-emption of CRR and SLR requirement and including the credit made out of the
proceeds of the bonds in computation of ANBC.
50. The Committee feels that Bond is a potent weapon which can hit the required target
of getting fund from the market.  If, the maturity period is kept medium i.e. 5-7 years,
desired result could be achieved. The Committee appreciates the steps taken by RBI to
allow banks to go for credit flow through issuing bonds.  The Committee recommends that
the Government should strive for long term bonds for a period of 20 to 25 years to
commensurate with the concession period which may be able to achieve the set target.
(d) Financing of Cost Overruns in Project Loans
51. Internationally, project finance lenders sanction a ‘standby credit facility’ to fund cost
overruns if needed. Such ‘standby credit facilities’ are sanctioned at the time of initial financial
closure; but disbursed only when there is a cost overrun. Such ‘standby credit facilities’ may rank
paripassu with base project loans and their repayment schedule may also be the same as that of
the base project loans. Reserve Bank has also introduced a concept of ‘standby credit facility’ to
fund cost overruns. Accordingly, where banks have specifically sanctioned a ‘standby credit
facility’ at the time of initial financial closure to fund cost overruns banks they may fund cost
overruns as per the agreed terms and conditions. However, where the initial financial closure does
not envisage such financing of cost overruns, banks have been allowed to fund cost overruns,
which may arise on account of extension of Date of Commencement of Commercial Operations
(within the time limits of two years and one year for infrastructure and non-infrastructure project
loans respectively), without treating the loans as ‘restructured asset’ subject to certain conditions.
52. The Committee finds that the “Standby credit facility” is a very supportive tool for
borrower if this Clause has been taken into consideration during the initial financial closure
to fund the cost overruns.

have been set up by the Government to facilitate financing of Infra and road projects. India
Infrastructure Finance Co. Ltd (IIFCL) was set up in 2006 as a wholly owned GoI company and
as an NBFC-ND-IFC for providing long term finance, direct lending, Take-out finance, Credit
enhancement and refinance to other financing institutions. Similarly, National Investment and
Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) was set up recently as an Alternate Investment Fund (AIF) with an
initial corpus of `20,000 crore (49% from Government). In addition, Infrastructure Debt Funds
(IDFs) were set up under the private sector with active encouragement from the Government for
the purpose of taking over completed projects from the banks. Recently, the Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has proposed to set up a new dedicated financial institution for
financing highways and associated infrastructure or infuse further equity in the existing FIs.
54. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is involved in development of road
sector which is the life-line of the economy of the country.  It supervises projects worth
thousands of crores rupees but it does not have its own source or a mechanism of
generating revenue, although it gets budgetary support from the Government.  But, as we
know that much support is not sufficient.  The Committee recommends that RBI and
Ministry of Finance may help the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to set up their
own dedicated financial institutions to generate own funds for development of road sector.
(ii) Delays and disputes:  Highway and road projects get delayed, impacting the asset
quality of bank loans, due to various reasons, such as problems cited in para 20 ibid , litigations
by different parties, court orders stalling the project, problems in clearances from Ministry of
environment and other agencies, forest clearance, defence land handovers etc. RBI is seized of
these issues and has taken a number of regulatory steps to address the concerns arising from
impact of delays on such project loans. Recently, the Government has proposed to constitute a
High Powered Committee (HPC) on Infrastructure under the Chairmanship of Hon’ble Minister of
Finance for amicable resolution of highways related issues that cannot be resolved within the
existing framework provided in the Concession Agreement.
55. The Committee is aware of the reasons for delayed projects.  The Committee
recommends that before awarding the project to concessionaire, the Ministry should
complete the processes of getting land, environmental clearance, relocation  of utilities and
rehabilitation issues etc. Such problems not only delays the project but also enhances the
budget of the project.  The Committee notes that the lack of dispute resolution is one of
the major hurdles in clearing the stressed or delayed projects.  It is time consuming and
the cost involved is too much in the absence of a formal mechanism for dispute redressal.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government need to put in place a dispute
redressal mechanism for resolving the issues related to road project.
(iii) Intangible Nature of Securities: In case of road projects, while the assets created
are tangible, securities created in favour of banks by project authorities are mostly intangible in
nature. Such securities are assignments, rights to receive toll/annuities, etc. Taking into account the

19
requests of banks and Government, RBI has allowed loan to road projects against such intangible
securities to be treated as ‘secured’, subject to certain conditions .
56. The Committee appreciates the step taken by the RBI.  It is a morale booster for
the concessionaire.  But adequate cautions should be taken to ensure that the interests of
the financial institutions which have funded the project should be protected by all means.
View of Ministry of Finance on infrastructure lending
57. The Committee enquired from the  Ministry of Finance whether the Government is thinking
of coming out with some financial institutions for infrastructure lending, or only banks will do the
lending in the road sector.
58. On this question the representative of Ministry of Finance stated that earlier they used to
have, the ‘development financial institutions’, the DFIs.  So, at one point of time there were IFCI,
IDFC, IDBI, and so on.  Now, over the time, either these got converted into banks or they just
withered away.  So, today, the number of DFIs is actually very, very limited.  Only the EXIM Bank
in the export sector, and IIFCL, are there. But the fact is that to recreate those institutions which
had the capacity to take on long-term assets of 20-25 years in terms of financing is going to take
a considerably longer time. Because the kind of requirements that are there in terms of money, the
sheer quantum of money which is required because of a booming infrastructure sector, no single
institution will be able to handle it and, therefore, multiplicity is needed.  Bond market remains
shallow and it is difficult to tap the efficiencies which come out of corporates being able to raise
money outside the banking system.  Now, this is something which the Ministry of Finance is
conscious about.  So, the NIIF, which has recently been launched, looks at the equity side of
things, and the bond market is to be looked forward in consultation with the RBI.  The attempts
therefore, are to address the problems sectorally, rather than looking at one broad-brush solution
for the entire infrastructure sector.
59. Ministry of Finance further added that:-
“the solution would be, one is on the NIIF, which was announced in the last year’s
Budget.  The equity part is coming out through one of the sub-funds, which is on the
stress assets kind of situation, to be able to take equity positions.  Second, is on the
steps to be taken on the bond market side.  Securitization of receivables is one part
of it.  Ways are to be found out by which infusion of funds can come into such
projects, which do not affect the quality of the loan itself.  This would mean that
banks actually get back some money.  So, there are various options on which work
is going on.  It would still take some more time by which it could be presented in
such a way that it satisfies all the concerns of the stakeholders.  That is the direction
in which Ministry of Finance is moving”.
60. From the views of Ministry of Finance the Committee notes that although the
Ministry is taking various measurers to bring financial institutions into infrastructure
lending. The Committee however, does not find any concrete solution from the submission
of Ministry of Finance that the financial institution would come up in near future to rescue
the road sector.  Till the banks remain the sole lender, the situation will not improve
substantially.  The Committee recommends that Ministry of Finance should in consultation
with RBI, explore Bond Market more vigorously to generate money for the road sector.

61. The Committee was informed by NHAI that they have taken various measures to rectify the
problems affecting the road projects. Some of the initiatives are summarized below:-
(a) Project Preparation :-  Much of the issues affecting project execution and delayed
project execution, by hindsight, can be attributed to the fact that NHAI even before
completing its requirement related to conditions precedent had awarded projects.
This inordinate stress on awards without proper project preparation has been
detrimental to the interest of the road sector as a whole. NHAI has decided not to
award projects until all regulatory approvals are obtained for the project and the
required land is available in possession to avoid post-bid delays and litigations.
(b) In the matter of Environment and Forest clearance, after NHAI moved the
Supreme Court, in March 2013 MoEF changed their policy which addressed all of
NHAI’s concerns.
(c) Society for Affordable Redressal of Disputes: It was found that the arbitration
process, through which all unresolved disputes were tried to be resolved, was
proving to be far too expensive and also highly time consuming. Hence NHAI in
association with NHBF formed a society for speedy and affordable redressal of
disputes.  This society is called as Society for Affordable Redressal of Disputes
(SAROD)registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860.  Builders/Contractors are
the Primary members and Consultants have been made as associate members.
Mainly qualified technocrats of highway sector have been empanelled as arbitrators.
It is intended that time bound completion of arbitration proceedings will now be
possible.
62. The Committee appreciates the corrective steps taken by NHAI.  The Committee
feels that NHAI should learn from its past experience.  Many of the projects got held up
due to bad-planning and showing haste in awarding the projects to developers.  The
Committee recommends that before awarding any project to concessionaire the project
should be technically examined, cost be estimated and all the clearness, viz. statutory,
environment and forest, railways etc. may be obtained first.
DISPUTE RESOLUTION
63. The Ministry submitted that the item rate  EPC awards which was used for project awards
for much of the GQ and part of the corridor has left NHAI with unsettled claims amounting to
more than `18,000 crs.  While much of these are inflated claims, the process of dispute resolution

which these disputes can be quickly resolved. Hence NHAI created a mechanism for speedy
resolution of long pending disputes. A tribunal was formed headed by a retired High Court justice,

st  March 2015 resolved 84
packages for a value of ` 17,524 crs, settling these for an amount of ` 1,404 crs.  The balance

64. The Committee recommends that unsettled claims may be settled speedily and it
should be ensured that while settling  the claims due diligence may be taken of the project,
against which the claim has to be settled. Adequate measures should be taken to ensure
that unscrupulous elements do not swindle away the Government money.
(d) Loans to Highway projects classified as “secured” by Lenders:- Unsecured loans
are generally considered as relatively riskier and hence banks limit their exposure on
unsecured loans to 15 to 20% of their debt portfolio. Given the high risk perception
such unsecured loans also carry higher interest rates. At NHAI’s initiative, Reserve
Bank of India has directed a policy shift that the Financial Institutions now should
consider loans to Highway projects as secured to the extent covered by termination
payment provisions under the Concession Agreements. Due to this changed
classification, road sector projects would now be able to access debt funds from
a larger pool for secured loans (as against the restricted pool available for unsecured
loans) and also get the benefit of lesser interest rates.
65. The Committee feels that this policy shift is a wise decision by the RBI,  which has
allowed financial institutions to consider loans to Highways projects as secured to the extent
covered by termination payment provisions under the concession agreement.  The
Committee hopes that interest rates also will come down accordingly in such case.
66. Steps taken by the Ministry for revival of Stalled Projects:
(a) Securitization of future cash flows in BOT Projects:
67. With a view to ameliorate the shortage of equity and improve liquidity of the prospective
bidder, NHAI board has approved granting of permission by NHAI to the Concessionaires of PPP

subordinate loan on the strength of future surplus cash flows of their operational BOT Road
projects.
(b) Premium Deferment in stressed projects:
68. To salvage the stressed projects, the Government has allowed restructuring of premiums
committed by Concessionaires during the bid stage in Highway projects for the awarded projects.
Such a renegotiation is permitted only once through the life of the Concession.
(c) Harmonious Substitution in Financially stressed projects:
69. In view of the difficulties being faced by the Concessionaire in PPP projects Government
has decided to permit substitution of existing Concessionaire or the selected bidder/consortium
member of such project SPV in a harmonious manner. An event of financial default will include
situations where the Authority and/or the senior lenders have reason to apprehend in their
considered opinion that the concessionaire is likely to face financial stress and is likely to default
in the compliance of the terms of the Concession Agreement.
(d) One time fund infusion to revive and physically complete languishing BOT projects:
70. For any languishing highway project in BOT (Toll /Annuity) mode that has achieved at least
50% physical completion and it is also established that infusion of moderate funding can quickly

bring this project to completion, NHAI will provide financial assistance in the form of a loan at
bank rate + 2% subject to first charge on the Toll/Annuity receivables of these projects.
(e) 100% equity divestment after two years of construction completion for all BOT
projects irrespective of year of award:
71. This would facilitate concessionaires to invest in:
(i) complete National Highways Authority of India projects;
(ii) any other highways projects;
(iii) to retire their debts to Financial institutions in any other infrastructure projects.
(iv) Authorizing NHAI for rationalized compensation to Concessionaires in case of delays
not attributable to Concessionaires for languishing highway projects on BOT mode:
72. The Committee observes that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways have

77. The Committee is concerned to note that the concessionaire is short of equity and
the bankers are also not disbursing the sanctioned loan.  The Committee fails to understand

a point, obtaining additional debt is certainly difficult.  The Committee recommends that

78. The Secretary, Ministry of Road, Transport and Highways who appeared before the
Committee, submitted that during 2010-12, a large number of road projects were awarded and it
was primarily on BoT Toll Model because that was the default mode at that point of time.  The

peculiar to the individual projects.  The Committee recommends that these projects may be

Problems associated with toll collections:
 Transition from EPC to BOT:  Most BOT project operators are companies that
have evolved from EPC contractors into BOT concessionaires just because of their
experience in constructing mega road projects. However, these companies had either
no knowledge or very basic knowledge of tolling when they entered the tolling
business. Awareness is now dawning upon them that tolling is a very technical and
complex activity and many varied factors contribute towards its success.
 Unwillingness to pay toll:  Road users feel this service should be provided free by
the Government as they are already paying taxes.
 Support from local authorities:  The concept of BOT projects is not understood
by the lower levels of administration with whom the concessionaires have to deal
with on a daily basis.
 Pilferage:  According to a rough assessment, toll pilferage on ill managed plazas can
be as high as 25%. Even a momentary failure of toll IT system can result in
considerable toll pilferages.
 Detours:  With wide-spread development of roads, taking a toll detour has become
a standard practice by most road users. In a large number of concession
agreements, there are no safeguards like check plazas. Thus, to avoid loss of toll
collections, choosing the correct location for the plaza becomes critical.
 Political interference:  This generally commences from protests against land
acquisition and finally culminates in obstruction of tolling activities. Explicit clauses
for addressing the issue of disruption of tolling activities needs to be included in the
agreements. The present, ‘Force Majeure’ clause, does not provide adequate
safeguards due to the lengthy time stipulations. Toll plazas are usually the target of
political agitation in the near vicinity culminating in impacting toll operations.
 Unauthorised exemptions:  A large percentage of exemptions consists of road users
who have to be necessarily exempted in order to ensure smooth and unhindered
tolling operations. These road users have the potential to create problems.

sort out the issues such as unwillingness of the public to pay toll, pilferage of toll, political

grant permission to quarry and mines.  They have also complained that there was a hurry
in awarding the projects without any due diligence which resulted in stalling of the projects
and the promoters leaving mid way.  In many of the cases, the promoters are forming their
equity on the basis of the loan taken from the financial institutions which results in failure
of the projects.  The banks are typically encouraged to raise money for a period of 5 to 7
years whereas the need of the infrastructure industry is for a longer period of 20 to 25
years. This is acting as a blockage in the entire infrastructure lending.  Development of
long time bonds is also an option which can be experimented for financing the projects.  In
the present regulatory scenario, the insurance funds and the pension funds are not
permitted to fund the infrastructure projects.  An easing of the regulations may help the
industry as a whole.  Another suggestion was that the concessionaires may be given an exit
clause if they want to.  NHAI informed the Committee that out of the 150 projects in the
PPP mode during the period 2006-12, only 16 projects were stalled and many of these were
due to land acquisition problems, utility shifting, delay in granting permission by the local
authorities and delay in giving in formal clearances and various approvals.  The
representatives of the RBI informed the Committee that the Government is seized of the
matter and they are contemplating to ease many of the guidelines applicable to the banks
for infrastructure lending. (Para 35)
The overall impression created by the banks is that along with public funding there
should be private participation for the growth of the Indian economy. Highway projects need
to be completed in time within the estimated cost.  It was also pointed out that the held-
up projects should be started immediately and banks and financial institutions may be
sufficiently compensated for the NPAs created by them by lending to the infrastructure
sector. (Para 36)
The Committee was also informed that the model concession agreement of NHAI is
not acceptable to the banks and it need to be restructured in a way that the banks should
not end up in accumulating NPAs. (Para 37)
The Committee recommends that the model concession agreement may be circulated
to all the banks and the financial institutions and the input and feedback received from
them may be incorporated appropriately.  Every effort may be made to ease out the bad
debts.  It is good that the RBI has already taken steps for converting debts into equity and
the contractors are allowed to get out of the projects in case of a default.  Need for higher
Government allocation is also emphasised  and the banks NPAs may be supported by
Government allocation.  Making the recovery of bad debts easier by empowering the bank
adequately should be considered. For example  in case of a default, the banks may be
allowed to take over the entire company.  The Committee was informed that as of now,
there is a total NPAs of `````2,60,000 crores due to defaulting infrastructure projects.  By the
end of 2015-16, it is estimated that it may go up to more than 4 lakh crore.  The banks’
demanded that the money of the loan given to the road sector  to be allowed to be
restructured for a longer duration may be considered along with proposal for making
adequate provisions in the model concession agreement to for the cost escalation of the

31
projects.  In case of time overrun due to the reasons which are beyond the control of the
promoters the projects may be re-assessed and the project cost may be refixed accordingly
also needs to be seriously considered for adoption. (Para 38)
CBI AND VIGILANCE
The Committee finds it bizarre that the banks work under the fear of CBI and CVC.
The Committee recommends that the banks should take a decision on its own whether a
particular NPA is to be financed or not and it should be done on the bank’s own wisdom
and under the permissible capacity of the banks.  The Committee also suggests that the
bank should see viability of the project i.e. whether lending some more money will give
their due returns. The Committee recommends that every decision if taken in a transparent
way and approved by a Committee consisting of more than two officials based on laid down
principles, there should not be any cause for fear of investigation by CVC, CBI and other
enforcement agencies. (Para 40)
RESTRUCTURING OF LOANS
The Committee finds a disconnect between views of NHAI and RBI because RBI has
said that continuous repeated restructuring is not restructuring and it is also not considered
as NPA, then the problems prohibiting NHAI on this issue, have to be sorted out by NHAI
itself.    The Committee suggests that NHAI resolve this issue with the Banks under the
guidance of RBI. (Para 45)
The Committee observes that initiatives taken by RBI recently has broaden the
scope for borrowers to get more funds on account of enhanced infrastructure finance.  It
is further heartening to note that banks have been allowed to treat annuities under BOT
model in respect of road projects and toll collection rights where there are provisions to
compensate the sponsor. Change of norms in PPP projects are also a welcome move where
debts due to the lenders has been allowed to be considered as secured. Lenders have got
first charge over escrow account and also a right of substitution of concessionaire if he
defaults.  The Committee hopes that these changes in existing models will help lenders and
it will pave the way for getting the stalled projects completed soon. (Para 48)
(d) LONG TERM BONDS
The Commi ttee feels that Bond is a potent weapon which can hit the required
target of getting fund from the market. If, the maturity period is kept medium i.e.
5-7 years, desired result could be achieved. The Committee appreciates the steps taken
by RBI to allow banks to go for credit flow through issuing bonds. The Committee
recommends that the Government should strive for long term bonds for a period of 20 to
25 years to commensurate with the concession period which may be able to achieve the
set target. (Para 50)
(e) FINANCING OF COST OVERRUNS IN PROJECT LOANS
The Committee finds that the “Standby credit facility” is a very supportive tool for
borrower if this Clause has been taken into consideration during the initial financial closure
to fund the cost overruns. (Para 52)

32
ISSUES RELATED TO INFRASTRUCTURE LENDING IN HIGHWAYS
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is involved in development of road
sector which is the life-line of the economy of the country.  It supervises projects worth
thousands of crores rupees but it does not have its own source or a mechanism of
generating revenue, although it gets budgetary support from the Government.  But, as
we know that much support is not sufficient.  The Committee recommends that RBI and
Ministry of Finance may help the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to set up
their own dedicated financial institutions to generate own funds for development of road
sector. (Para 54)
The Committee is aware of the reasons for delayed projects. The Committee
recommends that before awarding the project to concessionaire, the Ministry should
complete the processes of getting land, environmental clearance, relocation  of utilities and
rehabilitation issues etc. Such problems not only delays the project but also enhances the
budget of the project.  The Committee notes that the lack of dispute resolution is one of
the major hurdles in clearing the stressed or delayed projects.  It is time consuming and
the cost involved is too much in the absence of a formal mechanism for dispute redressal.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government need to put in place a dispute
redressal mechanism for resolving the issues related to road project. (Para 55)
The Committee apprecia tes the step taken by the RBI. It is a morale booster for
the concessionaire.  But adequate cautions should be taken to ensure that the interests
of the financial institutions which have funded the project should be protected by all
means. (Para 56)
VIEW OF MINISTRY OF FINANCE ON INFRASTRUCTURE LENDING
From the views of Ministry of Finance the Committee notes that although the
Ministry is taking various measurers to bring financial institutions into infrastructure
lending. The Committee however, does not find any concrete solution from the submission
of Ministry of Finance that the financial institution would come up in near future to
rescue the road sector.  Till the banks remain the sole lender, the situation will not
improve substantially.  The Committee recommends that Ministry of Finance should in
consultation with RBI, explore Bond Market more vigorously to generate money for the
road sector. (Para 60)
The Committee appreciates the corrective steps taken by NHAI.  The Committee
feels that NHAI should learn from its past experience.  Many of the projects got held up
due to bad-planning and showing haste in awarding the projects to developers.  The
Committee recommends that before awarding any project to concessionaire the project
should be technically examined, cost be estimated and all the clearness, viz. statutory,
environment and forest, railways etc. may be obtained first. (Para 62)
DISPUTE RESOLUTION
The Committee recommends that unsettled claims may be settled speedily and it
should be ensured that while settling  the claims due diligence may be taken of the project,

33
against which the claim has to be settled. Adequate measures should be taken to ensure
that unscrupulous elements do not swindle away the Government money. (Para 64)
The Committee feels that this policy shift is a wise decision by the RBI,  which has
allowed financial institutions to consider loans to Highways projects as secured to the extent
covered by termination payment provisions under the concession agreement. The Committee
hopes that interest rates also will come down accordingly in such case. (Para 65)
The Committee observes that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways have
taken certain steps to strengthen the construction work in road sector.  The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should keep eye on toll collection and channelize the surplus
money towards stressed projects. (Para 72)
STATUTORY CLEARANCE
The Ministry has informed the Committee that the picture on land acquisition front
is more clear now and it has become easier to acquire land from its owners.  Environmental
clearances are also given in a shorter period. (Para 76)
The Committee is concerned to note that the concessionaire is short of equity and
the bankers are also not disbursing the sanctioned loan.  The Committee fails to understand
the intention of bankers.  NHAI too has defaulted in fulfillment of its conditions and has
failed in many cases for acquiring land, environment clearance, utility shifting etc.  The
Committee may be apprised of the reasons for not fulfilling the requirement by the NHAI.
The Committee also finds that insistence of NHAI for the first change on toll/annuity in the
project which is 50% completed is not practical.  The Committee recommends that NHAI
should offer its help to complete the half built project rather then claiming rights of
collecting revenue.  The Committee recommends that the NHAI may pay full attention to
its duty towards extending all facilities /help to concessionaire in completing the projects.
The Committee notes that if there is a delay in construction from any sides, whether it is
NHAI or concessionaire, the cost of interest is going to be high and if it reaches beyond
a point, obtaining additional debt is certainly difficult.  The Committee recommends that
delay from both sides may be avoided so that already infused in incomplete project does not
turn into NPA. The Committee notes that the Government and its agencies are under
pressure of various limitations imposed by the systemic rules and rigidity in financial
regulations. The Committee recommends that the Government should have relook at the
various rules and regulations from the overall perspective to ensuring that road
construction is completed in time. This is not to say that those misusing the financial
system should not be punished and brought to book. (Para 77)
The Committee noted observations of the Secretary and recommends that the
Government should thoroughly inquire into all the 77 projects which were languishing in
2014 to understand the quantum of money siphoned away by the unscrupulous contractors
in connivance with various agencies of the Government and financial institutions. The
quantum of money lost should be quantified and action should be taken to recover the lost
money and a report to this effect may be submitted to the Committee. (Para 82)

34
The Committee notes that there were an economic downtown that took place in the
last 3 or 4 years and as we are slowly coming out of this, there is a possibility to use the
infrastructure in construction sector as one of the major vehicles for revival of the
economy.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the BoT Toll should not be the sole
model for awarding the road projects. The Committee recommends that each project length
has to be analysed and examined on its merits and demerits depending on the revenue
streams that are possible and determine whether it should be taken up on BoT Toll or BoT
annuity or on EPC Model. (Para 83)
The Committee notes that the Government has allocated a huge budget for the
road sector but this excessive flow of Government money cannot sustain over a long
run.  The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Government to devise ways and means
and establish appropriate financial institutions and models to encourage the return of
the private investment to the road sector. The Committee notes that the new hybrid
annuity scheme introduced by the Government is attracting many players in the field
but the Committee feels that the players are the same during the various models over
a period of time.  Therefore, the Government needs to be over cautious and what has
happened to the PPP Model in the past, should not be repeated in case of Hybrid Annuity
Projects also. (Para 84)
Yet another complaint the Committee received during its interaction with various
stake holders is that the NHAI typically underestimates the project costs and the
concessionaires who bid out a project on L1 basis approaches banks and financial
institutions with an inflated project cost for taking loans.  The Committee observes that
NHAI should be realistic while calculating the total project cost (TPC) so that the
concessionaire may not get opportunity to project the inflated cost and obtain loans from
the financial institutions in a nefarious way.  The Committee believes that the total project
cost should be realistic irrespective of the model of the project. (Para 85)
The Committee wants to know the issues on which 19 projects are yet to be solved.
The Committee recommends that the impending issues may be solved at the earliest and
the projects should be completed in minimum time period.  The Committee is aware of the
fact that each of the project will have its own peculiarities and problems specific to it.
Therefore, the Committee notes that solution to the problems will also be specific and
peculiar to the individual projects.  The Committee recommends that these projects may be
infused fund by all means so that the languishing projects which are presently NPAs could
be made viable by incurring just limited expenditure keeping in view the broader national
interest in mind. (Para 86)
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE PROJECT COST ESTIMATED BY NHAI AND BANKS
The Committee finds its strange as to how the concessionaire who has got a project
for `````1,000 crore gets `````1,400 crores for the same project.  The NHAI has submitted that the
bank does their own calculation.  The Committee wants to know why there is a big gap
between the cost calculated by NHAI and the bank for the same project?  The Committee
further would like to know whether there is any discussion between NHAI and banks

35
regarding estimation cost for a particular project after awarding the project to a
concessionaire?  Why the concessionaire has been given a free hand to get the banks’ loan
as per their wish?  The Committee recommends that the NHAI  should keep a watch over
the excess loan amount over the estimated cost obtained by the concessionaire from the
bank. The Committee recommends that the TPC arrived at by the NHAI should be the
project cost for all purposes. If at any time the Banks, Financial Institutions or
concessionaires feel that the TPC need to be revised then they should approach NHAI for
the purpose and NHAI can do it in a transparent way, wherever required. The conditions
under which TPC can be revised should be specifically laid down. (Para 88)
TOLL COLLECTION
The Committee recommends that the Government should take adequate measures
to sort out the issues such as unwillingness of the public to pay toll, pilferage of toll,
political interference in the functioning of toll booths and unauthorized exemptions at toll
plazas. (Para 91)
MAINTENANCE AND OTHER AMENITIES AT HIGHWAYS
The Committee feels that   construction of road is a difficult job but to maintain it
is rather more difficult.  It is a proven fact that condition of road goes from bad to worse
in a very short period.  The Committee was informed that for maintenance and repair, the
budget allocated in `````2834 crore for the financial year 2016-17 which meets only 60% of
total requirement.  Ministry further submits that maintenance being a non-plan activity
there is also a tendency by the Government to apply adhoc cuts in the face of resource
constrains. (Para 92)
The Committee finds that with this budgetary provision, the Ministry is not giving
adequate attention to maintenance and repair of highways.  The Committee recommends
that the maintenance upkeep of the roads should be given higher priority and a higher
allocation be made at RE stage. (Para 93)
ROAD SAFETY
Road safety is a major issue in view of increasing road accidents throughout the
country.  There are many factors responsible for it.  According to one report inputs given
by National Crime Records Bureau, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, there are 4.5
lakhs road accidents annually causing 1.4 lakhs death and 4.8 lakhs injured.  It’s a sad face
of our development. The Committee feels that there may be many reasons for road
accidents, but road is also a factor.  Road’s faulty design, pot holes, absence of signage and
speed breaker, blind turn always cause accidents. (Para 94)
The Committee insists that road design and its maintenance may be given top
priority. If road is maintained properly, the chances of accidents minimizes. (Para 95)
The Committee also recommends that utilizing a part of petrol and diesel Cess on
Road Safety may seriously be considered. (Para 96)

36
MEDICAL FACILITIES AT HIGHWAYS
The Committee has discussed the availability of medical facilities to accident victims
on highways with the Ministry.  The Committee recommends that the trauma centres  may
be opened at every 40-50 Km. on a highway  and ambulance should be made available to
accident victims.  It has been experienced that after an accident many lives could be saved
by giving them medical aid during golden hour.  Every road accident victim should be given
required medical treatment at nearest place whether they are insured or not. (Para 97)
Besides medical facilities, the Committee recommends that places of public amenities
like restaurants, toilets, petrol pump etc. may be opened at reasonable distance so that
commuters should not face any difficulty. (Para 98)
The Committee notes that every company registered under companies Act is bound
to allocate and spend a portion of their profit for Corporate Social Responsibility. The
Committee recommends that the road safety should be included as an area for spending the
money from the Corporate Social Responsibility. Providing Ambulance, hospitals, emergency
services, public amenities such as toilet complexes, etc. can be included in the CSR
activities of the companies. In this regard, the Committee recommends that the Ministry
of Road Transport and Highways should take up this issue at the appropriate level to
implement it. (Para 99)

(iii) Regulatory mechanism by RBI for lending to the infrastructure projects in road sector.
3. First of all Shri Ritabrata Banerjee, Member of the Committee raised the issue of four months delay
in submitting the replies by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to the queries raised by Members
in the meeting held on 1st October, 2015. On this issue Secretary, Road Transport and Highways apologized
to the Committee and ensured that such delay would not happen in future.
4. The Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways informed the Committee that earlier there
were problems with PPP model in road sector but now the situation has improved. He further added that
private sector is now showing interest in BOT Toll Projects. He stated that hybrid annuity projects have a
bright future and that positive response has started coming. On land acquisition and environment clearance,

47
he informed the Committee that the situation has improved. States are also co-operating vis-a-vis statutory
clearances.
5. The Secretary in his submission further added that the Ministry has now a single window system
for the road sector. The Cabinet has delegated substantial powers to the Ministry for sanction of projects.
6. A power point presentation was given by the Ministry on the subject. The Chairman raised the issue
or lacking of co-ordination between NHAI and Banks and offered the role of the Committee towards solving
the problems raced by the road sector. The Chairman also pointed out towards a big difference in the total
value assessed by the NHAI and the concessionaires for some of the projects.
7. A power point presentation was then made by the NHAI. After presentation Chairman, NHAI submitted
that Banks are reluctant to consider the funds generated by the concessionaire by securitization of future
cash flows of completed projects and that they were not ready to treat that as equity for other road projects.
8. The Chairman then allowed Deputy Governor, RBI to clarify the points raised by the Chairman,
NHAI on banks’ about their reluctance to further lend in ongoing projects. Deputy Governor apprised the
Committee that every bank has got its own risk appetite based on its financial strength. It is upto the bank to
take extra risk or not while lending to any sector. RBI has put no bar on the banks.
9. Chairman, NHAI gave an account of such projects which are of an amount of less than ` 500 crores
needed for restructuring of infrastructure loans which are allowed only for loan accounts more than ` 500
crores. He opined that lowering the threshold will assist small projects to start servicing the debt and provide
relief to the concerned banks in recovering loans.
10. Deputy Governor, RBI further elaborated that bank funds are for short term finance and not for long
term. Banks have increased funding from 2 lakh crores to ` l 0 lakh crores in last 7-8 years. He submitted
that if bank starts giving ` 200 crores or less amount, then they will not get the required generation of funds.
Deputy Governor, RBI agreed to look into the matter whether it is possible for the banks to lend more and
more funds for longer period.
11. Chairman, NHAI advocated for treating road sector as priority sector for the sake of social and rural
development, as a measure of social justice, bringing about equality and women empowerment but Deputy
Governor submitted before the Committee that if major loan is sanctioned to roads only then the other
smaller sector would suffer and further added that without priority sector label, road sector is getting 16 per
cent of total funds.
12. Chairman, NHAI submitted that loan accounts having an interest or scheduled payment overdue for
more than 90 days turns to NPAs and once the promoter turns as NPA. it is not possible for him to secure
loans from other banks and financial institutions. He requested RBI to relax PA norm from 90 to 180 days.
Committee was informed that India is a signatory to Basel Convention and they cannot break this rule; or
else bank’s rating will go down and Letter of Credits (LCs) will not be accepted internationally and there will
be a higher cost for raising the funds overseas.
13. Executive Director, Punjab National Bank submitted that Public Sector Banks come under the purview
of CVC and CBI and they are under the fear that if they finance NPA account, these agencies may doubt
their integrity and that is the reason why the banks are reluctant to lend for NPA. Deputy Governor further
added that if Banks feel safe in financing NPA, they can do it. Restructuring of loan under 5/25 is permissible
and it is not considered NPA. On cost escalation, he added that 10 per cent is allowed as a normal one and

48
beyond that it is problem loan. 10 per cent is at third stage because at first level the automatic price escalation
clause is there and at second level funded interest loan.
14. Joint Secretary, Ministry of Finance informed the Committee that earlier there were Development
Financial Institutions (DFls) viz., IFCI, IDFC, IOBI etc; but today they have got converted into Banks and
such new Financial Institutions will take longer time to become functional. He emphasized to improve the
bond market in consultation with RBI and also looking for other means to support the road sector.
15. The Secretary informed the Committee that the number of languishing projects has come down to
19 at present. Members raised various issues related to the subject in various parts of the country and gave
some suggestions also. Deputy Governor, RBI suggested that if a project is ready by 80 or 85 per cent and
some problem has arisen due to some reasons, then the completed segment may be opened for use and then
the bank will not consider it as an NPA.
16. The Chairman and Members of the Committee raised different queries and these were answered by
the concerned officers. Chairman allowed the Ministry to send the replies of unanswered questions in 10
days.
17. A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept.
18. The meeting was adjourned at 5.35 
P.M.
