REPORT 
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the 
observations/recommendations as contained in its Two Hundred and Thirtieth Report on “Issues 
related to Security at airports in India” which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 
21st December, 2015. 
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on the 21st June, 2016 in 
respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. The replies have been 
categorized as follows:– 
(i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government: 
 
Paragraph Nos:- 104, 105 and 110 Total: 3 
(ii) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of 
the Government replies: 
Paragraph Nos:-   101, 102, 103, 109 and 111 Total: 5 
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been 
accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos:- Nil Total: Nil 
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are still 
awaited. 
Paragraph Nos: 49, 54, 63, 64, 65, 66, 85, 86, 90, 95, 96, 97, 100, 106, 107 and 108 Total: 16 
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of those recommendations/observations 
which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished at the earliest. 
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each 
item of Action Taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry. The recommendations of the Committee  
contained in the Two Hundred and Thirtieth Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and 
recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the  
succeeding paragraphs: 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
5. The Committee condemns the violent incident at Karipur Airport. The Committee demands 
that the Government should ensure that such incidents do not occur in future. The Committee 
notes that six months is more than sufficient time to complete the investigation. The Committee 
recommends that the investigations may be completed at the earliest and the guilty may be 
punished. Findings of investigations may be shared with this Committee as soon as it is submitted. 
(Para 49) 
 
1 

2 
 
Reply of the Government 
6. As regards the incident happened at Karipur Airport, Kozhikode, 13 CISF personnel and 15 
AAI staff were arrested, who are under bail. Four FIRs were registered against AAI staff and CISF  
Personnel. Out of the total 4 cases registered in the matter, investigations in to 2 (two) cases have 
been completed. Investigations in the remaining two cases are near completion. Kerala Police has 
been requested to expedite their investigation and submit the final report to this Ministry, urgently. 
However, the details of the measures taken subsequent to the Kozhikode airport incident are as 
under:- 
➢ ADG/APS held a meeting with Member (Ops), AAI and Director Security, AAI. 
They were assured that Zonal DIGs have been directed to ensure there is smooth 
inter agency co-ordination and functioning of airport operations. Zonal DIGs have 
been asked to visit airport extensively, have meeting with stakeholders, address the 
men and ensure that there is no friction to ensure smooth airport operations. 
➢ Addl. DG, Airport Sector visited Calicut Airport to take stock of the situation and 
also met Addl. DG (Law & Order), Kerala Police. 
➢ During the visit, ADG/APS informed Regional Executive Director, AAI  and Airport  
Director, Kozhikode airport about necessary measures to ensure that there is no 
friction between CISF and the other stake holders during the mandated course of 
duty, so that airport operations are not happened. 
➢ All Chief Airport Security Officers have been directed that it is their bounden duty to 
ensure that there is no source of friction amongst the stake holders and that they 
should take proactive and corrective measures, if there is any problem. 
➢ Supervisory officers have visited all airports with a view to ascertain and resolve inter-
agency friction, if any. 
➢ Instructions have been issued to all formations to be courteous during the mandated 
tasks of security which should be followed in letter and spirit. 
➢ A special drive to have refresher courses in soft skill training for CISF personnel, 
deployed at airports has been initiated. So far, 21, 604 no. of persons have been 
trained from 03.08.2015. 
➢ Motivational tasks are being delivered to the personnel of all ASGs. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
7. The Committee notes that the violent incident in Karipur, Kozhikode airport was a 
serious issue. However, the Government and various security agencies did not take   it  
seriously. Even after a long lapse of time the police agencies failed to complete the 
investigations and bring the guilty to book. The Committee recommends that   the   guilty  
should be punished and the amount of loss occurred due to the rampage by officials should 
be recovered from the salary of concerned officials after conducting an enquiry   in   this  
regard by an appropriate authority. The Committee desires that the investigation in the 
remaining two cases should be expedited and that the final report should be submitted 
without delay. 

3 
 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
8. The Committee noted the suggested co-ordination mechanisms and hope that it will be 
implemented soon to prevent any loopholes in the security apparatus. 
(Para 54) 
Reply of the Government 
9. The following committees are in existence for co-ordination on the matter of security 
aspects at airports:- 
(i) Standing Committee for reviewing security arrangements at airports with   Secretary 
–Home as Chairman with  Secretary MOCA, Director, IB, DG, CISF, Commissioner,  
BCAS Chairman, AAI as members and Addl. Secretary (LWE) as members 
Secretary. To meet on quarterly basis. 
(ii) National level Facilitation Committee chaired by Cabinet Secretary. 
(iii) Facilitation committee at Airport level. 
(iv) Airport Security Committee (APSC) at airport level. 
Zonal level and Sector level committees of CISF are also there. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
10. The Committee  takes  note of the reply  and hopes  that the mechanism  will  
strengthen the security apparatus at the airports. The Committee may be apprised of the 
details of the meetings held by the Co-ordination Committee during   the   last   one   year  
period. 
Recommendations/Observations of   the   Committee 
11. The Committee expresses its serious concern over the grey area and security related 
problems as mentioned by Delhi Police. It is equally appalled to see the existing interface between 
the Delhi Police and DIAL in  respect of security related issues at the Airport. It reflects a lack of 
mutual confidence in one another as well as required co-ordination between the two. Otherwise, 
Delhi Police, instead of taking up these issues with the Parliamentary Committee and DIAL giving point-
wise clarification before it, the two should have mutually resolved them. BCAS and the Ministries of 
Civil Aviation and Home Affairs also appeared to have remained unconcerned in this regard. IGI Airport 
being one of the most sensitive Airport in the existing security scenario, such gaps are sure to lead 
to any disaster at any time. 
(Para 63) 
Reply of the Government 
 
12. Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), an attached office of this Ministry formed a 
Facilitation Committee at airport level to resolve the issues between Delhi Police and DIAL. In 
addition, a meeting of Airport Security Committee (APSC) is held on monthly basis. 
13. A meeting was also held to resolve the issues of CISF and airport operator and have better 

4 
 
coordination, in the meeting, it is decided that BCAS should review the requirement of the gadgetry 
and authorize the same. Based on authorization, airport operator will provide gadgetry. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
14. The Committee notes the various concerns expressed by the Delhi Police as regards the 
security at Delhi International Airport. The  committee observes that the issues are very serious and 
need immediate attention of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Home Affairs and various other 
stakeholders involved. The Committee recommends that all the issues need to be considered for 
immediate redressal and status note be submitted to the Committee containing steps taken in these 
regards. 
(Para 64) 
Reply of the Government 
15. ED (Security), DIAL was communicated to resolve the issues raised by Delhi Police. Other 
aspects as mentioned at Para 63 above. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
16. The Committee recently visited the Delhi airport and noticed that the situation 
prevailing earlier has not changed as far as the points raised by the Delhi Police are 
concerned. The Committee notices an element of apathy by the agencies involved such as 
the DIAL, Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Home Affairs as far as the grievances 
of Delhi Police are concerned. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the points 
raised by the Delhi Police should be taken seriously and resolved at the earliest. The 
Committee may be apprised of the specific steps taken to resolve the issues between DIAL 
and the Delhi Police and the outcome thereof. The Committee desires that time bound 
action should be taken to resolve these issues. 
17. During further interaction with all the involved agencies, the Committee could learn 
that the hotels at the aerocity are a potential security threat to the runway and the airport. 
The Committee is of the view that all the hotels in the aerocity should be considered as 
equally important as any other airport asset.   However,   the   Committee   learnt   that   the  
access to the hotels inside the aerocity are being managed by the private security guards. 
The security at these hotels should be given utmost importance because unknown persons 
are accessing such points. Considering the strategic importance of the hotels which are so 
nearby to the functional runway, the Committee recommends that   CISF  should   be   the  
default security agency for all the access points to the   hotels   in   the   aerocity.   The 
Committee also recommends that since the hotels are a separate business, the payments for 
the deployment of CISF security may be borne by the hotels themselves. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
18. As regards payment of rent and electricity charges by Delhi Police to DIAL for space 
occupied by them and signing of License Agreement, the committee recommends that the Ministry 
of Home Affairs may take immediate decision in those matters as the Delhi Police is under that 
Ministry, discharging sovereign function of maintenance of security in and around the IGIA. 
(Para 65) 

5 
 
Reply of the Government 
19. As per Operations, Maintenance and Development Agreement (OMDA) all Government 
agencies, including Delhi Police had to be pay these charges as per the rates fixed. MHA has 
requested DIAL to waive off ` 46.1 lakhs as electricity charges.   DIAL has suggested for signing 
of an agreement by Delhi Police. Matter under consideration. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
20. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that Delhi Police is doing the 
sovereign function and they should not be charged for basic facilities provided to them. The 
Committee may be apprised of the progress made in this regard. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
21. As regards providing space to the Delhi Police in the Delhi International Airport, the 
Committee directs the Ministry of Home Affairs to find out a workable solution in consultation with 
the Ministry of Civil Aviation and BCAS to provide an adequate space to discharge their sovereign 
duty of security in the International Airport at Delhi. 
(Para 66) 
Reply of the Government 
 
22. MHA has Approved during the current plan period a proposal of Delhi Police for 
construction of Police Station and DCP office at IGI Airport at an estimated cost of ` 20.93 crore. 
It has been intimated by Delhi Police that 90% work has been completed and remaining 
construction work is expected to be completed shortly. 
Further Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
23. The Committee takes note of the reply and desires that it may be informed of the 
progress made in this regard. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
24. The Committee finds it pertinent that the issue of encroachment of airport land and 
adjoining hillock by slum dwellers is settled at the earliest. In this regard, the Committee took note 
of the replies furnished by MIAL and the Housing Department Government of Maharashtra on 
various aspects of the encroachment. The Committee observes that the 35 pockets of slums in 
airport and the slums hillock along the Mithi River are potential threat to the aircrafts and the CSIA 
airport. The problems are persisting for the last so many years. The Committee feels that the 
Governmental agencies, both at the Centre and the State level, could not rationally judge the menace 
of slums inside the airport area as a potential security threat. Mumbai is the commercial capital of 
the country. Any breach of security at the airport will have far reaching consequences. The threat 
is perennial and no amount of policing could provide adequate security to the airport if the slums 
are allowed to exist and flourish inside the airport. The committee feels that the Government 
agencies are happily unconcerned about the airport security at CSIA, Mumbai. In Mumbai 
International Airport, a disaster is waiting to happen at any moment in view of these dangerously 
placed encroachments overlapping operational areas, of the Mumbai Airport. The Committee calls 

6 
 
upon all the agencies such as AAI, Ministry of Civil Aviation, BCAS, State Government of 
Maharashtra and MIAL to wake up from their slumber and see the danger looming large on the 
Mumbai Airport. The Committee expresses its serious concern on this and strongly recommends 
that all the slums must be removed and relocated from the airport area. There is no justification for 
allowing encroachers inside the airport area and Committee is of the view that so long as this area 
is occupied by the slum dwellers, the Mumbai airport is sitting on a ticking bomb until it is 
relocated. Therefore, the Committee recommends that MIAL along with   Government   of 
Maharashtra should come forward immediately with adequate proposals to rehabilitate the slums 
taking support of various Government agencies. 
(Para 85) 
25. The Committee understands that MIAL has been pursuing with the Government of 
Maharashtra (GoM) for rehabilitation of hutment dwellers at CSIA since taking over operations of 
CSIA in 2006. The Committee hopes that the Government of Maharashtra will expedite its approval 
for the Airport Specific Slum Rehabilitation Scheme for CSIA, to enable the slum rehabilitation 
process quickly. 
(Para 86) 
Reply of the Government 
 
26. As per the State Government Support Agreement (SGSA), entered into between the State 
Government of Maharashtra and M/s Mumbai International Airport Pvt. Ltd. (MIAL), rehabilitation 
of slums from the airport land shall be carried out in accordance with the applicable slum 
rehabilitation scheme of the State Government. MOCA has written to the State Government for 
preparation of an airport specific slum rehabilitation scheme. The State Government has prepared a 
draft scheme and is in the process of finalizing it. As soon as the slum rehabilitation scheme is in 
place, the rehabilitation process shall be undertaken by MIAL on priority basis in consultation with 
the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and the State Authorities. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
27. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the slums are a threat to the 
Mumbai airport. The slums should be removed from the airport premises. The Committee 
desires that the airport specific slum rehabilitation scheme may be finalized at the earliest 
and that the process of rehabilitation of slums from the airport land at Mumbai may be 
carried out without delay. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
 
28. The Committee compliments the CIAL, CISF and other security agencies for providing 
security to the Cochin Airport. 
(Para 90) 
28.A. The Committee observes that National Security cannot be compromised. Civil Aviation 
Security is a very integral and important element of national security. Airport  complex is a crucial 
infrastructure. Any large scale damage/terrorist attack on the airport complex will be catastrophic 
with far reaching grave implications for the citizens and the economy. Investments flowing into the 
country depend on the state of the security and safety. The Committee further notes that the 
airports have been categorized as hyper-sensitive, sensitive and normal. Operational airports in

7 
 
hyper-sensitive categories are 26 out of which only 18 airports have been provided with CISF 
security cover. Which means that eight hyper-sensitive airports are not provided the security cover 
of CISF. In sensitive category, there are 56 airports, out of which 37 are covered by CISF and 19 
are not covered. In the normal category of 16 airports, only 4 are provided with CISF security and 
12 are not covered. Thus, out of 98 functional airports, only 59 are covered with CISF security 
cover and 39 are not under CISF. Explanations given to the Committee was lack of funds for 
providing CISF security cover at all the 98 airports. 
(Para 95) 
 
Reply of the Government 
 
29. Pursuant to the recommendations made by Committee of Secretaries (CoS) and based on 
prioritization of Airports,  CISF has been deployed at 59 airports in India till date. Based on the 
assessment, security cover at all airports has been provided.    Many Airport Operators including 
AAI, have reported shortfall in the collection of Passenger Service Fee (Security Component), 
which are utilised to meet the revenue expenditure on deployment of security agencies such as 
ASG, APSU etc. for security at airports. 
30. The cost of deployment of CISF and other security agencies, mainly State Government at 
the airports is met out of the PSF levied on embarking passengers. PSF is presently charged @ 
` 200/- per ticket, out of which ` 70/- is utilized by the airport operator for passenger facilitation 
and balance ` 130/- for payment to the designated security agency either of Central Government or 
State Government. 
31. The Ministry has also taken certain measures to streamlining the system pertaining to PSF. 
Ministry of Civil Aviation has already taken up the matter with Ministry of Finance to consider the 
security of airport as sovereign function and expenditure be allowed from Consolidated Fund of 
India. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
32. The security must be adequate and in proportion to the threat perception. Funds should not 
come in the way of providing security. The Committee recommends that the security component of 
PSF needs to be enhanced to commensurate with the security expenditure and ensure that security 
is not compromised at all the airports in India and the PSF security component must be deposited 
in the Consolidated Fund of India. 
(Para 96) 
Reply of the Government 
 
33. Ministry of Civil Aviation has already taken up the matter with Ministry of Finance to 
consider the security of airport as sovereign function and expenditure be allowed from Consolidated 
Fund of India. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
34. The Committee is of the view that lack of funds should not be a reason for not 
providing CISF security cover at the airports. The Committee may be apprised of the

8 
 
response of the Ministry of Finance in this regard. The Committee reiterates that the 
security of the airports should be treated as a sovereign function. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
35. The Committee recommends that Airport Security should be absolute. The Committee observes 
that Security of the Airports  is an integral part of national Security and therefore, recommends that 
providing security should be a sovereign function. Adequacy  of PSF Security component collections 
should not be the criteria for providing security. If CISF security cover can be given to the Delhi Metro,  
why cannot all the operational airports be provided with CISF security cover? 
36. The Committee feels that ideally, the CISF security cover should be provided to all the 70 
odd airports which are having normal scheduled operations. But to begin with, the Committee 
recommends that all the Airports rated hyper-sensitive airports. In view of shortages of manpower 
and logistics available with CISF, security of normal airports can continue with State Police for the 
time being. But these airports also be given all modern equipment, training etc. 
(Para 97) 
Reply of the Government 
 
37. Ministry of Civil Aviation has already taken up the matter with Ministry of Finance to 
consider the security of airport as sovereign function and expenditure be allowed from Consolidated 
Fund of India.   Decision on further deployment of CISF shall be taken in accordance with the Civil  
Aviation Policy approved recently by the Cabinet. 
Further Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
38. The Committee may be apprised of the final outcome of the proposal to consider the 
security of airport as sovereign function and expenditure be allowed from the Consolidated 
Fund of India. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
39. The Committee noted the arguments of Home Secretary and Secretary, Civil Aviation and 
observes that there is no need for a separate Civil Aviation  Force at this juncture and that Airport  
Security can remain with the CISF and Ministry of Home Affairs especially in view of the fact the 
IB, NSG and other Police Forces have a substantial role to play in airport security are also under 
the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
(Para 100) 
Reply of the Government 
40. The proposal is being examined. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
41. The Committee may be apprised of the outcome of the examination of the proposal. 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
42. The Committee, after examining the papers/documents submitted to it and hearing the 

9 
 
arguments of various stakeholders on the subject, could understand that there are multiple agencies 
involved in providing security at Indian airports. 
(Para 101) 
Reply of the Government 
43. There is a coordination mechanism in various agencies and BCAS is designated agency for 
security at airport to take all steps. 
Further Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
44. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
45. The Committee notes that Bureau of Civil aviation Security responsible for laying down the  
standards for pre-embarkation security and anti-sabotage measures in respect of civil flights and 
ensuring their compliance through regular inspections and security audits.   Commissioner   of  
Security, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security has been empowered to issue Directions under Section 
5A of Aircraft Act, 1934 with respect to civil aviation security matters. 
(Para 102) 
Reply of the Government 
46. BCAS being the designated agency, is already performing these functions. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
47. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
48. The Committee also notes that whereas BCAS frames the rules and regulations for civil 
aviation security, the Central Industrial Security Force which is functioning under the Ministry of 
Home Affairs acts as the implementing agency for the guidelines framed by BCAS. The Intelligence 
Bureau plays an important role in providing intelligence inputs related to civil aviation security. 
National Security Guard (NSG) under the Ministry of Home Affairs is also the primary Contingency  
Response Force for anti-terrorist operations at airports. 
(Para 103) 
Reply of the Government 
49. No comment 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
50. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
51. The Committee was at a loss to find that the post of the Commissioner of Security, BCAS, 
the Appropriate Authority for the development, implementation and maintenance of National Civil 

10 
 
Aviation Security Programme of India, is lying vacant for the last two-and-a-half years. The 
Committee would like to know the reasons for keeping this important and sensitive post vacant for 
more than two years. The Committee may also be apprised on the steps taken to fill up the post on 
priority. 
(Para 104) 
Reply of the Government 
52. Shri Kumar Rajesh Chandra, IPS has assumed the office of Director General, BCAS on 
17.05.2016. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
53. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. 
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
54. The Committee finds that the violent incident involving employees of Airports Authority  of 
India and the Central Industrial Security Force at Karipur Airport in Kozhikode on 10th June, 2015 
raises a question mark over the effectiveness of the existing co-ordination mechanism between 
carious agencies involved in providing security at Indian Airports. When the issue was raised during 
the deliberation, both the Home Secretary and Civil Aviation Secretary assured the Committee to 
look into the matter and to address the shortcoming in the system. The Committee hopes that apart 
from conducting various meeting to address the issues related to airport security with agencies 
involved in the process, both the Ministries will have a periodical review of the performance of the  co-
ordination mechanism so that any grey areas identified could be addressed immediately. 
(Para 105) 
Reply of the Government 
55. There is an Airport  Security Committee (APSC) at each airport which meets once in every 
month and security related issues are discussed and addressed in the meeting. BCAS issues 
necessary instructions in accordance with the discussions held in the meeting.       Further,  Ministry 
of Home Affairs have set up a Standing Committee with members from Minist ry of Civil Aviation,  
Intelligence Bureau (IB), CISF, BCAS and AAI,  to review the security arrangements at airports on 
quarterly basis. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
56. The Committee takes note of the reply and hopes that the existing mechanism would 
strengthen the security apparatus at the airports. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
57. The Committee also feels that the issues of deficiency of security gadgets and installation of 
CCTV cameras of shadow zones at various airports should be taken up on priority so that such 
deficiencies do not become a cause for concern in the Indian airports security system. As it is said 
that the performance in the battlefield is obviously known before hand if we are not fully equipped 
with the modern equipments to fight with the enemy. The Committee, therefore, hopes that PIDS 

11 
 
which is currently operating on pilot basis at Delhi Airport Should be reviewed and efforts should 
be made to remove the flaws found in the system. The Ministry of Civil Aviation should also look 
out for such PIDS technology which could function properly in the Indian conditions. 
(Para 106) 
Reply of the Government 
58. BCAS informed that a Committee has been constituted to study the grey area in the CCTV 
areas and security lapses at IGI airport and the observations of the committee has been 
communicated to DIAL for compliance report. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
59. The Committee may be apprised of the steps taken by DIAL to comply with the 
observations of the Committee constituted to study the grey areas at the IGI Airport. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
60. The Committee desires that the areas of concern on providing security to Delhi Airport, 
expressed by the Delhi Police should be given due consideration. The Ministry of Civil Aviation and 
Delhi International Airport Limited are urged to look into the problems faced by the Delhi Police on 
the city side as well as within the T-3 terminal building of Delhi Airport. 
(Para 107) 
Reply of the Government 
61. Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), an attached office of this Ministry formed a 
Facilitation Committee at airport level to resolve the issues between Delhi Police and DIAL. In 
addition, a meeting of Airport Security Committee (APSC), of which Delhi Police is also member, is 
held on monthly basis. 
62. In addition, ED (Security), DIAL was also communicated to resolve the issues raised by 
Delhi Police. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
63. The Committee may be apprised of the updated status of the issues between DIAL 
and Delhi Police. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
64. The Committee also hopes that the issue of relocation and rehabilitation of slum dwellers 
from the vicinity of Mumbai International Airport will be settled as soon as possible so that the 
encroachment land is brought within the control of airport operator and the necessary expansion 
works of Mumbai Airport are commenced shortly. Upon that, the present security threat to the 
Mumbai Airport will automatically wither away. The Committee after cross examination of the 
Governments and concerned organizations has come to the conclusions that the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation, State Government of Maharashtra, Mumbai International Airport Limited and Airport 
Authority of India should sit together to sort out the long pending issues which have presently 
become the major issue of threat to Mumbai airport. The Committee also requests the Ministry of 

12 
 
Civil Aviation and Government of Maharashtra to take a lead in settling the issues with no loss of 
time. 
(Para 108) 
Reply of the Government 
 
65. Removal of the encroachment from Mumbai airport land is a crucial project as the slums 
are not only serious security threat to the airport but also the encroached land is required for 
development of the airport. Therefore, MOCA, Airports Authority of India and MIAL are keen to 
take all the necessary steps for removal of the encroachments from the Airport  Land. MOCA has  
already taken up the issue with the State Government of Maharashtra and has requested them to 
formulate an airports specific slum rehabilitation scheme. The State Government is in the process 
of finalization of the scheme based on which the removal process shall be initiated. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
66. The Committee hopes that the airports specific slum rehabilitation scheme will be 
finalized by the State Government of Maharashtra in a time bound manner and that the 
removal of the encroachments from the airport land at Mumbai will be initiated without 
delay for development of the airport. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
67. The Committee desires that vacant posts in the Aviation  Security Group of CISF which is 
manning the Indian airports through the length and breadth of the country are filled up at the 
earliest so that the existing security apparatus is strengthened. 
(Para 109) 
Reply of the Government 
 
68. The released strength of CISF at 59 airports is 24261 and posted strength is 22904. With 
over 94% posts filled, CISF is able to handle the situation without compromising security or 
causing inconvenience to public.   Recruitment and training of additional personnel, as requirements 
of CISF increase, is an ongoing process. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
69. The Committee is of the view that vacancies cannot be afforded in the vital Aviation  
Security Group of CISF and desires that the vacancies may be filled up at the earliest. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
70. There is an involvement of multiple agencies in providing securities at Indian airports and 
the Committee has found a lack of proper co-ordination between the agencies. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that a think tank may be created to bring out a proper co-ordination 
involving all the stakeholders to help the Commissioner of Security, BCAS to perform his duties 
satisfactory. 
(Para 110) 

13 
 
Reply of the Government 
71. There are different security responsibilities such as anti-sabotage checks, screening of hold 
baggage and all items carried in the bally of aircraft, access control to aircraft, carriage of security 
items from SHA etc.  to different agencies i.e. airlines. Airport  operators, Regulated agent, catering 
companies and all these agencies area subject to audit on regular basis  by BCAS teams  to see the  
compliance of the task assigned to them by appropriate authority i.e. DG, BCAS. 
72. Following are some of the arrangements to review the same: 
(i) Standing Committee for reviewing security arrangements at airports with   Secretary 
–Home as Chairman with  Secretary MOCA, Director, IB, DG, CISF, Commissioner,  
BCAS Chairman, AAI as members and Add,. Secretary (LWE) as members 
Secretary. To meet on quarterly basis. 
(ii) National level Facilitation Committee chaired by Cabinet Secretary 
(iii) Facilitation committee at Airport level 
(iv) Airport Security  Committee (APSC)  at airport  level 
73. Zonal level and  Sector level  committees of CISF  are also  there 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
74. The Committee hopes that the existing mechanism will ensure proper co-ordination 
among all the stakeholders involved in airport security. 
Recommendations/Observations   of   the   Committee 
75. The Commissioner finds it quite scary to know that the security of 8 of our hyper-sensitive 
and 19 of our sensitive airports are not covered by the CISF which has now become the only 
specialized force for aviation security; now question is who is then guarding these airports and how 
secure these airports are? In these existing threats perceptions at our airports, the country can ill- 
affords such a situation to continue any more. The Committee finds that aviation security has not 
received the attention and importance that it deserves. The Committee feels that in view of several 
gaps and lack of unified command and control for the multiple agencies involved, there is an urgent 
need for having an Aviation  Security policy in the country for ensuring fool proof security at our 
airports before a major untoward incident takes place in the Country. 
(Para 111) 
Reply of the Government 
76. It is felt that adequate mechanisms already exist to ensure coordination between various 
agencies. Further action on the issue would be taken in accordance with the National Civil Aviation 
Policy approved recently by the Cabinet. 
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee 
77. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry. 

14 
 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS ––– AT A GLANCE 
 
The Committee notes that the violent incident in Karipur, Kozhikode airport was a 
serious issue. However, the Government and various security agencies did not take   it  
seriously. Even after a long lapse of time the police agencies failed to complete the 
investigations and bring the guilty to book. The Committee recommends that   the   guilty  
should be punished and the amount of loss occurred due to the rampage by officials should 
be recovered from the salary of the concerned officials after conducting an enquiry in this 
regard by an appropriate authority. The Committee desires that the investigation in the 
remaining two cases should be expedited and that the final report should be submitted 
without delay. (Para 7) 
The Committee  takes  note of the reply  and hopes  that the mechanism  will  
strengthen the security apparatus at the airports. The Committee may be apprised of the 
details of the meetings held by the Co-ordination Committee during   the   last   one   year  
period. (Para 10) 
The Committee recently visited the Delhi airport and noticed that the situation 
prevailing earlier has not changed as far as the points raised by the Delhi Police are 
concerned. The Committee notices an element of apathy by the agencies involved such as 
the DIAL, Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Home Affairs as far as the grievances 
of Delhi Police are concerned. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the points 
raised by the Delhi Police should be taken seriously and resolved at the earliest. The 
Committee may be apprised of the specific steps taken to resolve the issues between DIAL 
and the Delhi Police and the outcome thereof. The Committee desires that time bound 
action should be taken to resolve these issues. (Para 16) 
During further interaction with all the involved agencies, the Committee could learn 
that the hotels at the aerocity are a potential security threat to the runway and the airport. 
The Committee is of the view that all the hotels in the aerocity should be considered as 
equally important as any other airport asset.   However,   the   Committee   learnt   that   the  
access to the hotels inside the aerocity are being managed by the private security guards. 
The security at these hotels should be given utmost importance because unknown persons 
are accessing such points. Considering the strategic importance of the hotels which are so 
nearby to the functional runway, the Committee recommends that   CISF  should   be   the  
default security agency for all the access points to the   hotels   in   the   aerocity.   The 
Committee also recommends that since the hotels are a separate business, the payments for 
the deployment of CISF security may be borne by the hotels themselves. (Para 17) 
The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that Delhi Police is doing the 
sovereign function and they should not be charged for basic facilities provided to them. The 
Committee may be apprised of the progress made in this regard. (Para 20) 
 
14 

15 
 
The Committee takes note of the reply and desires that it may be informed of the 
progress made in this regard. (Para 23) 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the slums are a threat to the 
Mumbai airport. The slums should be removed from the airport premises. The Committee 
desires that the airport specific slum rehabilitation scheme may be finalized at the earliest 
and that the process of rehabilitation of slums from the airport land at Mumbai may be 
carried out without delay. (Para 27) 
The Committee is of the view that lack of funds should not be a reason for not 
providing CISF security cover at the airports. The Committee may be apprised of the 
response of the Ministry of Finance in this regard.    The Committee reiterates that the 
security of the airports should be treated as a sovereign function. (Para 34) 
The Committee may be apprised of the final outcome of the proposal to consider the

The Committee may be apprised of the steps taken by DIAL to comply with the

The Committee may be apprised of the updated status of the issues between DIAL

The Committee hopes that the airports specific slum rehabilitation scheme will be

Around Plan has not been provided for Air India. This was the case in 2015-16 also where there
was a short fall of ` 977 crores. The Committee feels that this reduction in equity infusion might
adversely affect the financial and operational performance of the company since it may be forced
to take loans from banks and financial institutions at a higher interest rate to meet the short fall,
which was not contemplated under the Financial Restructuring Plan. The Committee, therefore, is
of the considered view that such short fall, at this stage when the company is presently placed at
a critical position in achieving the TAP targets, should be avoided. Since the committed financial
support from the Government is vital to sustain the momentum of performance of Air India, the
Committee strongly recommends that the full amount of equity infusion should be restored to Air
India. The Committee recommends as a matter of fact that in future, the amount committed under
the TAP should be allocated at the BE stage itself.
(Para 23)
Reply of the Government
24. Air India had sought an Equity Infusion of ` 3901.49 crores in the Annual Plan 2016-17
submitted to the Ministry of Civil Aviation. However, against this demand, an amount of only
` 1713.00 crores has been allocated as Equity Infusion for FY 2016-17. 
25. Accordingly, during FY 2016-17 there will be a shortfall in Equity Infusion of ` 2188.49
crores viz ` 3901.49 crores. This reduction in Equity Infusion would impact the financial and
operational performance of the company as the same will create liquidity issues for the company
whereby the company will be unable to meet it’s financial commitments and maintain the
operational efficiency of the company.
26. In order to meet the shortfall, a proposal for grant of additional funds of ` 2188.49 Crore
has been included in the first Batch of Supplementary Grant for 2016-17.

55. The Committee notes that the senior level positions in BCAS are occupied by deputationists.
The Committee is given to understand that the BCAS officials acquire a lot of operational
experience during their services in the organization. However, the senior level positions are given to
novices with little or no experience in aviation security on deputation basis ignoring the experience
and qualifications of BCAS officials. The Committee has been given to understand that by doing so,
we are endangering the entire civil aviation security of the country as the deputationists leave the
organization after a brief stint of 3 years in the organization. The Committee, therefore, in principle
agrees with the view that the senior positions of BCAS may be held exclusively for career officials
of BCAS. The Committee, therefore, wants the Ministry to submit a note on this aspect for
consideration of the Committee.
(Para 55)
Reply of the Government
56. After the approval of ‘re-structuring of BCAS’, one additional post of Joint Director General
(formerly known as Joint Commissioner of Security (CA) is being created, with the approval of the
Cabinet. Further, the re-structuring plan provides for an additional post of Deputy Director General
(the erstwhile post of Additional Commissioner of Security (CA) in BCAS. These senior level posts,
including that of the Director General, BCAS (Head of the Organisation), are filled up purely on the
basis of ‘deputation’. In view of this, the post of DDG and Jt. DG cannot be treated to be a
‘feeder post’ to the post of Jt. DG and DG , respectively.
57. This Ministry have already taken note of the representations received in the matter,
requesting for creation of further promotional avenues to the cadre officers of an organisation (at
senior level) for their promotion to the level of DDG , JDG and DG. The suggestion/viewpoint of the
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture in this
regard has also been taken on record.

Recruitment Rules  of various posts in BCAS, which has been initiated pursuant to the approval of
‘restructuring of BCAS’, is presently under consideration of this Ministry in consultation with
BCAS. The said suggestions and viewpoints will be kept in view while amending the RRs, and
decision on the same would be finalized after due consultation with relevant stakeholders.

111. Central Government granted ‘in-principle’ approval to the project subject to certain
conditions for setting up of Greenfield airport at Kushinagar in September, 2010. Government of
Uttar Pradesh (GoUP) had invited applications from prospective developers for developing the
airport in PPP mode. However, the project could not attract the interests of developers. GoUP and
Airports Authority of India (AAI) are in talks for implementation of the project.
112. AAI team along with State Government officials visited kushinagar on 6
th November, 2015
to assess the quantum of land required for the development of Kushinagar Airport. The minimum
land requirement was assessed and the Revenue Officials were asked to examine the feasibility of
acquiring the land. The Revenue Officials after carrying out the detailed field study has forwarded
the revenue map showing the tentative land which can be acquired. Based on this, AAI has
prepared the draft Master Plan and forwarded to the State Government for acquisition of land.
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
113. The Committee may be apprised of the progress made in this regard.

long time causing tremendous inconvenience to the travelling public. The Committee desires that the
renovation work at the Calicut airport may be completed at the earliest and that the senior officers
of AAI should continuously monitor the progress of the work.
(Para 105)

115. Noted.
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
116. The Committee desires that the renovation work at the Calicut airport may be
completed within a definite timelimit.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
117. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by AAI to ensure green airports/offices. The

16
Committee notes that there are lots of vacant lands in the numerous airports of the country where
no other construction could be carried out. The Committee observes that such vacant land needs to
be utilized for generating solar energy which can be used for the functioning of the airports as well
as the nearby areas if there is surplus level. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the
airports of the country should endeavour to develop solar power plants with a futuristic plan.
(Para 107)

118. AAI endeavours to maximum installation of solar power plants by utilizing vacant land at
various airports for generating Solar Energy. For  ground Mounted Solar Power Plants at
available land of AAI airports, AAI has already initiated action and works are in progress at Kolkata
(15000 KWp), Jaipur (1800 KWp) and Chandigarh (3000 KWp) Airports. For other Airports, AAI
shall be taking up solar projects subject to availability of “Net Metering” facility. At present most of
the States are not having solar policy for Ground mounted solar plants.  Policy is available for roof
top solar power plants that too for a small limited capacity.
119. In view of above, AAI is taking  up ground mounted solar power plants only where “Net
Metering” facility is available and AAIs captive load also exists.
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
120. The Committee takes note of the reply furnished by the Ministry.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
121. The Committee welcomes the incentives agreed to be provided for MRO activities as
mentioned above. Given the huge growth/expansion, Indian Civil Aviation Sector is going to be the
world’s largest civil aviation sector within a few years. We need to tap the opportunity of related
sectors to become an aviation giant of the 21
st century. The Committee observes that India has the
human resources and conducive environment for development of state of the art MROs. The
Government should aim at exploiting the ` 5000 crores MRO business so that not only Indian
carriers but foreign aircrafts also get this facility within India only. The Committee feels that India
has the potential to be an MRO hub given the demand as well as the availability of skilled
manpower in the country. The Committee desires that immediate steps should be taken to set up
and expand the MRO infrastructure presently available in the country by providing conducive
business environment and legal framework.
(Para 110)
Reply of the Government
122. Approval of MRO is granted by DGCA under the regulation CAR-145.
123. At present DGCA has approved 92 MROs in the country under the above regulation. Out of
these there are 8 number of large MROs, which can carry out maintenance of large aeroplane and
helicopter.
124. DGCA is also taking required actions for grant of approval of MRO’s  whenever request of
approval is received and the applicant is complying with the regulations.

17
125. The National Civil Aviation policy also provides for further incentives for MRO; in addition
to the financial incentives already announced in the Budget Speech of the Hon’ble Finance Minister
for the year 2016-17. The other incentives are as under:-
126. Service tax on output services of MRO will be zero-rated.
127. The tools and tool-kits used by the MRO are specific to aircraft industry. Aircraft
maintenance tools and tool-kits will be exempt from Customs duty. The exemption shall be given
on the basis of list the tools and tool-kits notified by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation from
time to time.
128. MROs are at present required to provide proof of their requirements of parts, or orders
from their client airlines. However, aircraft parts are used exclusively in the aircraft and are
designated  by part Numbers as given by aircraft and related Original Equipment Manufacturers.
Therefore, the process for the clearance of the parts shall be simplified by allowing for self-
attestation by the MROs.
129. To enable economies of scale, the period for which the spare parts  imported by MROs can
be stored tax-free shall be extended to 3 years.
130. To allow import of unserviceable parts by MROs for providing exchange /advance
exchange,  the concerned notification shall be reviewed and revised to also enable advance export
of serviceable parts.
131. Foreign aircraft brought to India for MRO work will be allowed to stay for the entire period
of maintenance or up to 6 months, whichever is lesser, provided it undertakes no commercial
flights during the stay period. The aircraft may, however, carry passengers in the flights at the
beginning and end of the stay period in India. For stay beyond 6 months, DGCA’s permission will
be required.
132. Foreign MRO experts will be provided visas promptly, especially in cases of an Aircraft on
Ground (AOG) situation.
133. Foreign Pilots operating an aircraft to and from India for the purpose of servicing at an
Indian MRO entity will be issued Temporary Landing Permits.
134. The provision under AIC 3 of 2010 of DGCA shall be reviewed to declare MRO (Aircraft
Servicing) as a separate category instead of clubbing with Ground Handling (GHA) for security
procedures and remove restrictions on foreign registered aircraft for MRO work.
135. MOCA will persuade State Governments to make V AT zero-rated on MRO services.
136. Provision for adequate land for MRO service providers will be made in all future airport
projects.
137. Airport royalty and additional levies on MRO service providers will be rationalised in
consultation with Airport Operators.

142. The Committee is happy that a comprehensive civil aviation policy is likely to be put in
place, which was long overdue. The proposed policy contains all the essential aspects that are
badly needed to be provided/expanded/strengthened to meet the demand in future. But the
Committee finds that most of these items included in the policy have not had the required emphasis
about which even this Committee had been pointing out regularly through its various reports. For
implementing these, apart from funds, several other bottlenecks/shortages will have to be tackled.
For example, concern for aspects each as aviation security, regional connectivity, safety, use of
helicopters, MRO facilities, aviation education and training and last but not the least, affordability of
air journeys has never been reflected in allocation during the previous years as well. If it remains
so, any policy is likely to remain on paper only, unless significant provisioning of funds etc. is done
for realizing the objectives contained in the Policy. The Committee, therefore, recommends the
Ministry of Finance to make adequate funds available for sustaining the sentiments that may be
generated due to adoption of new Civil Aviation Policy. It should realize that growth and expansion
of aviation facilities would have cascading effects for growth in other sectors of our economy as
well as job creation.
(Para 116A)

Committee hopes that this would give a boost to the civil aviation sector.

various unserved and underserved airports to make them functional.  The Committee is aware that

hopes that the revival of these airports would boost the Indian economy and therefore,

adequate funding for starting the revival of unserved and underserved airports, at the RE stage.

and that it can be compared to any other developed nation.  The Committee also feels that it is high
time to set aside the sign of a colonial past and acquire a new call sign which appropriately denotes
the Indian civil aviation sector.
(Para 126)

Reply of the Government
155. As contracting state to International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), India has to follow
the requirements of ICAO Annex 7, which deals with the aircraft nationality and registration mark.
156. As per Para 2.3 of Annex 7, nationality mark shall be selected from the series of nationality
symbols included in the radio call signs allocated to the State of Registry by the International
Telecommunication Union. The nationality mark shall be notified to the International Civil Aviation
Organisation.
157. India has been allocated three series (“ATA-AWZ”, “VTA-VWZ” and  “8TA-8YZ”) by the
international Telecommunication union and in accordance with the above paragraph 2.3 of Annexe
7, India can chose aircraft registration mark from these series and notify to International Civil
Aviation Organisation. The aircraft nationality and registration mark ‘VT’ is at present used from
the “VTA-VTZ” series allocated by International Telecommunication Union.
158. Additionally Rule 37 of Aircraft Rules, 1937 also specifies “the nationality mark of the
aircraft shall be the capital letters VT in Roman character”.
Further Recommendations/Observations of the Committee

basically low paid workers. The exorbitant ticket fares are causing lot of financial troubles for
already troubled workers due to poor wages due to economic slowdown and other related issues.
The Committee, therefore, observes that Air India has a social responsibility towards its population,
that they are protected from predatory airfares. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government of India should ensure that all the Indian carriers operating in Gulf Sector provide a
reasonably low fare for its citizens. The Committee desires that these issues may be looked into
and appropriate remedial action may be taken in this regard.
(Para 128)
Reply of the Government
161. Under the provisions of Rule 135, the Aircraft Rule 1937, every airline is required to
establish tariff having regard to all relevant factors including the cost of operation, characteristic of
service, reasonable profit and generally prevailing tariff. Generally, airlines offer low priced tickets
for booking made considerably in advance. Government normally does not interfere in a day to day
commercial aspects of airlines. In case of Indian carrier operating in Gulf sector, are asked to
provide much lower fare for Indian citizen, the issue may translate in to discriminatory or
predatory pricing practices and invite litigation by foreign carriers. Also, the issue of international
operations by domestic airlines are covered under bilateral agreements between Government of
India and foreign Governments. However, in case of extra ordinary situations such as natural
calamities, civic unrest etc. airlines have positively shared their social obligations in the past.

which are also causing hindrance to passenger flow in the country. The Committee recommends

there should be more flights to accommodate the passenger rush. The Committee also recommends

should fix an upper limit especially in the economy class of airfares so that there should not be
unhealthy practice of raising fares exorbitantly by the airlines.  The Prime Minister in one of his
visits to Middle East has already asked the Ministry of Civil Aviation to do something about such
prices.  The Committee would like to know about the efforts made in this regard so far.

among Indian carriers to their foreign competitors and also may attract litigation on predatory
pricing by foreign airlines.

of regulating airfare after the repeal of Air Corporation Act in 1994.  Predatory pricing of airfare is
hurting not only the individual passenger but country’s economy as well.  The explanation given by
the Ministry of Civil Aviation is purely technical suggesting that they are unable to do anything
under existing laws. The Committee observes that this is amounting to abdicating their basic
responsibilities of protecting the citizens of the country. The Committee fails to understand whose
interest is sought to be sub served by taking such a stand that too before a Parliamentary
Committee which is empowered to suggest necessary modification in our rules, regulations that are
coming in our way for correcting airfares. Let us not compare Indian case with any other country.
India has a specific case which needs a specific solution that is best suited to it in a given
situation.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation
should specify the limitations, legal and otherwise, which need to be amended or other measures to
be put in place to tackle this problem after consulting all the stakeholders.
(Para 134)

172. In the matter of civil aviation, governing regulations are generally framed in accordance
with ICAO Standard and Recommended Practices (SARPs). At present DGCA, India is in process
to harmonise the domestic regulations at par with standards and practice followed globally. Any
difference with ICAO SARPs is required to be notified to ICAO as India is a contracting member
and signatory to conventions of International Civil Aviation Organisation, it is binding on us to
promulgate regulations as per ICAO guidelines.

otherwise, which need to be amended or other measures to be put in place to tackle the
problem of predatory airfares.  The Committee desires that the Ministry may furnish a
detailed reply in this regard.

st December, 2013 and was ` 35127 per kilo litre as on 1 st March, 2016. The Committee could

that the Ministry should take effective steps to ensure that the airlines pass on the benefit to the
travelers by reducing the air fares and inform the Committee about the specific steps taken in this

176. The Committee desires that the Ministry may inform the Committee about the

RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
5. The Committee observes that there is a mismatch between the total outlay for the 
Ministry of Tourism for the 12 
th  Five Year Plan and the annual allocation. Even tho ugh 
the total outlay was Rs. 15190 crore, the annual bu dgetary allocations remained far from 
the proportionate allocation required as per the to tal outlay. Similarly, BE allocations 
were reduced substantially every year at RE stage a s shown in Table 3.  This reduction 
was significant in 2015-16, almost 57% reduction. T he actual expenditure right from the 
first plan year (2012-13) to the fourth plan year ( 2015-16) was also far from  the desired 
level. During none of the year except 2015-16, fund  could be utilized optimally.  During 
2014-15, it was the lowest expenditure of allocatio n. Moreover, every year the actual

not convincing.

Plan was taken up with erstwhile Planning Commissio n and Ministry of Finance at the

9. Out of the main reasons for significant reductio n in the allocation at RE stage in 
2014-15 & 2015-16 is that a major part of the Budge t Estimate for the year 2014-15 & 
2015-16 was earmarked for two new schemes announced  in July, 2014 the Budget 
Speech of 2014-15, i.e. Rs.600 crore and Rs.700 cro re respectively. These two new 
Schemes of Ministry of Tourism namely Swadesh Darshan & PRASAD were launched in 
January, 2015 after the formulation and approval of  the scheme guidelines in pursuance 
of the Budget Announcement in July, 2014. After for mulation/approval of the Scheme

in January, 2015. The reduced RE allocation for 201 4-15 i.e. Rs.20 crore for Swadesh 
Darshan & Rs.15.60 crore for PRASAD was fully utilized. 
10. Being new schemes, it took some time to sensiti ze the States/UTs and get the 
project proposals in accordance with the objectives  of these schemes. Besides, for new 
projects, the 1 st  installment of funds released by the MOT is only 2 0% of the sanctioned 
cost. Therefore, the pace of expenditure upto September, 2015 (on the basis of which RE, 
are prepared by the Ministry of Finance) remained s low this resulted in huge reduction in 
allocation at RE stage. The reduced RE allocation o f Rs.310.00 crore for Swadesh 
Darshan & Rs.40.00 crore for PRASAD has been fully utilized under both the schemes.

11.  The Committee notes the reply. The Committee howev er is not satisfied with 
the reply as the onus of under utilization of funds  squarely lies on the Ministry. The

new schemes but this time the matters were taken in  a lackadaisical manner which 
resulted in messing up of things. The Committee rec ommends that the deficiencies 
on the part of the Ministry should be taken as a lesson for future actions.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
30. The Committee notes the achievements made by th e Ministry of Tourism during 
2015-16 in the domestic as well as world tourism fi eld. The Committee observes that 
during 2015-16 there was a drastic cut at the RE St age i.e. from Rs. 1483.20 crore of BE, 
it has been reduced to Rs. 850.00 crore. Even Rs.14 83.20 crore was only 51.89% of the 
Ministry’s demand of Rs 2897.15 crore during 2015-1 6 as per the information furnished 
by the Ministry. Now, the actual expenditure stands  at Rs. 667.16 crore. Compared to the 
original demand of Rs.2897.15; the actual expenditu re of Rs. 667.16 crore is very 
negligible as far as the Ministry of Tourism is con cerned, which is contributing to 
12.36% growth of the economy.         
                       (Para 23 of  ibid )        
31. The Committee further observes that the Secreta ry Tourism himself has admitted 
that allocating such a large amount of funds to Swa desh Darshan and PRASAD when 
they were launched should have been avoided. In fac t the process of making the 
guidelines, forming committees etc for these entire ly new schemes took some time.  The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Touri sm should have anticipated these 
basic things relating to implementation of the sche me and utilization of the grants. There 
was no need of earmarking huge budgetary allocation s for that schemes.  As a result, this 
fund was blocked which would have been utilized for after important ongoing schemes.   
(Para 24 of  ibid ) 
32. Even though Tourism Circuit had got Rs.600.00 c rore allocation at BE stage, it 
was reduced drastically to Rs. 245.00 crore at RE. However, the Ministry could spent 
Rs.276.76 which is Rs.31.76 crore  more than the am ount allocated at RE stage. 
Similarly, under Assistance to IHMs/FCI/PPTTM/NIWS/ NIAS/NCHMCT Scheme also 
Ministry has spent more than the amount allocated a t the RE stage. The Committee 

observes that at the RE stage, cuts were made in ma ny of the schemes during 2015-16 
without taking the actual situation and demand into  consideration which has resulted into 
shortage of funds to many of major projects. The Co mmittee recommends that a realistic 
approach should be taken while making modifications BE allocations. 
(Para 25 of  ibid ) 
Reply of the Government  
33.  As submitted, the new Schemes namely Swadesh D arshan & PRASAD were 
announced in the Budget Speech of the Hon’ble Finan ce Minister for the year 2014-15 
and accordingly, the Budget Allocation under Swades h Darshan & PRASAD were 
earmarked by the Ministry of Finance for the year 2014-15 & 2015-16. 
34. During 2015-16 at the RE stage the allocation w as reduced to Rs.310.00 crore for 
Swadesh Darshan and Rs.40.00 crore for PRASAD and t he expenditure under Swadesh 
Darshan is Rs. 309.55 crore and under PRASAD the sa me is Rs. 39.99 crore. Hence the 
budget allocation under both the Schemes has been f ully utilized. The total provisional 
expenditure of MOT during 2015-16 is Rs.826.53 cror e, which is about 97% of the total 
allocation of Rs. 850.00 crore.  
35.  Under Assistance to IHMs/FCI/PPTTM/NIWS/NIAS/N CHMCT Scheme MOT 
has utilized 100% of RE allocation which is Rs. 95.00 crore.  
36. As mentioned already MOT is regularly pursuing the matter for enhancement of 
Budget allocation with the Ministry of Finance.

should not reduce the BE for important tourism projects at RE stage as this practice

Budget Estimates of the Ministry of Tourism in 2016 -17. Even though the projected

demand was less and the Ministry of Tourism needs to explain the reasons for it.

39. The demand of Rs. 2897.15 crore was projected b y keeping higher allocation for

32. The Zaffar Mahal and Qutub Minar complex are bo th centrally protected monuments 
of national importance under the jurisdiction of Ar chaeological Survey of India.   As per the 
report called from the field office of the Archaeol ogical Survey of India, Delhi Circle it is 
informed that so far as Prohibited area (within 100  metres of protected monument) of 
Centrally protected monument and  Regulated area (2 00 metres further beyond prohibited 
area) are concerned, there are as many as 93 number  of unauthorized constructions within 
prohibited/regulated areas of Zaffar Mahal and 139 number of unauthorized constructions 
within prohibited/regulated areas of Qutub complex.   The Archaeological Survey of India has 
initiated action for removal of such unauthorized c onstructions as per the provisions of the 
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Rema ins Act and Rules.  It is also to 
mention here that as per records, there is no encro achment in the protected areas of Zaffar 
Mahal and Qutub complex.

constructions within prohibited/regulated areas of Zaffar Mahal and 139 unauthorized 
constructions within prohibited/regulated areas of Qutub Complex are removed at the 

earliest. The Committee may be informed about the a ction taken within three month’s 
time.  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
34. The Committee, although is not against the view  that ASI can effectively fulfill its 
mandate if it has adequate statutory backing to rem ove and prevent encroachments, it, 
however, is of the considered opinion that it would  not help to any great extent, until we are 
able to strike at the nexus between the unscrupulou s elements and local authorities including 
the police, leaving ASI helpless in this regard.  I f the proposed amendment is for breaking the 
unholy nexus, the Committee would welcome this.  Th e Committee hopes that the 
amendments proposed in the AMASR Act would equip AS I to execute its demolition orders 
and also that the Act would stipulate the action to  be taken against the District Authorities in 
case of laxity or non- co-operation on their part in executing the demolition orders.   
(Para No. 31 of ibid ) 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
35. As per the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological  Sites and Remains Act, 1958, 
Collector to cause to remove the encroachment, if a ny from protected area of centrally 
protected monument.  There is a restriction under t he Act that even the owner of protected 
area of monument cannot take any construction witho ut the permission of Central 
Government.  The local authorities are required to be sensitized which would be achieved 
through State Level Co-ordination Committee.  If th e State machinery implements 
demolition/removal of encroachment, the goal to rem ove the encroachment from the 
monument could be achieved. View of Ministry of Law  would be obtained on powers to ASI 
for demolition with regard to action on District Au thorities in case of laxity or non co-
operation on their part in executing demolition orders it is to mention here that the section 30C 
of the Act specifies that “if any officer of the Ce ntral Government enters into or acquiesces in 
any agreement to do, abstains from doing, permits, conceals or connives at any act or thing 
whereby any construction or re-construction takes p lace in a prohibited area or regulated area, 
he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term  which extend three years, or with fine, or 
with both.”  As such non action by District Authori ty may fall under the ambit of existing 
provision.  However, a legal view shall be obtained.

Achievement of Target  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE 
8. The Committee notes Ministry’s claim of achievin g target completely without any 
shortage of funds. On the other hand, it has cited many factors which delayed the projects 
that are largely beyond its control viz. problem in land acquisition, shifting utilities, obtaining 
statutory clearance etc. Performance of contractors  is also poor and other major concern in 
some areas is law and order problem. The Committee suggests the Ministry should 
proactively work as coordinator/facilitator in all these respects. It should take up the matter 
with concerned agencies before hand to solve these problems. Although, the Ministry has set 
a high target of constructing 10,000 km road in the  year 2016-17, the Committee has 
apprehension how this mammoth task could be completed in the given situation. 
(Para 9 of  ibid ) 
Reply of the Government 
 
9. It is submitted that at the stage of preparation  of detailed project report(DPR) of the 
highway project, consultations with local people ar e done regarding land acquisition and 
proposed alignment of NH stretch. At the DPR stage only, the liaisoning is done with 
concerned departments of Central / State Government s for utility shifting/ 
Environment/Forest/Wildlife clearances is done. Fur ther, there is a State Level Coordination 
Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of Chi ef Secretary of each State/UT for 
expeditious clearances/approvals.    
10. At Central level, a high level “Group of Infras tructure” has been constituted to sort 
out the inter-Ministerial issues, under the Chairma nship of  Hon’ble Minister of Road 
Transport and Highways with Hon’ble Ministers of Ra ilways, Civil Aviation, Minister of 
State (IC) of Environment, Forest and Climate Chang e, Principal Secretary to Prime 
Minister, Cabinet Secretary, Secretary(RT&H), Chair man (Railway Board), Secretary 
(Environment & Forests), Secretary(Shipping) and Se cretary (Civil Aviation) as its 
Members.   
11. NHAI has finalised Contractor/Concessionaire ra ting system alongwith key 
performance indicators; the allied IT system archit ecture and design is under preparation. 
The pilot phases of the system will be put for evaluation by 31.12.2016. 
12. Concerted efforts are being made to proactively  facilitate resolving the hindrances. 
Keeping in view the past achievements and consideri ng recent initiatives by the Ministry in 
last two years (like – exit policy, revival of lang uishing projects by one time fund infusion, 
promotion of Hybrid Annuity Model, amendments to MC A for BOT projects) and also 
looking at the quantum of the ongoing NH works, the  target of 10,000 km construction of 
road should  be achievable. All efforts shall be made to maximize the length of completion. 
13. Ministry has received enhanced funds during BE 2016-17 of Rs.55,000 crore. The 
actual requirement and additional fund requirement,  if any, shall be projected at the time of 
Revised Estimate proposal.

46. The Maintenance and Repair (M&R) of NH stretche s are carried out for the stretches 
not covered under any programme or completed stretc hes where there are no liabilities of

contracts have been taken up for a definite time pe riod (4 to 9 years) on Operate, 
Maintenance and Transfer (OMT) basis. The maintenan ce of the project highway under

during 2016-17 is Rs.2,853.57 crore against the pro jected requirement of Rs.7,070 crore.

requirements of funds.  This leads to the compulsio n of thin spreading of available resources 
for the NH stretches in need of M&R.  This is one o f the main reason for inability to take up 
timely maintenance interventions.  The issue is bei ng taken up every year with Ministry of 
Finance.  The concerns of the Committee is noted.  All efforts shall be made to ensure better 
upkeep of NH infrastructure.

Treatment of Accident Victims  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATION   OF THE COMMITTEE 
183. The Committee feels that accidents on NH is ve ry frequent and it has been seen that 
road accident victims are left to die due to lack of medical facilities during golden hours. The 
Committee recommends that trauma centres be opened at the NH stretch after a gap of 40-50 
km. and patrolling van and ambulance may be deploye d in sufficient number to provide 
medical facilities to accident victims immediately.  The Committee learnt that uninsured 
victim of hit and run cases, do not get required tr eatment. In view of increase ins uch 
accidents, something has to be done to ensure that such victims get at least basic treatments 
during golden hours to save their lives. They shoul d not be denied treatment by any hospital, 
nursing homes, etc, who should have surely to be co mpensated afterwards. Govt. and 
insurance companies and other can be roped in to do something in this regard. 
(Para 100 of ibid ) 
Reply of the Government 
 
184. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been  implementing a scheme 
‘establishment of an integrated network of Trauma C entres’ along the Golden Quadrilateral, 
North-South and East-West Corridors of the National  Highways by upgrading the trauma 
care facilities in 140 identified State Government hospitals during 11th Five Year Plan. The 
Scheme covers entire Golden Quadrilateral, North-South and East-West corridors. 
185. The Network has been so designed that no traum a victim has to be transported for 
more than 50 kilometer.  It will bring down the mor bidity and mortality on the road by 
observing the golden hour concept. The project comp rises of well equipped life support 
Ambulances at every 50 Kilometer of the completed stretches of the National Highways with 
well-equipped & staffed trauma centre at every 100- 200 Kilometer of the National 
Highways.  
186. During 12th Five year plan, Ministry of Health  and Family Welfare has to establish 
85 Trauma centres (5- Level-I, 25 Level-II, and 55 Level-III) in Government Hospitals on 
National Highways, at the total cost of 534.64 crore. They have also proposed to complete 27 

Trauma Care which was sanctioned during 11th Five Y ear Plan with the estimated cost of 
Rs.  306.81 crore. 
187. As regards ambulance under National Highways A ccidents Relief Service Scheme 
(NHARSS) the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways have supplied 134 Advanced Life 
Support Ambulances (ALSA) to the identified Trauma Care Centre being set up by M/o 
Health & Family Welfare during 2010 to 2013.  
188. Ministry of Road Transport & Highways is imple menting the scheme namely 
“Cashless Treatment” on pilot basis on following stretches:- 
i. Gurgaon - Jaipur stretch of National Highway (NH) N o.8. (Implemented by ICICI 
Lombard General Insurance Company) (Being implemented since July 2013)  
ii. Vadodara – Mumbai stretch of NH No. 8 (Implemented by IFFCO Tokio General 
Insurance Company Limited.) (Implemented during September 2014 to 31.03.2016) 
iii. Ranchi – Rargaon – Mahulia stretch of NH No. 33. (I mplemented by ICICI Lombard 
General Insurance Company) (Implemented during September 2014 to 09.03.2016) 
189. The project envisages transport of accident vi ctims from the accident scene to 
hospital and, where required, from one hospital to another for treatment at a public or private 
hospital for the first 48 hours or Rs. 30,000/-, wh ichever is earlier so that lives of accident 
victims by providing prompt and appropriate medical  care during 'Golden Hour" may be 
saved.  
190. The pilot project will provide guidance in wor king out a proper pan-India scheme. 
Based on the findings of the pilot project, the sch eme for cashless treatment to road accident 
victims would be finalized for country-wide roll ou t. The experience and data gathered 
during the pilot project will provide:  
• Likely average cost of treatment for (A) simple injuries (B) serious injuries.   
• Modalities of treatment and of meeting expenses if the accident victim is not fit for 
discharge after 48 hours. 
• Size of the fund required to be established by MoRT&H 
191. In case of Gurgaon-Jaipur stretch, on an avera ge an ALS ambulance takes 8 minutes 
to reach the road accident victims and 18 to 19 min utes are required to drop the victims to 
the nearest empanelled hospital. BLS ambulance take s 3 minutes to reach the victims and 13 
minutes are required to drop the accident victims t o the nearest hospital.  Till February 2016, 
9869 accidents were attended which includes 12,738 accident victims. The average 
expenditure on one road accident victims is around Rs. 13,500/-.  
192. In case of Ranchi-Mahulia Stretch of NH-33, it  was informed that average time taken 
by a patient to reach the hospital is still 43 minu tes because of inequitable distribution of 
hospitals.  Till February 2016, 784 accidents were attended which includes 1283 accident 
victims. The average expenditure on one road accident victims is around Rs. 11,500/-.  
193. In case of Vadodara – Mumbai stretch of NH No.  8, on an average an ambulance 
takes 7-8 minutes to reach to the road accident vic tims and 15 minutes are required to drop 
the patient to the nearest hospital. Till March 201 6, 1554 accidents were attended. The 
average expenditure on one road accident victims is around Rs. 10,000/-.

221.  The Committee is happy to note the proposed steps to be taken by the Ministry

Road Connectivity to Minor Ports 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATION   OF THE COMMITTEE 
222. The Committee feels that the connectivity to m inor ports is of utmost importance 
since the minor ports are now growing faster and lo ad and unload substantial volume of 
cargo/containers. The Ministry has chalked out the plan to develop 2 lane roads in  nearby 
areas of 50 minor ports. The Committee would like t o know the progress of the projects 
taken up by the Ministry through State PWDs. 
(Para 120 of ibid ) 

Reply of the Government  
223. This Ministry is primarily responsible for dev elopment and maintenance of National 
Highways across the country.  Hence, there is no se parate proposal in the Ministry for 
connectivity to minor ports through State PWDs.  Ho wever, the Ministry is considering to 
take up a new scheme which inter-alia envisages to provide connectivity in a length of about 
1,000 kms to minor ports handling Export-Import car go.  However, the scheme is yet to be 
launched formally.  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
224. The Committee notes the reply.
